chunks.title: Verdicts
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
Each question is one chat call to the model's own backend with `max_tokens: 1`, `temperature: 0`, `logprobs: true` and `top_logprobs: 20`. Booleans answer `yes` or `no`; choice options (in sorted name order) and score levels get the letters `A` to `Z`, which are single tokens in common vocabularies. The first token's probabilities over those labels become the answer.

The state goes in a system message that is identical for every question in the request, and all questions go to one endpoint at once. With prefix caching on the backend (vLLM `--enable-prefix-caching`, SGLang), the state is processed once and each further question costs about one cache hit and one output token. Ask every question about one state in the same request.

**Thinking and harmony models.** A model that opens with a `<think>` block or a harmony channel token spends its first token there, not on an answer. When less than 5% of the first-token probability lands on answer labels, the gateway retries that question once: with an empty `<think></think>` block already closed (`continue_final_message`, supported by vLLM and SGLang), or, for harmony models such as gpt-oss, through the backend's `/v1/completions` with the final channel already open. The form that works is remembered per model for the life of the process, so later requests skip the first attempt. Both attempts are billed, and the answers often still come back with low confidence, so prefer an instruction-tuned model and make one the verdicts defau

chunks.title: Verdicts
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
`POST /v1/verdicts`
  A chat model whose backend returns logprobs (vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp)
  About one cached prefill and one output token per question
  Playground › Verdicts

Send a **state** (a ticket, a document, a record, your application's current state) and a map of typed **questions**. Each question comes back as a typed verdict with a probability distribution and a confidence. The answer is read from the model's first-token probabilities over a fixed set of labels, so it cannot come back malformed.

Use it where you now ask a model a question and parse its reply: triage (is this urgent, which team owns it), gating (escalate, block or approve, with a probability to threshold on), rubric scoring, record matching and batch labeling. [Verdict examples](/docs/clients/verdict-examples) has requests to copy for several of these.

chunks.title: Verdicts
chunks.heading: Question types
chunks.text:
| `type` | `criteria` | `value` | `probabilities` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `boolean` | Optional `{"true": …, "false": …}` | `true` or `false` | `{"true": p, "false": p}` |
| `choice` | Required: option name to description (or `null`), 2 to 255 options | The chosen option name | Option name to probability |
| `score` | Required: level descriptions, lowest first, 2 to 10 levels | The level, from 1 | An array in level order |

A choice with more than 26 options is answered with two-letter codes (see How it works). A request holds 1 to 32 questions, and may mix types. Question ids are up to 256 bytes and option names up to 200. The rendered state may be up to 2 MiB.

chunks.title: Verdicts
chunks.heading: The response
chunks.text:
```json
{
  "model": "qwen3-8b",
  "verdicts": {
    "department": {"type": "choice", "value": "billing",
      "probabilities": {"account": 0.0007, "billing": 0.9962, "technical": 0.0031}, "confidence": 0.97},
    "frustration": {"type": "score", "value": 2,
      "probabilities": [0.11, 0.78, 0.09, 0.02], "confidence": 0.62, "expected_value": 2.02},
    "is_urgent": {"type": "boolean", "value": true,
      "probabilities": {"false": 0.06, "true": 0.94}, "confidence": 0.71}
  },
  "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 430, "completion_tokens": 3, "total_tokens": 433}
}
```

- `model` is the model that answered, with aliases and `auto` resolved.
- `value` is the most likely answer. `probabilities` sum to 1 over the answer labels.
- `expected_value` (score only) is the probability-weighted level, a smoother signal when neighbouring levels split the probability.
- `confidence`, from 0 to 1, says how decisively the model answered. It is near 0 for a 50/50 split, and also low when most of the model's probability went to tokens that are not answer labels.
- `usage` sums every call the request made, retries included.
- `answered` appears only on a question the model gave no answer to, when the request set `on_no_answer` to `low_confidence` (see below).

Gate automated actions on both: `probabilities` say how likely the answer is, `confidence` says whether the model engaged with the labels at all. Floats are written as plain decimals at full precision, never in scientific notation.

chunks.title: Verdicts
chunks.heading: When the model gives no answer
chunks.text:
Sometimes none of the model's likely first tokens is an answer label, for example on a question that makes no sense. By default the request then fails with 502 and names the question. Set `on_no_answer` to answer it anyway:

| `on_no_answer` | A question with no answer label |
| --- | --- |
| `error` (default) | The request returns 502 |
| `low_confidence` | The question comes back with every answer equally likely, `confidence` 0 and `"answered": false`; the other questions are unaffected |

```json
"is_urgent": {"type": "boolean", "value": true,
  "probabilities": {"false": 0.5, "true": 0.5}, "confidence": 0.0, "answered": false}
```

Use `low_confidence` when you score many questions in bulk and would rather count an unanswered question as wrong than retry the whole request. Backend failures (a timeout, an unreachable model) still return an error.

chunks.title: Video generation
chunks.heading: Billing and admission
chunks.text:
A create is charged the model's `cost_per_video` once the backend accepts the job and the gateway has recorded it, as request type `video` with no token counts.

- A create the backend rejects is not charged.
- A reply with no usable job id returns 502 `the upstream did not return a video job id`, not charged.
- If the job cannot be recorded, the gateway deletes it on the backend (best effort) and returns 503, not charged. You never get a job id that was not recorded.
- A create is never served from the [response cache](/docs/models/response-cache).

The create takes a slot in the model's pool only while the create call runs, so fairshare limits how fast jobs are created, not how many render at once. Budgets reserve and settle on the create like any request. Input [guardrails](/docs/routing/guardrails) scan the `prompt`; a reference image is not scanned.

Records live in the Postgres `video_jobs` table rather than Redis, because the Redis eviction policy could drop a key with a TTL mid-render. Every gateway replica prunes records older than `OBLETH_VIDEO_JOB_RETENTION_HOURS` (default `24`; Helm `obleth.videoJobRetentionHours`) once an hour. A follow-up for a pruned job returns 404.

Job ids are the backend's. The gateway accepts any id of 1 to 256 printable ASCII characters except one containing `/`, `\`, `?`, `#` or `%`, or `.` and `..`, and forwards it percent-encoded as one path segment.

A multipart create is sent once and never retried. A JSON create follows the model's

chunks.title: Video generation
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A backend that implements the OpenAI Videos API
  Register the model with `model_type: "video"`
  A flat `cost_per_video` per created job
  The key that created it, by default

A video is a job, not one request and one response. The create call returns a job id at once, the backend renders in the background, and the client polls the job until it can download the file.

```
POST   /v1/videos               create a job (prompt, optional reference image)
GET    /v1/videos/{id}          job status, as the backend reports it
GET    /v1/videos/{id}/content  the finished video
DELETE /v1/videos/{id}          delete the job
GET    /v1/videos               the caller's own jobs
```

chunks.title: Video generation
chunks.heading: Run a job
chunks.text:
```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model_name": "video-gen",
    "model_type": "video",
    "upstream_model": "my-video-model",
    "api_base": "https://video.example.internal/v1",
    "cost_per_video": 0.50,
    "enabled": true
  }'
```

`api_base` ends in `/v1`; the gateway appends `/videos`. You can also set `cost_per_video` in the model's form on the Models page.

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8088/v1/videos \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "video-gen", "prompt": "A paper boat on a rain-soaked street", "seconds": "4", "size": "1280x720"}'
```

To send a reference image, use `multipart/form-data` with OpenAI's `input_reference` field:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8088/v1/videos \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_KEY" \
  -F model=video-gen -F prompt="The boat sails out of frame" \
  -F input_reference=@first-frame.png
```

The response is the backend's own video object. The fields a job accepts and the statuses it goes through are the backend's; the gateway does not check them.

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8088/v1/videos/$VIDEO_ID -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_KEY"
curl -s http://localhost:8088/v1/videos/$VIDEO_ID/content -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_KEY" -o video.mp4
curl -s -X DELETE http://localhost:8088/v1/videos/$VIDEO_ID -H "Authorization: Bearer $OB

chunks.title: Video generation
chunks.heading: What follow-up calls do
chunks.text:
The gateway records every job it creates: its id, model, tenant, the key that created it and the endpoint that accepted it. Polls, downloads, deletes and listings are served from that record.

- **They go back to the same endpoint**, whatever its health now. If the model has since been disabled or removed the call returns 503; if the endpoint is gone from the model, 502.
- **The backend's answer passes through.** A download while the video is still rendering returns whatever not-ready response the backend gives.
- **Downloads stream.** The file comes through chunk by chunk with the backend's `Content-Type`, `Content-Length` and `Content-Disposition`.
- **Delete** drops the record once the backend confirms (or answers 404). Any other answer keeps it, so you can retry.
- **List** asks each backend holding one of your jobs and returns only your entries, newest first. With no jobs you get an empty list.
- **They are free.** Follow-ups check the key and tenant but take no slot, reserve no budget and write no usage row.

chunks.title: Video generation
chunks.heading: Who can see a job
chunks.text:
`OBLETH_VIDEO_JOB_SCOPE` (Helm `obleth.videoJobScope`) decides who may follow up on a job:

| Scope | Poll, download, delete | `GET /v1/videos` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` (default) | Only the key that created the job | Only the caller's own jobs |
| `tenant` | Any key of the same tenant | Every job of the caller's tenant |

A job id you don't own returns 404 `no such video job`, the same as an id that never existed, and the backend is never asked. Another tenant's job is always a 404. Any other value falls back to `key` with a warning at startup.

Each user is one key: a person with a secret key, or an SSO caller with a per-user [identity key](/docs/clients/identity-tokens). Under `key`, each user sees only their own videos. Choose `tenant` when a tenant's keys deliberately share renders. The scope applies at request time, so changing it affects existing jobs immediately.

Under `key`, a disabled key is refused before the lookup, and a rotated or recreated key is a new key, so neither reaches the old key's jobs. Those jobs finish or expire on the backend.

chunks.title: Audit log
chunks.heading: Find a change
chunks.text:
Open **Audit**. Each change reads as a sentence that names what changed and links to its page, newest first and grouped by day. A run of the same change by the same person within a minute folds into one line, such as "changed 3 models". Deleted things keep their names, taken from the log's own records.

![The Audit page: tiles for changes in 7 days, people, the most changed kind and deletions, above filters and a day-by-day list of changes written as sentences](/dashboard/audit.png)

- Search by a name, an id, or what changed.
- Filter by time (24 hours, 7 days, 30 days or all), by who (**Anyone** or one person), and by kind (**Anything** or one kind of thing). The filters are kept in the address, so a filtered view can be shared.
- Open a line's details to see which fields changed from what to what, with the raw JSON behind **Raw JSON**.
- **Load older** pages back through the whole log.
- **Export** downloads the current view as CSV.

A model's **Audit log** link opens the log filtered to that model.

chunks.title: Audit log
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Every change made through the Management API
  Audit in the dashboard, or GET /api/v1/audit
  In Postgres, append-only

chunks.title: Audit log
chunks.heading: Read it through the API
chunks.text:
```bash
curl "http://localhost:9180/api/v1/audit?entity_type=tenant&since=2026-09-01T00:00:00Z&limit=200" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

Rows come back newest first. Each has `id`, `ts`, `actor`, `action`, `entity_type`, `entity_id` and `detail`, a JSON object with the specifics of the change.

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `limit` | Rows to return. Default 100, at most 1,000 |
| `actor` | An exact actor, such as an email or `admin` |
| `entity_type`, `entity_id` | The kind of thing and its id |
| `action` | One action, or several separated by commas |
| `since`, `until` | RFC 3339 times; `since` is inclusive, `until` exclusive |
| `q` | Free text over actor, action, entity id and detail |
| `before_id` | Page back from this row id |

The rows are stored in the Postgres `audit_log` table. See [Postgres schema](/docs/reference/postgres-schema).

chunks.title: Audit log
chunks.heading: What is not recorded
chunks.text:
Secrets stay out of the log: a model's upstream key is not recorded when the model is created, and configuration backups record only entity counts (and, for a restore, the source's export time, gateway version and warnings), never the backup itself, which carries secrets and key hashes. See [Backup and restore](/docs/operate/backup-restore).

Data-plane traffic is not audited here. Requests are in [Request logs](/docs/dashboard/control-plane#request-logs).

| Entity type | Actions |
| --- | --- |
| `tenant` | `create_tenant`, `update_tenant`, `delete_tenant`, `update_quota`, `update_weight`, `update_tenant_group`, `set_tenant_status`, `set_tenant_budget`, `set_tenant_schedule`, `set_tenant_allowlist`, `set_tenant_guardrails`, `set_tenant_compression`, `set_tenant_synthetic`, `enable_tenant_tracing`, `disable_tenant_tracing` |
| `fairshare_group` | `create_fairshare_group`, `update_fairshare_group_weight` |
| `api_key` | `create_key`, `update_key`, `delete_key`, `move_key`, `enable_key`, `disable_key`, `enable_key_tracing`, `disable_key_tracing` |
| `model` | `create_model`, `update_model`, `delete_model`, `activate_model`, `set_model_status`, `set_model_capacity`, `set_model_capacity_mode`, `set_model_weight`, `set_model_cache`, `set_model_reliability`, `set_model_knowledge_collections`, `update_model_health_config`, `autotune_model`, `apply_autotune_capacity`, `clear_lost_replicas` |
| `model_endpoint` | `create_model_endpoint`, `update_model_endpoint`, `delete_model_endpoin

chunks.title: Audit log
chunks.heading: Who is recorded
chunks.text:
| Actor | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| An email address | The signed-in dashboard or portal user who made the change |
| `system` | The Slurm provisioner, for changes it makes itself |
| `admin` | A Management API call that named no actor. The dashboard shows it as "admin token" |

Callers name the actor with the `x-obleth-audit-actor` header. The dashboard sends the signed-in user's email on every write, including those made from live pages such as Fairshare. A script calling the Management API can set the header to attribute its changes, or leave it out to record `admin`.

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: API keys
chunks.text: Every key with its tenant, last use, requests, spend and budget. A new key's secret is shown once. Open a key to change it, replace it, move it to another tenant or delete it; select several to act on them together. See [Tenants and keys](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys#keys).

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Audit
chunks.text: Every configuration change, written as a sentence with who made it, filterable and exportable. See [Audit log](/docs/dashboard/audit-log).

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Batches
chunks.text: Every tenant's [batches](/docs/clients/batches), newest first. Tiles count the batches running now, the requests still to go, those waiting for capacity and those done. Show active, done, ran out of time, couldn't start, cancelled or all of them, or search by batch, model, tenant or key. Each row shows a progress bar, who submitted it, its model, and what it is doing in plain words: running with the time left at its pace, waiting because the model is busy with interactive work, done with how many requests failed, or out of time. **Cancel** stops one for its owner and is recorded in the audit log. The page refreshes every few seconds while anything runs. The API behind it is [`/api/v1/batches`](/docs/reference/management-api#batches).

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Deployments
chunks.text:
Models on your own compute: Kubernetes models obleth watches and sizes from their ready replicas, and models it launches as Slurm jobs. Each deployment shows its status, replicas, where it runs and pool load. A Slurm deployment's page scales, pauses and resumes it; **New deployment** launches one in three steps, from a recipe or a Hugging Face repo; recipes are a tab here.

![The Deployments page: a watched Kubernetes card and a Slurm card, tiles for deployments, ready replicas, what needs you and full pools, and three serving Kubernetes deployments](/dashboard/deployments.png)

See [Pool sizes](/docs/models/pool-sizes) and [Slurm provisioning](/docs/deployments/slurm-provisioning).

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Fairshare
chunks.text: Every model pool, fullest first, with who holds its slots, who is waiting, and each group's use against its share. Open a pool to see each tenant's running requests against its fair share, or a tenant to change its weight or cap. **Groups & weights** edits group weights with a preview. See [How fairshare works](/docs/sharing/how-fairshare-works#read-the-fairshare-page).

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Knowledge
chunks.text: Collections of documents models can retrieve from, with retrieval settings for the whole gateway. Each collection has a page with its documents, a test search, and the models attached to it. See [Knowledge base](/docs/boons/knowledge).

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: MCP servers
chunks.text: Each server is checked when the page opens, with its tools, the models that use it, and its recent calls. Open one to grant it to models, edit or remove it. See [MCP gateway](/docs/clients/mcp-gateway).

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Models
chunks.text:
A searchable table of every model (press `/`) with health, load, requests, time to first token, price, context and router tags. Select rows to check, switch, export or delete them together.

![The Models list: tiles for models, failing health checks, pools under pressure and the response cache, above a table of models with type, health, load, requests, first token, price, context and router tags](/dashboard/models.png)

Each model has a page at `/models/<name>` with its activity and every setting, with **Find a setting** (`⌘K`) and one save bar. **Add model** checks the endpoint and fills in what it serves; new models start switched off and turn on when their first health check passes, and start [staged](/docs/models/model-lifecycle) until you make them active. See [Model registry](/docs/models/model-registry) and [Health checks](/docs/models/model-health).

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
`http://localhost:3002` with Compose, or your Ingress host
  The break-glass admin, or SSO
  The Management API only

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The Overview answers "is anything wrong" first. One 1h / 24h / 7d control drives the page, and the header says in a line what needs attention.

![The Overview: a Needs attention card with a full pool and two tenants waiting below their share, tiles for requests, tokens, error rate, first token and spend, and the traffic chart](/dashboard/overview.png)

**Needs attention** lists failing models, full pools and tenants waiting below their fair share, each with a link to act on it. Five tiles compare requests, tokens, error rate, time to first token and spend with the previous window. Below are the traffic chart, every model's health and load, what is running now, top tenants and recent changes.

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Playground
chunks.text: Chat with or compare up to four models, see where `auto` would route a prompt, generate images, run verdicts and searches, and have the Assistant test a model. See [Playground](/docs/dashboard/playground).

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Reports
chunks.text:
Usage over a range, filtered by team, key and model, with totals against the previous period, a daily chart split by team or model, a sortable breakdown, and CSV **Export**. Reports read the permanent daily rollup, so they keep history after raw requests expire.

![Reports for this month: totals for requests, tokens, spend and success rate, spend per day split by team, and teams by spend beside models by tokens](/dashboard/reports.png)

**Model speed**, further down Reports, lists each chat model with a square per day (or per hour, over a day or two), shaded by how that period compared with the model's own usual speed, so a slowdown stands out whatever the model's speed. Its header counts the models that slowed by 20% or more against the previous period. Open a model for its median and slowest-tenth output speed, first token and prompt speed, a sentence on how its speed went, and a chart aligned with the squares. Models with too few requests to judge sit behind a **Show more** button. It reads raw requests, so it covers the request retention window; the API is `GET /api/v1/usage/speed`.

**Key access**, the second tab of Reports, shows where each key was used from in the last 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days: one row per key with its requests, networks, the names you gave your networks and countries, tagged when a key was seen from a country or network for the first time. A private address without a name says Private address. Open a key to see each network, with links to its reque

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Request logs
chunks.text:
Every request, live, with a chart you can drag across to zoom, filters typed into the search box (`status:error model:… team:…`), and saved views. "What's in this window" counts the busiest status codes, models, teams and keys, with their failures.

![Request logs: the search box and filters, a per-minute chart, the What's in this window panel with the most common failures, and the list of requests](/dashboard/logs.png)

A request opens in a side panel with a line saying what happened, a timeline of its steps, every number, and why the auto router picked its model. See [Observability](/docs/operate/observability).

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Self-service portal
chunks.text:
Accounts with the `user` role and a tenant land in the portal: the models their tenant may use, its keys (which they can create, turn off and delete), and its usage. A pending account, or one with no tenant, sees an awaiting-approval screen. See [Tenants and keys](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys#portal-users).

The dashboard reads and writes gateway state only through the Management API, so validation and the audit log live in one place. It keeps its own sign-in tables in Postgres (`DATABASE_URL`) and never touches the gateway's tables, Redis or ClickHouse.

| Variable | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL` | The Management API, such as `http://localhost:9180` |
| `OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN` | The admin token for every Management API call. Held on the server, never sent to the browser |
| `OBLETH_PROXY_BASE_URL` | The data plane, used by the Playground (default `http://localhost:8080`) |
| `DATABASE_URL` | Postgres for the sign-in tables |
| `DASHBOARD_SESSION_SECRET` | Session signing secret, at least 32 characters. Used as `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` when that is not set |

The sign-in variables are in [Sign-in and SSO](/docs/dashboard/dashboard-sso). With Compose they are all set in `deploy/docker/.env`, whose example admin token must be changed before the stack is reachable from a network.

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Settings
chunks.text:
One page for how the whole gateway behaves, with **Find a setting** (`⌘K`) and one save bar that saves only the sections you changed. It opens on **Needs you**. First come findings from the last day of requests: images sent to models that read only text, a caller repeating a request that fails, server-side failures, requests waiting for room, and Auto models whose answers run long. Each one shows its numbers, links to exactly those requests, and, where obleth can make the fix itself (such as turning on the vision boon for the models refusing images), has a button for it. Set a finding aside for a day or a week, or dismiss it. When a Verdicts default model is set (Settings › Routing), it rates each finding, and the list is ordered by those ratings; it never adds findings or changes their numbers. After these come settings that contradict each other, such as no alert channel or a boon that models ask for but is off.

![Settings: the section list, a Needs you card saying nobody is alerted, the Alerts section, and the Routing section with its readiness findings](/dashboard/settings.png)

| Section | What it sets |
| --- | --- |
| Alerts | Slack and email channels, the quiet period, and a test alert. See [Alerting](/docs/operate/alerting) |
| Routing | The classifier and weights for `auto`. See [Auto routing](/docs/routing/auto-model-routing) |
| Boons | One row per boon with its switch and settings. See [Boons](/docs/boons/overview) |
| Energy | Power readings and rates. See [Ene

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Signing in
chunks.text:
Sign in with the admin account seeded from `DASHBOARD_ADMIN_EMAIL` and `DASHBOARD_PASSWORD`, or through SSO; see [Sign-in and SSO](/docs/dashboard/dashboard-sso). Every dashboard page needs the `admin` role. Accounts with the `user` role see the [self-service portal](#self-service-portal) instead.

A footer on every page shows the last day's requests, tokens and cost. Many numbers link to the requests behind them in Request logs.

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Tenants
chunks.text:
Every tenant with its group and weight, keys, requests, spend against budget, limits and access hours. Each tenant has a page with its activity and every setting, from weight and limits to guardrails. See [Tenants and keys](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys).

![The Tenants list with each tenant's status, group and weight, keys, requests, spend and limits](/dashboard/tenants.png)

chunks.title: A tour of the dashboard
chunks.heading: Users
chunks.text: Dashboard and portal accounts. People waiting for approval come first: pick a role and a tenant, then **Approve**. See [Sign-in and SSO](/docs/dashboard/dashboard-sso#admin-approval-flow).

chunks.title: Sign-in and SSO
chunks.heading: Admin approval flow
chunks.text:
A first SSO sign-in creates an account with no access. Pending users see an awaiting-approval screen with **Sign out**.

On **Users**, accounts waiting for approval are listed first. Pick a role and a tenant, then **Approve**; **Not now** leaves them waiting. Below them, everyone else is listed with what they can reach and when they joined, and can be changed or deactivated.

| Role | Can reach |
| --- | --- |
| `admin` | The whole dashboard |
| `user` | The self-service portal for their tenant: its models, its keys and its usage. See [Tenants and keys](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys#portal-users) |

Two changes are always refused, so nobody locks the gateway out: removing admin from your own account, and demoting or deactivating the last active admin. The same rule covers the sign-in library's own admin endpoints under `/api/auth/admin/*`.

chunks.title: Sign-in and SSO
chunks.heading: Break-glass local admin
chunks.text:
One email-and-password admin is seeded at start-up and works even when the identity provider is down. Public sign-up is closed; every other account comes from a first SSO sign-in.

| Variable | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DASHBOARD_ADMIN_EMAIL` | `admin@example.com` | A real email address |
| `DASHBOARD_PASSWORD` | none | At least 8 characters. Required by Compose and Helm |

The account is created only when there is no active admin, so it is made on first boot and not recreated. A password shorter than 8 characters, or an existing non-admin account with the same email, is logged as an error and no account is made; the dashboard still starts and serves SSO. Change both values from any development defaults before the dashboard is reachable from a network.

chunks.title: Sign-in and SSO
chunks.heading: Kubernetes (Helm)
chunks.text:
```yaml
controlPlane:
  dashboardAdminEmail: "admin@your-org.example"
  dashboardPassword: ""        # at least 8 characters; pass with --set or a Secret
  dashboardSessionSecret: ""   # at least 32 characters; also used as BETTER_AUTH_SECRET
  betterAuthUrl: "https://dashboard.example.edu"
  trustedOrigins: ""
  oidcProviders: |
    [{"providerId":"globus","displayName":"Globus","discoveryUrl":"https://auth.globus.org/.well-known/openid-configuration","clientId":"ID","clientSecret":"SECRET","scopes":["openid","email","profile"]}]
```

In production, put these in a Secret you create and set `controlPlane.existingSecret`. The chart then renders no control-plane Secret, so yours must carry every key: `DASHBOARD_PASSWORD`, `DASHBOARD_SESSION_SECRET`, `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`, `DATABASE_URL`, `DASHBOARD_ADMIN_EMAIL`, `BETTER_AUTH_URL`, `TRUSTED_ORIGINS` and `OIDC_PROVIDERS`. See [Helm values](/docs/reference/helm-values).

chunks.title: Sign-in and SSO
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A local admin, email and password
  Any OIDC provider with a discovery document, such as Globus or CILogon
  Wait for approval on Users

This SSO signs people in to the dashboard only. It's separate from obleth-chat's sign-in and from the [identity tokens](/docs/clients/identity-tokens) the data plane accepts, so it needn't use the same provider as either.

chunks.title: Sign-in and SSO
chunks.heading: Provider fields
chunks.text:
| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `providerId` | Short name used in the redirect URI: letters, digits and hyphens |
| `displayName` | The label on the sign-in button |
| `discoveryUrl` | The provider's OIDC discovery document |
| `clientId`, `clientSecret` | From the provider's client registration |
| `scopes` | Defaults to `openid email profile`, which is enough |
| `claims` | Read `email`, `name` or `image` from a different claim. See below |
| `overrideUserInfo` | `true` re-applies the profile to existing users at every sign-in, not only the first |
| `pkce` | `true` sends a PKCE challenge, so an intercepted code cannot be redeemed alone. Off by default; turn it on where the provider supports it |
| `authentication` | How the client authenticates at the token endpoint: `"post"` (credentials in the body, the default) or `"basic"` |

The discovery URLs are `https://auth.globus.org/.well-known/openid-configuration` for Globus and `https://cilogon.org/.well-known/openid-configuration` for CILogon (register at cilogon.org/oauth2/register). An unknown `authentication` value or `claims` field is refused with an error.

chunks.title: Sign-in and SSO
chunks.heading: Reaching the dashboard from another host
chunks.text:
Sign-in checks the browser's `Origin` against `BETTER_AUTH_URL`, which defaults to `http://localhost:3000` (the Compose stack uses `http://localhost:3002`). Opening the dashboard by IP address or another hostname fails with an invalid-origin error, for the local admin as well as SSO, until you either set `BETTER_AUTH_URL` to the URL you browse to or list the other origins:

```bash
TRUSTED_ORIGINS=http://10.0.0.10:3002,http://obleth.example.internal:3002
```

A single `*` trusts every origin: acceptable on a trusted private network, unsafe anywhere reachable from the internet. `BETTER_AUTH_URL` still sets the host in redirect URIs, whatever `TRUSTED_ORIGINS` allows.

chunks.title: Sign-in and SSO
chunks.heading: Set up SSO
chunks.text:
Create a confidential client in the provider's developer console, requesting the `openid email profile` scopes, with this redirect URI:

```
https://<dashboard-host>/api/auth/oauth2/callback/<providerId>
```

`<providerId>` is a short name you choose, such as `globus`.

Set `BETTER_AUTH_URL` to the dashboard's browser-facing URL, such as `https://dashboard.example.edu`. The redirect URI you registered must match it exactly, scheme and port included.

Set `OIDC_PROVIDERS` to a JSON array with one object per provider:

```json
[{
  "providerId": "globus",
  "displayName": "Globus",
  "discoveryUrl": "https://auth.globus.org/.well-known/openid-configuration",
  "clientId": "YOUR_CLIENT_ID",
  "clientSecret": "YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET",
  "scopes": ["openid", "email", "profile"]
}]
```

The sign-in page shows a button per provider. Each person's first sign-in creates a pending account; approve it on **Users**. A provider sign-in is found again by the provider and its subject only, never joined to an existing account by email: a first sign-in whose email already belongs to a dashboard account, such as the break-glass admin, is refused.

Where the variables go depends on how you run the dashboard: `deploy/docker/.env` for Docker Compose, `control-plane/.env.local` when running it on the host with `npm run dev`, or the `controlPlane` values under Helm (see [below](#kubernetes-helm)). Moving from a test provider to a real one is only a change to these variables.

chunks.title: Sign-in and SSO
chunks.heading: Try it locally with Dex
chunks.text:
The Compose stack includes a [Dex](https://dexidp.io) test provider behind the `sso-dev` profile, with one user, `researcher@example.edu` / `password`. In `deploy/docker/.env`:

```bash
COMPOSE_PROFILES=sso-dev
OIDC_PROVIDERS=[{"providerId":"dex","displayName":"Dev SSO (Dex)","discoveryUrl":"http://host.docker.internal:5556/dex/.well-known/openid-configuration","clientId":"obleth-control-plane","clientSecret":"dev-dex-secret","scopes":["openid","email","profile"]}]
```

Run `docker compose up -d` in `deploy/docker` and open `http://localhost:3002`. The issuer uses `host.docker.internal` because it must resolve to the same address from your browser and from the control-plane container. If you change the dashboard's port, update Dex's `redirectURIs` in `deploy/docker/dex/config.docker.yaml` and `BETTER_AUTH_URL` to match.

When the control plane runs on the host (`npm run dev`, port 3000) and only Dex runs in Docker, use `http://localhost:5556/dex/.well-known/openid-configuration` as the discovery URL and set `BETTER_AUTH_URL=http://localhost:3000` in `control-plane/.env.local`. More test users go under `staticPasswords` in the Dex config, with bcrypt-hashed passwords; restart Dex after editing.

Some providers send an `email` that is not the identifier your institution keys accounts on. Globus, for a university identity, can send a display alias such as `Ada.Lovelace@example.edu` as `email` and the canonical `alovelace@example.edu` as `preferred_username`. Without a mapping, t

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: 3D
chunks.text:
3D runs a job on a `mesh` model through [`/v1/meshes`](/docs/clients/mesh-generation): choose, drop or paste an image of one object and press **Generate 3D**. The settings panel holds the quality, the number of faces, the texture size and a seed, which the backend may ignore. While the job runs you see its stage, progress and place in the queue; the finished model opens in a viewer you can turn and zoom, with **Download .glb**.

A job takes minutes, so the session keeps its id: switch modes or reload and the job picks up where it was. The model itself is fetched again from the backend while the backend still holds it, so download anything you want to keep.

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Chat and compare
chunks.text:
Pick one model, or up to four to compare. The model picker shows each model's context window, capabilities, price, router tags and live load, and also offers **Automatic routing** (`auto`) and the **Assistant**. With several models, the **Send to** row chooses which of them get the next message; each keeps its own conversation.

Each answer shows time to first token, tokens per second, tokens and cost, with a link to its trace in Request logs. In a comparison, the answers with the fastest first token, the fewest tokens and the lowest cost are marked.

A reasoning model's thinking shows in a **Thinking** block above its answer, which folds once the answer starts. It is never sent back to the model.

The settings panel holds the system prompt, temperature and max output tokens. A blank field uses the model's default. You can attach one image to a prompt.

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Get code
chunks.text: **Get code** turns the current request into cURL, Python or JavaScript against the gateway's data-plane URL (`OBLETH_PROXY_BASE_URL`), reading the key from `$OBLETH_API_KEY`. Router mode gives the `auto` request it simulated. The Assistant has no public API, so it has no code.

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: How Playground traffic is handled
chunks.text:
Chat, Image, Verdicts and Search requests, and the Assistant's calls, go through the normal data plane as the gateway's reserved internal tenant. Admission, budgets, boons and tracing apply as for any client, so a boon on a model fires here too. The internal tenant is synthetic: its traffic is recorded as request type `benchmark` and left out of usage and cost figures unless you include internal traffic. Its key stays on the dashboard server and never reaches the browser.

**Settings › Assistant**, or `GET` and `PUT /api/v1/settings/charo`:

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `true` | Shown as **Playground**. Off hides the Playground and the Assistant |
| `brain_model` | none | The Assistant's model. None makes it a plain model tester |
| `tools_enabled` | all on | Per-tool switches, keyed by tool name; a missing key is on. The dashboard shows **May run benchmarks** for `run_benchmark` |
| `bench_max_concurrency` | `40` | Most concurrent requests a benchmark may ramp to |
| `bench_max_duration_s` | `120` | Longest benchmark run, in seconds |
| `bench_max_requests` | `500` | Most requests one benchmark may send |

The benchmark limits are enforced on the dashboard server, so a prompt cannot talk the Assistant into a larger load test. The agent loop runs at most four tool rounds per turn.

`search_docs` reads an index of this site that is built into the dashboard image, so it works without outbound network access. A dashboard answers from the docume

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Image
chunks.text: Image drives `POST /v1/images/generations` on an `image` model directly. The settings panel holds the size (256 to 1024 pixels square), images per run, and the backend-only negative prompt, steps and seed, which the backend may ignore. Each result shows its latency and cost and can be reused, run again or downloaded. When a `mesh` model is registered, **3D** on an image sends it to 3D mode.

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The `admin` role
  Chat, Image, Speech, 3D, Router, Verdicts, Search
  Settings › Assistant › Playground
  Real requests, kept out of usage figures

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Router
chunks.text:
Router shows where `auto` would send a prompt, without sending it: the classify, filter, score and pick stages, and each candidate's score split into capacity, cost and tag.

![The Router tab: a coding prompt routed to qwen3-coder-30b, the four stages, each candidate's score broken down, and the weight sliders in the settings panel](/dashboard/router.png)

**Live classifier** (on by default) asks the configured classifier, as real requests do; off, the keyword heuristics run. The weight sliders change only the simulation, with live and draft scores side by side. **Apply to gateway…** lists the changes and asks before saving them to Settings › Routing, **Reset to live** discards the draft, and **Open in Chat** sends the prompt to the chosen model. See [Auto routing](/docs/routing/auto-model-routing).

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Search
chunks.text: Search sends a query to a [search tool](/docs/clients/search-api) through `/v1/search`, as a client would, with how many results, how recent, and an optional list of sites to keep to (a minus in front leaves one out). Results show as a client gets them, and **Copy JSON** copies the response.

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Start a session
chunks.text:
Open **Playground**. A new session opens on a launcher that describes each mode, or you can type straight into the box at the bottom to chat through `auto`. **Try in Playground** on a model's page opens a session on that model, in Search mode for a search tool.

![The Playground launcher: cards for Chat, Image, Router and Verdicts, a box to start chatting through automatic routing, and a prompt to have the Assistant test a new model](/dashboard/playground.png)

Every mode has the same layout: sessions on the left, the work in the middle, and a settings panel on the right that stays open until you hide it. Switch modes with the tabs at the top. A session remembers its mode, models and inputs.

Sessions are kept in this browser, for your account only. They are grouped by day and searchable; export one as a file with the download button, and bring it back with **Import**. Generated images, 3D models and Router and Verdicts results are not saved with the session.

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: The Assistant
chunks.text:
The Assistant is a helper that runs real work against the gateway and reports what happened, with the trace. Start it from **Test capabilities** or **Benchmark** on the launcher or in a chat's settings panel, or add **Assistant** from the model picker. It opens its own session, and each activity is a step-by-step card where you pick the model and options.

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `test_capabilities` | Sends a real request for each capability the model is set up with (a ping, tool use, JSON mode, vision) and reports which [boons](/docs/boons/overview) fired |
| `run_benchmark` | A concurrency ramp against the model, with latency and throughput per step, the capacity knee, and a 0 to 100 score. Asks for your approval before it sends anything |
| `test_mcp` | The MCP handshake against registered servers, with each server's tools. See [MCP gateway](/docs/clients/mcp-gateway) |
| `search_docs` | Answers from this documentation, citing the pages it used |

Asking in plain language works too: "test gemma4" starts the capability test on that model. For the vision probe, attach a test image; without one, a small built-in image shows that the vision boon fires, not that the description is right.

The Assistant needs a model to think with. In **Settings › Assistant**, pick **Its model**: a model with function calling. With **None**, it passes your prompt to the model you name and returns the reply with its timings, without tools.

chunks.title: Playground
chunks.heading: Verdicts
chunks.text: Verdicts is a builder for the [Verdicts API](/docs/clients/verdicts), read left to right: the state (text or JSON), the questions (up to 32, each boolean, choice or score, with an id and instructions), and the results. Each result shows its value, probabilities and confidence, with token use, latency and a link to the trace.

chunks.title: Recipes
chunks.heading: Cluster values
chunks.text:
A default can name a cluster value, so no recipe hard-codes a path. Each comes from **Cluster defaults** on the [Slurm connection](/docs/deployments/slurm-provisioning#connect-slurmrestd):

| Token | Cluster default |
| --- | --- |
| `{{cluster.cache}}` | **Weight cache** |
| `{{cluster.images}}` | **Images folder** |
| `{{cluster.image.<engine>}}` | **Image per engine**: a full path, or a file name in the images folder |
| `{{cluster.logs}}` | **Job logs** |
| `{{cluster.setup}}` | **Load before launch**: lines run where the token stands; empty when unset. Put it before `set -euo pipefail` |

A launch is refused while a value the script needs is unset, and says which one to set.

chunks.title: Recipes
chunks.heading: Header fields
chunks.text:
| Field | Required | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | yes | | Shown on the Recipes tab and in New deployment |
| `description` | no | | A short summary |
| `engine` | yes | | For example `vllm`, `sglang`, `llamacpp`, `ollama` |
| `kind` | no | `model` | `model` serves one model; `engine` serves any model and asks for it at launch |
| `model` | no | | The Hugging Face repo or Ollama tag served, for the picker and the fit check |
| `weights_gb` | no | | Size of the weights, for the fit check |
| `requires` | no | | What the image must provide, such as a minimum engine version |
| `model_type` | yes | | The model's type, such as `chat` |
| `api_model_name` | yes | | The API model name suggested at launch, and the name the server must serve |
| `context_window` | no | the `context` input | The context the server starts with, in tokens: a number, or an input such as `{{context}}`. The model obleth creates gets it, so the gateway's limits match the server |
| `capabilities` | no | | What the model can always do when served this way, from `function_calling`, `tool_choice`, `response_schema` and `vision` |
| `port` | no | `8000` | The base of each replica's port window, not a port the server listens on |
| `health_path` | no | `/` for `ollama`, otherwise `/health` | The path that must answer 2xx before a replica serves |
| `target_replicas` | no | `1` | Replicas to keep running |
| `min_replicas` | no | `1` | Serving replicas needed before the model counts as

chunks.title: Recipes
chunks.heading: Inputs
chunks.text:
Each input is a setting someone launching the recipe may change. It has a `name` (a letter or underscore, then letters, digits or underscores), and optionally a `label`, `help` text, a `default` and `required` (`true` or `false`; `yes`, `no`, `on` and `off` work too, and any other word is refused).

| `type` | What it takes |
| --- | --- |
| `text` | Any text; the default type |
| `choice` | One of `options`; the default must be one of them |
| `number` | A number within `min` and `max`, shown with `unit` |
| `path` | A path on the cluster |
| `flag` | On or off, with a `true` or `false` default. On, `{{name}}` becomes `adds`, which a flag must have; off, it becomes empty |

A launch creates the model with the capabilities the recipe gives it, from `function_calling`, `tool_choice`, `response_schema` and `vision`:

- The header's `capabilities` lists what the model can always do, such as `[vision]` for a model that reads images.
- A flag's `capabilities` are added when the flag is on, and its `drops` are removed, such as a **Text only** flag that turns the vision encoder off with `drops: [vision]`. A flag with an empty `adds` and only `capabilities` just marks the model.
- The rendered script counts too: `--enable-auto-tool-choice` or `--tool-call-parser`, or `llama-server` with `--jinja`, outside comments, mark the model for function calling and tool choice wherever the flag came from, the **More flags** input included.

So a recipe whose tool flag adds a tool parser launche

chunks.title: Recipes
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Deployments › Recipes (`/deployments?tab=recipes`)
  A YAML header plus the job script obleth submits
  Administrators: a recipe runs any command on the cluster as the Slurm user

chunks.title: Recipes
chunks.heading: Record where it ran
chunks.text:
A recipe can list the runs that served it under `tested`, newest first:

```yaml
tested:
  - hardware: "1× 80 GB GPU"
    engine: "vLLM <version>"
    date: 2026-10-01
    result: "What you saw: time to ready, speed, tool calls."
```

`hardware` is required. New deployment shows each run as a sentence, and the Library and Engines lists say where a recipe last served.

chunks.title: Recipes
chunks.heading: The older `variables`
chunks.text: `variables:` (`name`, `label`, `default`, `required`) still works: each is read as a `text` input. When a name is in both lists, the typed input wins.

chunks.title: Recipes
chunks.heading: The Recipes tab
chunks.text:
The tab has three lists. Each row shows the recipe's engine, the values it asks for and the deployments launched from it; a library row also says where it last served. A recipe that can't be read is still listed, with the reason.

- **Saved** recipes are your team's, stored by the gateway: a library recipe or engine with the values that worked. Save one at launch with **Also save these settings as a recipe**, or from a serving deployment's page with **Save as recipe**, which writes its values into the source recipe's header and keeps cluster defaults as `{{cluster.*}}` references. A script edited at launch or on the deployment's page is saved as edited. You can **Edit** and **Delete** them; deployments launched from a deleted recipe keep running.
- **Library** recipes are the `*.recipe` files with `kind: model` in `OBLETH_RECIPES_DIR` (default: `recipes/` in the dashboard's working directory), named by their file stem. They can't be changed from the dashboard. The repository ships a set in `control-plane/recipes/`, each with where it was tested.
- **Engines** are the files with `kind: engine`: one per engine (vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp and Ollama) in the shipped set. They serve a Hugging Face model that has no recipe yet, and are offered after you pick one under **From Hugging Face**, saved copies of an engine first. The model input takes a repo id or a folder on the cluster that holds the weights. A Hugging Face model's task sets the model type: an embedding or speech recogniti

chunks.title: Recipes
chunks.heading: What the loader refuses
chunks.text:
A recipe that breaks one of these rules is listed with the reason and can't be launched:

- **A key it doesn't know**, in the header, an input, `variables` or `tested`, with a hint for a likely slip such as `max_model_len` for `context_window`. Recipes saved in the gateway before this rule show as invalid until the key is fixed.
- **A `{{name}}` no input declares** (`{{api_model_name}}` is built in), a malformed token, a `{{cluster.*}}` name that isn't a cluster default, or a token in an `env` value, which is exported exactly as written.
- **A script that never uses `$OBLETH_SERVING_PORT`** outside comments, or that passes a fixed `--port <number>`.
- **An `#SBATCH` line obleth can't send**, with what to write instead: `--mem-per-gpu` and `--mem-per-cpu` (use `--mem` for the whole node), `--ntasks` (a replica runs one task; set `--cpus-per-task`), `--job-name` (obleth names each job), and anything else not in the list above.
- **An API model name** that breaks the rule for model names, and a `context_window` that is neither a number nor an input token.

An input the script never uses, and an engine obleth doesn't know, are warnings: the recipe still launches.

chunks.title: Recipes
chunks.heading: Write a recipe
chunks.text:
On **Deployments** › **Recipes**, choose **New recipe**: it starts from a minimal recipe in the shipped shape. Paste in the server command from a script you already run on the cluster, and keep in mind that a job from obleth doesn't inherit your shell's environment: load modules in the script or the cluster's setup lines (see [Job scripts](/docs/deployments/job-script)). To change a library recipe, choose **Copy to edit**.

Put the YAML header between `---` fences above the script: at least `name`, `engine`, `model_type` and `api_model_name`. Declare what someone launching it may change as `inputs`, and write `{{name}}` where each goes in the script. The editor checks the recipe as you save; see [What the loader refuses](#what-the-loader-refuses).

Save it, then choose **Launch** on its row. See [Launch on Slurm](/docs/deployments/slurm-provisioning#launch-a-model).

```bash
---
name: Qwen3 8B
description: "Qwen3 8B on one GPU with vLLM."
engine: vllm
kind: model
model: Qwen/Qwen3-8B
weights_gb: 17
model_type: chat
api_model_name: qwen3-8b
port: 8000
health_path: /health
target_replicas: 1
max_job_failures: 2
env:
  VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S: "3600"
inputs:
  - name: context
    label: Context length
    type: choice
    options: [16384, 32768]
    default: 32768
    unit: tokens
  - name: tools
    label: Tool calling
    type: flag
    default: true
    adds: --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser hermes
    capabilities: [function_calling, tool_choice]
  - name: ex

chunks.title: Job scripts
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
`0.0.0.0` and `$OBLETH_SERVING_PORT`
  The deployment's API model name
  `PATH`, the Hugging Face token and the recipe's `env`; load the rest in the script

chunks.title: Job scripts
chunks.heading: The environment
chunks.text: The job's environment is not your shell's. A job submitted through slurmrestd gets only a fixed `PATH` (the usual system folders plus `/opt/apptainer/bin` and `/opt/singularity/bin`), `HF_TOKEN` and `HUGGING_FACE_HUB_TOKEN` when a Hugging Face token is set, the recipe's `env`, and the variables Slurm sets itself. Your modules, `MODULEPATH`, conda and site variables are not carried over as `sbatch` does. Start the script with `#!/bin/bash -l` so the login profile sets up the module system, and load what the server needs in the script or in **Load before launch**. Such jobs get `SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE`, `SLURM_GPUS_ON_NODE`, `SLURM_JOB_GPUS`, `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` and `SLURM_MEM_PER_NODE`, but not `SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK`, so size thread counts from `SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE`.

chunks.title: Job scripts
chunks.heading: What obleth adds
chunks.text:
The provisioner submits the deployment's script after adding a short block below its shebang. A script without a shebang gets `#!/bin/bash -l` and `set -euo pipefail` above it. The block:

1. Picks the first port in the replica's window that nothing on the node answers on at `127.0.0.1`, and exports it as `OBLETH_SERVING_PORT`. Each replica's window is `OBLETH_PORT_SPAN` ports (8), the first free window at or above the deployment's port, and no two live replicas share a window, across every deployment.
2. Records the port in the job's comment with `scontrol update JobId=$SLURM_JOB_ID Comment=obleth-port=<port>`, so the provisioner checks exactly that port. If the update fails, the provisioner checks the whole window. A script must not set its own job comment.

chunks.title: Job scripts
chunks.heading: What the server must do
chunks.text:
The server in the job must:

- **Listen on `$OBLETH_SERVING_PORT`, on all interfaces** (`--host 0.0.0.0`), not a fixed port and not `127.0.0.1`. llama-server, SGLang and Ollama listen on `127.0.0.1` by default, so pass the host. The provisioner and the gateway reach the server from outside the node.
- **Run on the first node of the allocation** (the batch host) when the job spans several nodes. obleth checks and routes to that node; a job on several nodes runs one task per node, and the script starts the other workers with `srun`.
- **Answer the health path with 2xx** once it is ready (`/health` by default, `/` for Ollama).
- **Serve the model under its API model name.** Once the health path answers, the provisioner reads `GET /v1/models`. If the server lists models and none is the API model name, the port doesn't count, and the replica's card says which model answered there instead. A server that doesn't list models passes on its health path alone.

chunks.title: Job scripts
chunks.heading: Working directory and output
chunks.text:
The job's working directory is its **Job logs** folder, or `/tmp` on the node when none is set, so use absolute paths. Each job writes `<job name>-<job id>.out` there, where the job name is `obleth-` (`OBLETH_PROVISIONER_JOB_PREFIX`) and the model name, with any character other than letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-` turned into `-`. With a **Job logs** folder, errors go to a matching `.err`; without one, they go into the `.out` in `/tmp` on the node that ran the job, which many sites clean when the job ends. Each replica's card shows its log path. Slurm does not create the folder: if it is missing or the Slurm user can't write to it, the job fails before it writes anything.

A server that never becomes healthy is covered in [Troubleshooting](/docs/deployments/slurm-replicas#troubleshooting). Recipes that follow these rules are in [Recipes](/docs/deployments/deployment-recipes).

chunks.title: Deployments
chunks.heading: A Slurm deployment's page
chunks.text:
The page shows the pool's load, 24-hour requests and failures, and a card per replica: **Queued** with Slurm's pending reason in a sentence, **Can't start** when that reason won't clear by waiting, **Loading** while obleth waits for the health path to answer, **Serving**, **Being replaced** while its replacement starts, or **Stopping**. Each card shows where its job writes its output, the port its server answers on and, while it serves, when its time limit ends and when a replacement starts. **Restart** starts a replacement job first and stops this one once the replacement serves. See [Replicas and failures](/docs/deployments/slurm-replicas).

- **Scale.** The **−** and **+** buttons change how many replicas obleth keeps running. Going down asks first when it would stop a serving or loading job, and says which one.
- **Pause and resume.** **Pause** stops the deployment's jobs and launches none until you choose **Resume**. Serving replicas leave the endpoints first and get 60 seconds to finish requests in flight. Requests fail once the last replica stops.
- **Apply to running replicas…** (in the **⋯** More actions menu) replaces each running replica with one started from the saved settings, one at a time, each new job before the old one stops, so the model keeps serving. It is the one way to replace every running replica. (Against an older gateway, which restarts by cancelling first, the menu offers **Restart all replicas…** instead.)
- **Remove deployment** stops launching th

chunks.title: Deployments
chunks.heading: A watched Kubernetes model's page
chunks.text:
The page shows the ready replicas, the pool's load, an hour of load, 24-hour requests and failures, and recent changes. **How obleth sizes it** lists the Service, namespace, ready endpoints, per-replica concurrency and headroom, and the pool they make: ready × per replica × headroom. **Change** opens the model's **Capacity** settings; see [Pool sizes](/docs/models/pool-sizes).

obleth doesn't start, stop or scale these replicas: the cluster does.

chunks.title: Deployments
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Deployments, under Operations
  Models obleth launches on Slurm, and Kubernetes models it watches
  Deployments › Set up Slurm (`/deployments?slurm=1`)

chunks.title: Deployments
chunks.heading: States
chunks.text:
| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Serving | At least **Healthy when** replicas serve (1 by default), or, on Kubernetes, the Service has ready replicas. The line under it says what else is queued or loading |
| Starting | Some replicas are queued in Slurm, with Slurm's reason, or loading |
| Can't start | Slurm refused the job, or holds every queued job for a reason that won't clear by waiting. Needs you |
| Paused | Paused on its page (Slurm), or turned off on Models |
| Stopped | Launches are paused after failed launches or a refused job; the line under it says when obleth tries again. Needs you |
| Not running | Nothing is running yet; waiting for the provisioner |
| No replicas ready | The Service has no ready replicas. Needs you |
| Not seen lately | Discovery has no current answer for the model, so its pool keeps its last size |

When the provisioner's passes are failing, the list and each deployment's page say so, with the reason, because replica states stop changing until it recovers.

chunks.title: Deployments
chunks.heading: The Deployments page
chunks.text:
![The Deployments page: a Kubernetes card with discovery every 15 seconds and a Slurm card with a Set up Slurm link, tiles for deployments, replicas ready, needs you and pools full now, then a table of three Kubernetes models, each serving with three replicas](/dashboard/deployments.png)

Two kinds of model are listed here:

- **Slurm, launched by obleth.** obleth submits the model's jobs to a Slurm cluster, keeps it at a replica count and routes to each replica once it is healthy. See [Launch on Slurm](/docs/deployments/slurm-provisioning).
- **Kubernetes, watched.** The cluster starts and scales the replicas. obleth reads the model's Service and sizes its pool from the ready ones: any model on the `kubernetes` [capacity source](/docs/models/pool-sizes#sources).

A model that only connects to an endpoint you run elsewhere isn't a deployment; it stays on [Models](/docs/models/model-registry).

At the top, a card for each kind shows how it is doing. The Kubernetes card shows the discovery interval and the namespaces in use. The Slurm card shows when the provisioner last checked in and the cluster's idle, busy and down nodes, or a **Set up Slurm** link. Tiles count the deployments, the ready replicas, what **Needs you** and the pools that are full now.

The table shows each deployment's status, replicas, where it runs (namespace and Service, or partition and resources), its pool's load, its 24-hour requests (linked to the request log) and the requests one replica takes. Search

chunks.title: Deployments
chunks.heading: The Slurm connection
chunks.text: The Slurm connection is a sheet on Deployments: **Set up Slurm** on the Slurm card (**Slurm connection** once it's set up), or `/deployments?slurm=1`. It is no longer in Settings, and old `/settings?tab=slurm` links open it here. See [Connect slurmrestd](/docs/deployments/slurm-provisioning#connect-slurmrestd).

chunks.title: Launch on Slurm
chunks.heading: Before you start
chunks.text:
- **slurmrestd with JWT auth.** slurmctld needs `AuthAltTypes=auth/jwt` and a JWT key (`AuthAltParameters=jwt_key=...`), and slurmrestd must run with `rest_auth/jwt`. obleth supports API versions v0.0.40 to v0.0.45; current Slurm releases serve only their newest few.
- **A Slurm user for the jobs.** Every job runs as this user. It needs an account and QoS that may use the partitions you launch on, and write access to the **Job logs** folder and the weight cache.
- **Network paths.** The gateway and the provisioner both reach slurmrestd, and both reach the model servers on the compute nodes. See [Network](#network).

chunks.title: Launch on Slurm
chunks.heading: Connect slurmrestd
chunks.text:
On **Deployments**, choose **Set up Slurm** on the Slurm card (**Slurm connection** once it's set up, or open `/deployments?slurm=1`).

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Slurm** | On, deployments are launched and kept running. Off, nothing new is launched or replaced; running jobs keep their nodes and are no longer watched |
| **slurmrestd URL** and **API version** | For example `http://slurm.example.internal:6820`. Leave the version on `auto` (the default): obleth reads the versions the server lists at `/openapi/v3` and uses the newest one it supports. Pin a version only if you need a particular one. A pin slurmrestd serves is kept; one it doesn't serve, for example after a Slurm upgrade, doesn't stop the provisioner: it uses the newest version the server serves and reports a warning on the Slurm connection ("slurmrestd doesn't serve the configured API version …, so obleth uses …") |
| **Slurm user** and **Slurm JWT** | The user jobs run as and a token for it. See [Get a token](#get-a-token) |
| **Node addresses** | Only if obleth can't reach node names: map each node to an IP, and replicas are reached by IP |

The **Cluster defaults** tab holds the values [recipes](/docs/deployments/deployment-recipes#cluster-values) refer to, so none of them hard-codes a path:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Weight cache** | Where models are downloaded (`HF_HOME`): shared, fast storage every node can reach |
| **Images folder** and **Image per engine** | The folder of `.sif` ima

chunks.title: Launch on Slurm
chunks.heading: Get a token
chunks.text:
A plain `scontrol token` lasts 30 minutes. After that slurmrestd refuses every call, and obleth stops managing the deployments: nothing is launched, replaced or marked ended until a new token is saved. Mint one that lasts, as the Slurm user:

```bash
scontrol token lifespan=2592000
```

That is 30 days. To mint a token for another user, such as a service account, run `scontrol token username=alice lifespan=2592000` as root or the SlurmUser. A site can cap the lifespan with `max_token_lifespan` in `AuthAltParameters`. Paste the output as it is: the `SLURM_JWT=` in front is removed.

The sheet and the Slurm card show the token's user and when it expires, and warn when the user isn't the **Slurm user** you entered. obleth warns again as expiry nears:

- Saving a token that expires within 7 days returns a warning with the command above.
- Within 3 days of expiry, and once it has expired, **Settings › Needs you** has a finding, and each provisioner pass reports a warning on the Slurm connection.

**To rotate**, mint a new token and paste it into **Slurm JWT**, then save. The provisioner uses it on its next pass; nothing restarts. A script can rotate it too: `PUT /api/v1/settings/slurm` with only `slurm_jwt` changes the token and keeps every other field.

```bash
TOKEN=$(scontrol token lifespan=2592000)
curl -X PUT http://obleth.example.com:9180/api/v1/settings/slurm \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \

chunks.title: Launch on Slurm
chunks.heading: Launch a model
chunks.text:
On **Deployments**, choose **New deployment**, then a **Saved** or **Library** [recipe](/docs/deployments/deployment-recipes). Or choose **From Hugging Face** and enter a repo id: the dashboard reads the repo and lists the engines that can run it, vLLM and SGLang for safetensors, llama.cpp and Ollama for GGUF. A gated repo needs the Hugging Face token from **Cluster defaults**. When the repo can't be read, **Or launch with an engine and type the model** still offers every engine recipe.

One form holds every setting the launch sends: the partition (each shows whether a replica fits and how many fitting nodes are idle; leave it empty for the cluster's default partition), account, QoS, walltime, nodes, GPUs, CPUs and memory per node (`0` is the whole node), **Only on nodes with**, **Avoid nodes**, the recipe's inputs, **Job logs**, replicas and the health check. The **API model name** is the name clients send and the name the server must serve, so one recipe can be launched under several names.

Each value says where it came from: the recipe, a cluster default, **Learned** from past launches, or changed by you. **Edit as** › **YAML** edits the same settings as text, checked line by line. Only accounts the partition takes are offered, and account, QoS and walltime are checked before submit. A value a cluster default should fill but doesn't names the setting, and **Slurm connection** opens the sheet without leaving the form.

Check the job script with your values filled in, and w

chunks.title: Launch on Slurm
chunks.heading: Network
chunks.text:
| From | To | Port | For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The gateway (`obleth`) | slurmrestd | its URL's port | Test the connection, and the partitions, nodes and accounts New deployment offers |
| The provisioner | The Management API on the gateway | `9180` | Settings, deployments and replicas |
| The provisioner | slurmrestd | its URL's port | Submit, cancel and look up jobs |
| The provisioner | Each compute node | the replicas' port windows | Health checks, the model list and the warm-up request |
| The gateway (`obleth`) | Each compute node | the replicas' port windows | Requests and the gateway's own health checks |

Each replica gets a window of `OBLETH_PORT_SPAN` ports (8): the first free window at or above its deployment's port, in steps of 8. Windows never overlap across deployments, so two deployments on port `8000` get windows at 8000 and 8008. With every deployment on port `8000` and 6 replicas in total, the windows cover 8000 to 8047. Allow a window more per deployment for the replacement started during a handoff, restart or roll. See [Job scripts](/docs/deployments/job-script).

The provisioner resolves each node through **Node addresses** first, then the address Slurm reports for the node (`NodeAddr`), then DNS, and registers the replica's endpoint by that IP. The gateway sends requests to that same IP, so it must route there too: a provisioner that reaches the nodes on a network the gateway can't route to sees replicas serve while every request fails.

The jobs

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
slurmrestd with JWT auth, a long-lived Slurm token, the `obleth-provisioner` running, and network paths to the compute nodes
  Deployments › Set up Slurm
  Deployments › New deployment

chunks.title: Launch on Slurm
chunks.heading: Start the provisioner
chunks.text:
The provisioner is a separate process, `obleth-provisioner`. It reads the Slurm connection and each deployment from the Management API, submits and cancels jobs through slurmrestd, checks each replica on its node, and adds healthy ones to the model's endpoints. Saving a connection alone launches nothing.

- **Docker Compose:** add `slurm` to `COMPOSE_PROFILES` in `deploy/docker/.env`, then `docker compose up -d --build` from `deploy/docker/`.
- **Helm:** set `provisioner.enabled: true`. The chart runs exactly one replica with the `Recreate` strategy, so two provisioners never submit jobs for the same model; don't scale it. `provisioner.extraEnv` passes any other [provisioner setting](/docs/deployments/slurm-replicas#provisioner-settings).
- **systemd:** a unit ships at `deploy/systemd/obleth-provisioner.service`; put its variables in `/etc/obleth/provisioner.env`.

It needs only `OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL` and `OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN`; the Slurm connection comes from the dashboard. On a stop signal it finishes the pass in progress before it exits, so a submitted job is always recorded, provided the stop grace period is long enough for a pass: Helm gives it 60 seconds and Compose 120.

chunks.title: Launch on Slurm
chunks.heading: Test the connection
chunks.text:
**Test the connection** checks each step and lists every problem as a sentence with what to do:

- **slurmrestd:** whether it answered the ping, how fast, whether slurmctld is up, and the Slurm release. With slurmctld down, jobs can't be submitted.
- **API version:** the versions slurmrestd serves, and the one obleth uses. A pinned version the server doesn't serve is named, with the ones it does; the test reports it as a problem, while the provisioner falls back to the newest served version.
- **Sign-in:** an authenticated read of the partition list. slurmrestd can answer a ping without checking the token, so this is the check that the token works.
- **JWT:** when it expires, and whether its user matches the **Slurm user**.

The sheet also shows when the provisioner last checked in, whether its passes are failing and why, and the warnings from its last pass. Changes reach the provisioner on its next pass, without a restart. Turning Slurm off asks first; with replicas running, it also raises an alert naming who did it.

chunks.title: Replicas and failures
chunks.heading: Failures
chunks.text:
- **Failed launches.** A launch fails when its job ends before its server ever served, when it hits **Give up loading after**, or when it is stuck in the queue (below). A job that served and then reached its walltime, was preempted or lost its node is not a failure; nor is a job preempted, lost to a failed node or cancelled outside obleth before it served, or a replica you stopped. The count is kept with the deployment, and a launch that serves resets it.
- **Pauses.** When failed launches reach **Stop after failed launches** (`0` never pauses), the deployment stops submitting for 5 minutes, then tries again. Each further pause waits longer: 15, 30, 60 minutes, then every hour. Replicas already serving keep serving. The deployment shows **Stopped** with when it tries again, the page says why in a sentence with what Slurm said about the last job, and **Settings › Needs you** lists it. **Try again** lifts the pause and resets the count at once.
- **Refused jobs.** When Slurm refuses a submit, for example a wrong account, partition, QoS or a request no node can meet, the page leads with Slurm's sentence, such as "Slurm rejected the job: Invalid account or account/partition combination specified.", followed by the site's `job_submit` message if there is one, and says which setting to change. A refused submit pauses the deployment on the same ladder whatever its failure limit, so a job Slurm will never take isn't resubmitted every pass. Fix the setting, then **Try again**.
- **Stu

chunks.title: Replicas and failures
chunks.heading: How replicas run
chunks.text:
Each replica is one Slurm job running a script that follows [Job scripts](/docs/deployments/job-script). Every pass, the provisioner compares each deployment with its jobs:

1. **Submit.** Below the replica count, it submits jobs. Memory `0` is sent as the smallest node's memory in the partition less what Slurm keeps back for the node (`MemSpecLimit`), so a site's own default can't replace it; when the nodes can't be read, `0` is sent as is. A job on several nodes runs one task per node, and the server must run on the first node of the allocation (the batch host), which is where it is checked.
2. **Promote.** For a running job, it checks the port the job recorded, or each port in the window, from where the provisioner runs. When one passes, it sends one warm-up request and adds the replica as an endpoint at `http://<node IP>:<port>/v1`.
3. **Give up loading.** A running job whose server isn't healthy **Give up loading after** minutes (60 by default, counted from when the job started, not from submit) is cancelled and counts as a failed launch. `0` waits until the walltime.
4. **Replace.** A job that ends is marked ended, its endpoint is removed, and a new job is submitted.
5. **Scale down.** Above the replica count, it stops queued jobs first (newest first, so the oldest keeps its place in the queue), then loading ones (newest first), then serving ones (oldest first). A serving replica leaves the endpoints at once, shows **Stopping** for 60 seconds so requests in flight can f

chunks.title: Replicas and failures
chunks.heading: Needs you
chunks.text: **Settings › Needs you** lists the Slurm problems that wait for a person: a token that expires within 3 days or has expired, and each deployment paused by failed launches or a refused job, with the reason, the failed launches in a row and the next try.

chunks.title: Replicas and failures
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Every 15 seconds (`OBLETH_PROVISIONER_INTERVAL_SECS`)
  After **Give up loading after** (60 minutes), counted as a failed launch
  At **Stop after failed launches**, or when Slurm refuses a job: 5, 15, 30, 60 minutes, then hourly

chunks.title: Replicas and failures
chunks.heading: Preemption and node failure
chunks.text: Jobs are submitted with requeue off, so a job that is preempted or loses its node ends (`PREEMPTED`, `NODE_FAIL`): its endpoint is removed and a new job is submitted. `scontrol requeue` refuses such a job, so one is requeued only where a site's `job_submit` plugin forces requeue on. If a job does come back under the same id (it is requeued that way, it is suspended, or it starts again on another node), the replica leaves the endpoints at once and returns to **Queued** or **Loading** with a sentence saying why. It is added again when it serves at its new place.

chunks.title: Replicas and failures
chunks.heading: Provisioner settings
chunks.text:
| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_ADMIN_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:9180` | Management API |
| `OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN` | required | Management API token |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_INTERVAL_SECS` | `15` | Seconds between passes |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_SECS` | `5` | Timeout per port check |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_WARMUP_TIMEOUT_SECS` | `600` | Budget for the warm-up request; `0` turns it off |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_LOST_RETENTION_SECS` | `900` | How long an ended job stays on the deployment's page after it ends |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_RESTART_AFTER_FAILURES` | `20` | Net failing checks before a serving replica is replaced; `0` turns self-healing off |
| `OBLETH_PORT_SPAN` | `8` | Width of each replica's port window |
| `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_JOB_PREFIX` | `obleth-` | Slurm job-name prefix |

**Give up loading after** (`startup_timeout_mins`), **Start a replacement** (`handoff_mins`) and **Stop after failed launches** (`max_job_failures`) are set per deployment, on its page under **Service**.

Helm maps `provisioner.intervalSecs`, `provisioner.restartAfterFailures`, `provisioner.logLevel` and `provisioner.resources`, and passes anything else through `provisioner.extraEnv`:

```yaml
provisioner:
  enabled: true
  extraEnv:
    - { name: OBLETH_PROVISIONER_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_SECS, value: "10" }
    - { name: OBLETH_PROVISIONER_WARMUP_TIMEOUT_SECS, value: "900" }
```

See [Environment variables](/docs/reference/environment-variables).

chunks.title: Replicas and failures
chunks.heading: Restarts and new settings
chunks.text:
**Restart** on a replica's card starts a replacement job first. The replica keeps serving until the replacement does, then stops as above, so restarting the only replica doesn't take the model down. A replica that isn't serving yet is cancelled at once and replaced. When the replacement hasn't served after **Give up loading after**, the old replica stops anyway.

Saved changes reach new jobs only. **Apply to running replicas…** (in the **⋯** More actions menu) replaces every running replica this way, one at a time, oldest first, so the model keeps serving throughout. It is the one way to replace all of them; against an older gateway, which restarts by cancelling first, the menu offers **Restart all replicas…** instead.
