chunks.title: Replicas and failures
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.text:
**A job runs but the replica never serves.** First read the replica's card: it says when another model answers on the port, how long the server has been loading, and where the job's output is. The output usually says why: a missing module, a wrong image path, or the server listening on `127.0.0.1` or a fixed port. The provisioner's check runs from wherever the provisioner runs, not from the compute node, so a `curl` that works on the node proves nothing. The provisioner's image has `getent` and `bash` but no `curl`; check from inside it with bash's `/dev/tcp`:

```bash
kubectl exec deploy/<release>-provisioner -- bash -c '
  getent hosts gpu-node-01
  exec 3<>/dev/tcp/gpu-node-01/8000 &&
  printf "GET /health HTTP/1.0\r\nHost: gpu-node-01\r\n\r\n" >&3 && head -1 <&3'
```

With Compose, run the same `bash -c '…'` through `docker compose exec obleth-provisioner`. A first line such as `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` means the provisioner reaches the server; "Connection refused" means nothing listens there on an address the provisioner can reach; a hang means a firewall or route.

**It serves for the provisioner, but requests fail.** The gateway sends requests and runs its own checks from its own pods, to the IP the provisioner resolved, so both need to reach the node. Check from the gateway, whose image has `curl`:

```bash
kubectl exec deploy/<release>-obleth -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://10.0.0.21:8000/health
```

When the gateway can't reach the node, its checks fail a

chunks.title: Replicas and failures
chunks.heading: Walltime
chunks.text:
Slurm ends each job at its walltime. **Start a replacement** (15 minutes by default) starts a new job that long before a serving job's time limit, and stops the old one once the new one serves, so the model keeps serving across the limit. It is skipped for jobs whose time limit is at most twice that long, which would otherwise be replaced as soon as they serve, and for jobs with no time limit. `0` turns it off.

The replacement has to queue and load in that time. If it takes longer, the old job ends first and the model has fewer replicas, or none, until it serves. Set **Start a replacement** above your usual queue wait plus load time, use the longest walltime the partition allows, and keep two replicas so a late replacement doesn't take the model down. While launches are paused, no replacement starts.

chunks.title: Replicas and failures
chunks.heading: When a server stops answering
chunks.text:
A serving replica whose server stops answering is replaced. The provisioner counts its failed checks (a pass counts down one), and acts after `OBLETH_PROVISIONER_RESTART_AFTER_FAILURES` (20 passes, about five minutes). It also acts when the gateway's own check of the endpoint, a real request, has failed twice in a row within the last 30 minutes. A recent passing check from the gateway overrules the provisioner's failed ones.

When another replica serves, a dead one is cancelled, at most one per model per pass. The last serving replica, and any that fail the gateway's check, are replaced new job first. When every serving replica of every model (two or more) fails the provisioner's check in the same pass, the fault is almost certainly on the provisioner's path to the nodes, so nothing is restarted and the Slurm connection shows a warning.

chunks.title: Replicas and failures
chunks.heading: When slurmrestd or the token fails
chunks.text:
Each pass starts with an authenticated read of the partition list. When slurmrestd can't be reached, rejects the token, or fails a job lookup, the pass changes nothing: no job is submitted, cancelled or marked ended, and replicas already serving keep their endpoints. The Slurm connection says the provisioner's passes are failing and why, for example "slurmrestd rejected the Slurm token while reading partitions (HTTP 401)", and names when an expired token expired. After 10 minutes the `slurm_reconcile_held` alert fires; `slurm_reconcile_recovered` follows. Anything that ends meanwhile is replaced once passes work again.

- **A submit with no answer.** When a submit times out or slurmrestd fails mid-answer, Slurm may have the job. That deployment's submits wait up to 3 minutes while the provisioner looks for the job by name in Slurm's accounting database, and a job it finds is tracked as the replica. Without an accounting database, a warning names the job so you can check `squeue` for a second one.
- **Every job missing at once.** When slurmrestd reports none of the jobs obleth tracks (two or more), usually a wrong URL or cluster, the provisioner asks the accounting database. Jobs it confirms ended are replaced; the rest are left as they are, with a warning on the Slurm connection. If those jobs really ended, stop each replica on its deployment page and new ones start.
- **Failed actions.** A cancel or endpoint change that fails is retried on the next pass and reported as a war

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Other processes
chunks.text:
- **Dashboard** (`control-plane`): reads and writes gateway state through the management API only. Its own sign-in tables live in the same Postgres database.
- **Slurm provisioner** (`obleth-provisioner`, optional): a single reconciler that launches and watches models on Slurm through the management API. See [Slurm provisioning](/docs/deployments/slurm-provisioning).
- **Compression sidecar** (optional): a CPU-only scorer the compression boon calls. The gateway falls back to heuristics when it is absent.
- **Benchmark backend** (optional): a simulated model server for demos and load tests.

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The gateway is one Rust binary, `obleth`. It opens three listeners and connects to Postgres, Redis and ClickHouse at start. The dashboard is a separate Next.js app that talks only to the gateway's management API.

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Reads: two caches, then 401
chunks.text:
Models and MCP servers resolve the same way. A Redis error during key lookup returns `503 authentication backend unavailable`, never 401, so an outage doesn't look like a revoked key. Recently resolved keys keep working from the in-process cache while Redis is down.

The gateway fills Redis from Postgres at start, re-pushes it every `OBLETH_REDIS_REWARM_SECS` (default 300) and after every Redis reconnect, and prunes entries that no longer exist in Postgres. `POST /api/v1/resync` (Settings › Data and backups › Reconcile cache) does the same on demand.

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Replicas
chunks.text:
Gateway replicas are stateless apart from their in-process caches and admission queues, so you can run several behind a load balancer. Each replica runs its own fairshare scheduler; with more than one live, they share pool slots and caps through Redis so the configured limits hold for the fleet. See [Fairshare engine](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine#multiple-gateway-replicas).

The steps one request goes through are in [Request lifecycle](/docs/how-it-works/request-lifecycle).

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: The three listeners
chunks.text:
| Port | Serves | Authenticated with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8080 | The data plane: OpenAI routes, the Responses and Anthropic Messages APIs (translated to chat), Videos, Verdicts, the MCP gateway, and model discovery (`/v1/models`, `/model/info`) | Tenant keys (`sk_…`, as `Authorization: Bearer` or `x-api-key`), or identity-provider JWTs when `OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS` is set |
| 9180 | The management API under `/api/v1`: tenants, keys, models, settings, usage, the live fairshare state | The admin token |
| 9091 | Prometheus `/metrics`, with low-cardinality labels only | None |

Per-tenant and per-key breakdowns come from ClickHouse, not Prometheus labels. Routes are listed in [Data-plane routes](/docs/reference/data-plane-routes) and [Management API](/docs/reference/management-api).

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Where state lives
chunks.text:
| Store | Holds | On the request path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres | The source of truth for configuration and audit | Never |
| Redis | A cache of keys, models and MCP servers; token buckets and term budgets; response cache; shared fairshare slots | Yes |
| ClickHouse | One row per request, and trace spans | Written in the background |

Everything in Redis can be rebuilt from Postgres except live bucket and reservation state. See [Datastores](/docs/how-it-works/datastores).

chunks.title: Architecture
chunks.heading: Writes: one path
chunks.text: Every configuration change takes this path; nothing writes to Redis directly. The invalidation message makes every gateway replica drop its in-process copy, so a new weight or a disabled key applies on the next request without a restart. If removing a key, tenant, model or MCP server from Redis fails, the write returns 502 rather than leaving the old entry serving.

chunks.title: Datastores
chunks.heading: ClickHouse
chunks.text:
ClickHouse holds the usage ledger: one row per request with tenant, key, model, admission class, estimated and real tokens, queue wait, time to first token, total time, status, cache status, cost, energy and CO₂, request type and session. Rows are inserted in batches from a background task and never block a request. Two more tables sit beside it: `usage_daily`, a rollup per day, tenant, key and model that is kept forever while raw rows are pruned after the retention window (default 180 days), and `spans`, per-step traces kept 14 days. The gateway creates and migrates all three at start. Columns and queries are in [ClickHouse usage](/docs/reference/clickhouse-usage).

The gateway starts without ClickHouse. While it is unreachable, rows go to a local spill file (`OBLETH_WAL_PATH`) and are replayed, without duplicates, when it returns. On Kubernetes the chart gives that file a writable volume.

chunks.title: Datastores
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
| Store | Workload | Holds | If you lose it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres | Relational, durable | Configuration and audit, the source of truth | All configuration: back it up |
| Redis | In-memory, atomic | A cache of configuration, budgets, shared fairshare slots | Only live bucket and reservation state; the rest is rebuilt from Postgres |
| ClickHouse | Append-only, analytical | One row per request, spans | Usage history: back it up |

How to run each one is in [Install on Kubernetes](/docs/start/kubernetes#choose-where-the-datastores-live); backups are in [Backup and restore](/docs/operate/backup-restore).

chunks.title: Datastores
chunks.heading: Postgres
chunks.text:
Postgres holds everything that must be durable and consistent: tenants, API keys (hashes only, never the secret), fairshare groups, models and their endpoints, MCP servers, settings, knowledge collections and their chunks, Slurm deployments and recipes, video job records, health-check history and the audit log. The dashboard keeps its sign-in tables in the same database.

It is never read on the request path. The management API writes to it first and then updates Redis. It is needed at start: the gateway applies the migrations it has not recorded (`schema/postgres/`, embedded in the binary) before it listens. Tables are listed in [Postgres schema](/docs/reference/postgres-schema).

chunks.title: Datastores
chunks.heading: Redis

chunks.title: Datastores
chunks.heading: Why three stores
chunks.text:
Each workload breaks the others. Per-request rows at high volume would bloat Postgres tables and slow the configuration API. ClickHouse has no transactions or row updates, which configuration needs. Redis is fast and atomic but not a durable source of truth. Keeping them apart also bounds failures: a Redis outage costs live counters, a ClickHouse outage delays usage rows, and neither loses configuration.

- **Redis:** key lookups that miss the in-process cache return 503. Budget checks follow `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN`: admitted without enforcement when `true` (the default), 503 when `false`. With several replicas, fairshare falls back to dividing the limits between them.
- **ClickHouse:** requests are unaffected; usage spills to disk. Usage views miss those rows until they replay.
- **Postgres:** requests keep being served from the caches, but configuration writes fail, and a gateway can't start.

See [Reliability](/docs/operate/reliability).

chunks.title: Fairshare engine
chunks.heading: Choosing the next request
chunks.text:
Each tenant and key has a *served* counter in estimated tokens. `share_score` is served divided by weight: lower means further behind. When a slot frees, the scheduler picks at three levels.

**Group, then tenant** (`OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_ALGORITHM=hierarchical`, the default). The pool is split between the groups that have work by group weight, and each group's part between its active tenants by tenant weight, with largest-remainder rounding and at least one slot each when there is room. An 8-slot pool with groups of weight 500 and 50 splits 7 and 1. Among waiting tenants under their share, the scheduler takes the group with the lowest group score, then its tenant with the lowest `share_score`.

**Tenant only** (`weighted`). Every tenant competes directly on `share_score`: start-time fair queuing on token cost.

**Key.** Inside the chosen tenant, the key with the lowest served-per-key-weight goes next (key weight default 100), so one busy key can't starve its teammates.

A tenant's or key's `max_in_flight` caps its running requests in each model's pool, not across models.

**Shares are ceilings, not reservations.** If no waiting tenant is under its share but a slot is free, it is lent to whoever is waiting. The lending group gets its share back as those requests finish; nothing is preempted. The live state reports each group's `slot_cap` and `borrowed`.

**No saved-up credit.** A tenant is measured only against the tenants it competes with: all of the pool's under `weighted`, its

chunks.title: Fairshare engine
chunks.heading: Effective weight
chunks.text:
A tenant competes in a pool with its weight scaled by the model's `admission_weight` (a percentage, default 100):

```
effective weight = round(tenant weight × admission_weight / 100), at least 1
```

Every tenant in a pool is scaled alike, so their shares of it don't change. Group and key weights are not scaled.

chunks.title: Fairshare engine
chunks.heading: Multiple gateway replicas
chunks.text:
So that configured numbers hold for the fleet, replicas share them through Redis (`OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_SHARED_SLOTS`, default `true`). With more than one live, every pool size, the global ceiling and every tenant and key cap is a set of cluster-wide slots. A replica picks its next waiter as it would alone, then takes a slot in one Redis script call that checks the pool, ceiling and caps together against the configured values, never divided. Finishing gives it back in one call. A 20-slot model behind three replicas admits 20 requests wherever they land, and never a 21st. With one live replica there is no Redis call on this path.

| Held across replicas | Not shared |
| --- | --- |
| Pool sizes (configured, default and discovered) | Group, tenant, key and model weights, which are ratios |
| The global in-flight ceiling | Token and term budgets, already fleet-wide in Redis |
| Tenant and key `max_in_flight` | |

Fairness is exact within a replica; across replicas a freed slot goes to whichever claims it first. A crashed replica's slots stay taken until its heartbeat expires, up to `OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_REPLICA_TTL_SECS` (default 15).

Queues stay with the replica that holds them, so in shared mode each replica also publishes a view of its scheduler: every pool with work, with its totals and the groups, tenants and keys running or waiting there. It goes out every 500 ms, or every heartbeat if that is shorter, and lives for three intervals, so one slow publish doesn't drop a replica. The

chunks.title: Fairshare engine
chunks.heading: One scheduler task
chunks.text: One async task owns every pool, queue and count, so admission decisions never race; dropping a request's permit releases its slot. Weights travel with each request from the key cache, so a change applies on the next admission after cache invalidation, without a restart. A request still waiting after `OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS` (default 60) gets 503 with `Retry-After: 5`; one whose client left is dropped without charge. See [How fairshare works](/docs/sharing/how-fairshare-works).

chunks.title: Fairshare engine
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: This page covers the scheduler's internals. To set weights, groups and caps, see [Tenants and keys](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys), [API keys](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys) and [Priority boost](/docs/sharing/priority-boost).

chunks.title: Fairshare engine
chunks.heading: Per model
chunks.text:
A model can turn affinity on or off for its own pool, whatever the gateway default, and set its own hold time, held share and bypass limit. Anything it leaves out uses the gateway's values, which apply even while the gateway default is off. Set it on the model page under **Capacity → Session affinity**, with `PUT /api/v1/models/{id}/session-affinity`, or with `session_affinity` on model create, update and import:

```json
{ "enabled": true, "hold_ms": 5000, "max_held_percent": 50, "max_bypass_secs": 120 }
```

`{}` follows the gateway. `hold_ms` is 0 to 60000, `max_held_percent` 0 to 100 and `max_bypass_secs` 1 to 3600. A change applies to the model's next request; turning affinity off frees the slots its pool holds. This lets you try affinity on one agent-heavy model while every other model is scheduled as before.

A held slot that no step takes was idle for the hold time, so affinity trades some throughput for shorter agent steps. Turn it on where agent sessions compete for a pool, and compare `hold` with `redeem` in `obleth_fairshare_affinity_total`: when they are close, held slots are being used.

In shared mode a held slot lives in Redis, so the session's next step can take it on whichever replica it reaches. The finished step's slot leaves its replica's holdings and is kept under an id made of the pool and the session, still counted against every limit. Redis also records when each session's step last finished, so whether a step followed straight on from the one before

chunks.title: Fairshare engine
chunks.heading: Per-model pools
chunks.text:
Every model has its own pool of slots: its `max_in_flight`, or `OBLETH_DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (default 32). A model in the `discovered` capacity mode sizes its pool from its ready backend replicas ([Pool sizes](/docs/models/pool-sizes)). A request holds a slot from admission until the upstream response has finished streaming.

Fairness is worked out in each pool on its own: a full model never delays one with free slots, and heavy use of one model doesn't lower a tenant's standing on another. `OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (default 4096) caps the sum across pools and plays no part in fairness; when it binds, pools are served round-robin. Keep it above the pools you expect to be busy together; the gateway warns at start when it isn't.

Unregistered model names share one unrouted pool. A pool idle for 10 minutes, or whose model is no longer routed, is dropped.

chunks.title: Fairshare engine
chunks.heading: Session affinity
chunks.text:
An agent sends the steps of a session one after another, each over the same, growing prompt. The backend keeps that prefix in its prompt cache only until other work pushes it out. When many sessions share too few slots, a step that waits behind other sessions' steps often finds its prefix gone and is prefilled again from the start, so a step that should take seconds takes minutes. With `OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_SESSION_AFFINITY=true` (off by default), each pool favours sessions that are still warm.

A session is the request's [session id](/docs/clients/conversations-and-sessions), sent by the client or derived by the gateway, under the key that sent it. Requests with no session id, and requests to a model that load balances across several endpoints (so a session would not reach the same backend twice), are scheduled as before.

- **Order within a key.** A session with a step running, or whose last step finished within the warm window, goes ahead of older requests from the same key. Which group, tenant and key is served next is still decided as above.
- **Held slots.** When a step finishes that arrived within the hold time of the session's previous step finishing, as an agent's next step does and a person's next message does not, its slot is held for the hold time. The session's next step takes it at once; if none comes, the slot is freed. A held slot counts like a running request against the pool, the global ceiling and the tenant's and key's `max_in_flight`, and the step that takes

chunks.title: Fairshare engine
chunks.heading: Watching it
chunks.text:
The dashboard's **Fairshare** page lists pools fullest first; `/fairshare?pool=<model>` opens one.

![A full pool on the Fairshare page: 24 of 24 slots running, 56 waiting, three tenants at their fair share, and the pool's keys with their weights](/dashboard/fairshare-pool.png)

`GET /api/v1/fairshare/live` returns the same state per pool, group, tenant and key, with the replica's `mode` and, in shared mode, `cluster_in_flight`. Its `scope` says whose counts it holds:

- `cluster`: every live replica, merged, in shared mode. `replicas_reporting` says how many views it includes (fewer than `replicas` while a new replica has not published yet) and `state_age_ms` the age of the oldest.
- `replica`: the answering replica alone. Always so outside shared mode, and in shared mode when the other replicas' views can't be read, with the reason in `scope_reason`.

`replica_in_flight` and `replica_queued`, at the top and on each pool, are always the answering replica's own.

The dashboard judges **Below share** inside each pool: a tenant is below its share when it has requests queued, holds fewer slots than its fair share of that pool, and another tenant in the same pool holds at least a slot more than its own. Admission never takes a slot back, so without such a tenant the wait is the pool or a cap being full. When the live state covers only one of several gateways, Overview says the counts are "on this gateway".

`GET /api/v1/fairshare/history` returns 2-second samples for one `model`

chunks.title: Performance
chunks.heading: Cached responses
chunks.text: A request that hits the [response cache](/docs/models/response-cache) is answered by the gateway and never reaches the backend. Caching is set per model.

chunks.title: Performance
chunks.heading: Measure it yourself
chunks.text:
`obench score` runs capacity ramps, gateway overhead, streaming quality, overload, resilience and fairshare sections against the benchmark backend in the Compose stack, and grades each one. Scores are kept as baselines so later runs show regressions. See [Benchmarks](/docs/operate/benchmarks).

For a self-hosted model, the Models page can run a short load probe against the upstream and recommend a concurrency cap from the latency curve. Nothing changes until you apply it. See [Capacity auto-tune](/docs/models/capacity-autotune). For a model on Kubernetes, [discovered capacity](/docs/models/pool-sizes) sizes the pool from its ready replicas instead.

chunks.title: Performance
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
In-process caches, then Redis. Never Postgres or ClickHouse.
  No Redis call with one replica; one script call in and one out with several.
  `obench score` grades gateway overhead against a GPU-free backend.

chunks.title: Performance
chunks.heading: Streaming
chunks.text: Response chunks go to the client as they arrive. The fairshare slot is held until the stream ends, so the gateway's count of requests in flight matches what the backend is actually serving, not how long a connection happened to be open.

chunks.title: Performance
chunks.heading: What runs on every request
chunks.text:
Keys, models and MCP servers resolve from an in-process cache first and Redis second. The gateway warms Redis from Postgres at start, re-pushes it on a timer and after every Redis reconnect, and invalidates the in-process copies over Redis pub/sub, so a change made in the dashboard reaches every replica without a restart.

Admission is the fairshare scheduler in the same process. With several gateway replicas, the limits are cluster-wide slots in Redis: one script call when a request is admitted and one when it finishes. With a single replica there is no Redis call on this path at all. See [Fairshare engine](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine).

chunks.title: Performance
chunks.heading: What stays off it
chunks.text:
- **Telemetry.** Usage rows and spans are written in the background. While ClickHouse is unreachable they spill to a local write-ahead file and replay when it returns. See [Datastores](/docs/how-it-works/datastores).
- **Tracing.** Spans export to an OTLP collector through a background batch processor, so a slow collector never slows a request.
- **Per-tenant metrics.** Prometheus labels stay low-cardinality (admission class, status class). Per-tenant and per-key breakdowns come from ClickHouse instead.

chunks.title: Request lifecycle
chunks.heading: 1. Authenticate
chunks.text:
The credential comes from `Authorization: Bearer` or `x-api-key`. A JWT from a configured issuer is verified instead ([Identity tokens](/docs/clients/identity-tokens)). A key is hashed and looked up in the in-process cache, then Redis. Not found returns 401; a Redis error returns 503. The result carries the tenant and key ids, weights, group, limits, budgets, model allowlist and guardrails policy.

A disabled key returns 403, and so does a tenant that isn't active or is outside its access window, expiry or weekly schedule.

chunks.title: Request lifecycle
chunks.heading: 2. Resolve the model and enrich the request

chunks.title: Request lifecycle
chunks.heading: 3. Response cache
chunks.text: When the model has caching on with a TTL above 0, the gateway looks up a hash of the tenant, the model and the body. A hit is returned with `x-obleth-cache: hit` and ends the request: no slot, no budget and no upstream call, and the usage row says `cache_status = "hit"`. A Redis error counts as a miss. The cache is skipped for gateway tool loops and for tenants with output guardrails. See [Response cache](/docs/models/response-cache).

chunks.title: Request lifecycle
chunks.heading: 4. Fairshare admission
chunks.text: The request asks the scheduler for a slot in its model's pool, carrying its tenant, key and group weights and caps and the estimated cost. With a free slot it is admitted at once (`fast`). Otherwise it waits and is admitted (`queued`) when the scheduler picks it for a freed slot. After `OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS` (default 60) it returns 503 `timed out waiting for model capacity` with `Retry-After: 5`. A waiter whose client has gone is dropped without charge. See [Fairshare engine](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine) and [How fairshare works](/docs/sharing/how-fairshare-works).

chunks.title: Request lifecycle
chunks.heading: 5. Reserve budgets

chunks.title: Request lifecycle
chunks.heading: 6. Call the upstream
chunks.text:
The request goes to a healthy endpoint of the model, or its `api_base`, or `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_BASE_URL`. The client's credentials are never forwarded; the model's own `api_key` is sent as `Authorization: Bearer`. Each attempt is bounded by the model's `request_timeout_secs` or `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_SECS`, and any silence from the upstream, the wait for headers included, by `OBLETH_UPSTREAM_READ_TIMEOUT_SECS`. Connection errors, timeouts, 408, 429 and 5xx are retried with backoff and then fail over to the next endpoint, but only before the first byte reaches the client; other 4xx are returned as they are. See [Reliability and failover](/docs/operate/reliability).

Streams are passed through as they arrive, and the slot is held until the upstream stream ends. A successful response of 512 KiB or less is cached when step 3 applied.

chunks.title: Request lifecycle
chunks.heading: 7. Settle cost and record usage
chunks.text:
The real token counts come from the upstream's `usage` (the gateway always asks a streaming upstream for it and strips the extra chunk if the client didn't). The per-minute bucket is refunded or charged the difference from the estimate, and the term reservation is replaced by the actual tokens and cost, once. Failed requests are not billed: an error without usage records zero, and a 502 or 504 after retries refunds the reservations. A stream [cut short](/docs/reference/data-plane-routes#when-a-stream-is-cut-short) after output reached the client is recorded as 502 and billed for what streamed: the reported usage, else the text at about 4 characters per token, never the `max_tokens` estimate. Helper calls made for the request (vision, tool loops, drafts, image generation, structured output) count against the term budgets. See [How fairshare works](/docs/sharing/how-fairshare-works).

A usage record then goes onto a bounded in-memory channel and a background task inserts batches into ClickHouse every `OBLETH_TELEMETRY_FLUSH_INTERVAL_MS` (5 seconds by default), or as soon as 500 rows are waiting; the request doesn't wait for it. Rejected and failed requests are recorded too, and a client that disconnects mid-stream is recorded as 499. While ClickHouse is unreachable, rows go to a local spill file and replay later. With tracing on for the tenant or key, one span per step lands in the `spans` table. See [Datastores](/docs/how-it-works/datastores) and [ClickHouse usage](/docs/refer

chunks.title: Request lifecycle
chunks.heading: Errors by step
chunks.text:
| Step | Status | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Authenticate | 401 | Missing or unknown key |
| Authenticate | 503 | `authentication backend unavailable`: Redis failed during lookup |
| Authenticate | 403 | Key disabled, or tenant inactive or outside its schedule |
| Read body | 413 | Body over 64 MiB |
| Read body | 400 | Missing `model` or an invalid body; `store`, `previous_response_id` or `background` sent to `/v1/responses` |
| Resolve model | 404 | Model not registered, or unknown endpoint |
| Resolve model | 403 | Model disabled, or not on the tenant's allowlist |
| Resolve model | 503 | No model can serve an `auto` request |
| Guardrails | 400 | Blocked by input guardrails, or an endpoint the tenant's output policy can't scan |
| Guardrails | 503 | `content policy scanner unavailable` with a fail-closed policy |
| Admission | 503 | `timed out waiting for model capacity` (`Retry-After: 5`) |
| Budgets | 429 | Per-minute token budget exceeded |
| Budgets | 403 | Key or tenant term budget exhausted |
| Budgets | 503 | Budget check failed with `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN=false` |
| Upstream | 502 | Failed after every retry and endpoint, or the stream broke before its last chunk |
| Upstream | 504 | Every attempt timed out |
| Client | 499 | Client disconnected (recorded only) |

Every error string is in [Data-plane routes](/docs/reference/data-plane-routes).

Input guardrails run for every request from a tenant with a policy, including `x-obleth-boons: off`, unrouted and non-chat

chunks.title: Request lifecycle
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The Responses API (`/v1/responses`) and the Anthropic Messages API (`/v1/messages`) are translated to a chat request after step 1, run steps 2 to 7 as chat, and are translated back. A [verdicts](/docs/clients/verdicts) request runs the steps once for all its questions: one slot and one set of reservations cover the whole fan-out.

chunks.title: Capacity auto-tune
chunks.heading: Capacity modes
chunks.text:
| Mode | Pool size |
| --- | --- |
| `static` (default) | The **Max slots** you set |
| `tuned` | The value last applied from auto-tune; `capacity_tuned_at` records when |
| `discovered` | Follows the backend's ready replicas; see [Pool sizes](/docs/models/pool-sizes) |

`static` and `tuned` both use `max_in_flight`, so between them the mode is a record for you and the audit log. You can switch back to `static` without losing the value.

chunks.title: Capacity auto-tune
chunks.heading: How the probe works
chunks.text:
The probe runs in the Management API and sends requests straight to the model's API base, bypassing obleth's own admission, so it measures the backend rather than the current pool. It carries the model's [upstream headers](/docs/models/model-registry#upstream-headers).

1. It steps concurrency up 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on to a ceiling, holding each step for 2.5 seconds and recording throughput and p50 and p99 latency.
2. It sets a latency budget from the concurrency-1 baseline: the baseline p99 × the tolerance, never below 100 ms.
3. It always runs the whole ladder, so the result is reproducible; only the safety limits below, or a step where every request failed, cut it short.
4. It recommends the highest concurrency that stayed within the budget and still added throughput.

| Why it stopped | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `latency_degraded` | A step's p99 went past the budget |
| `plateau` | Throughput gained less than about 7% over the step before |
| `max_concurrency` | It reached the ceiling with no knee; the real one may be higher |
| `no_data` | No step produced usable samples: the upstream is unreachable |

The ceiling is `max_concurrency` if you give it (at most 512), otherwise 32 × **Replicas running**, otherwise 64.

| Workload | Prompt | Reply |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `chat` (default) | about 512 tokens | 128 tokens |
| `coding` | about 6,000 tokens | 512 tokens |

chunks.title: Capacity auto-tune
chunks.heading: Management API
chunks.text:
```bash
# Run a probe (changes nothing)
curl -X POST "http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/autotune" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"workload": "chat", "latency_headroom": 4.0, "replicas": 2}'

# Apply a recommendation
curl -X POST "http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/autotune/apply" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"max_in_flight": 32}'
```

The probe answers with `recommended_max_in_flight`, `knee_reason`, `baseline_p99_ms`, `latency_ceiling_ms`, `recommended_throughput_rps` and a `steps` array. Applying sets `max_in_flight`, switches the mode to `tuned`, stamps `capacity_tuned_at` and updates every gateway replica. Probes and applies are recorded in the audit log. See [Management API](/docs/reference/management-api#model-capacity-and-auto-tune).

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Wall clock | 60 seconds for all steps together |
| Total requests | 20,000 |
| Concurrency | 512 |
| `latency_headroom` | Clamped to 1.5–20; default 4.0 |
| Model types | Chat and embeddings |

chunks.title: Capacity auto-tune
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Chat and embedding models on servers you run
  A model's page › Capacity › Auto-tune capacity
  Up to 60 seconds of real load and its tokens
  Nothing until you apply the result

chunks.title: Capacity auto-tune
chunks.heading: Run a probe
chunks.text:
On the model's page, under **Capacity**, choose **Auto-tune capacity**. Run it in a quiet window: the probe sends real concurrent load to the model's backend.

Set **Replicas running**, the copies of the model serving now; **Latency tolerance**, how much slower than one idle request you accept at peak (Tight 2×, Balanced 4×, Relaxed 8×); and the **Workload**: short chat turns, or coding with a large context and longer replies.

Choose **Run probe**. The dialog shows the recommended slots, the throughput there, the latency budget, why the ramp stopped, and a row per step. **Apply** sets the model's pool to the recommendation and switches it to the `tuned` capacity mode.

Keep a model on a metered cloud API on a fixed pool instead: the probe would spend real money, and a fixed number bounds your spend. If the backend's replica count changes on its own, use the [`discovered` mode](/docs/models/pool-sizes#follow-the-backend), with the tuned value divided by the replicas as the per-replica concurrency.

chunks.title: Import from a provider
chunks.heading: Import a file
chunks.text:
**Import or export** on Models writes models to an `obleth-models` manifest and reads one back, on the same gateway or another. Use it to keep models in a repository or copy them between gateways. Import a file shows what would be created and changed before anything is written. A manifest is not a backup: for a whole-gateway copy, see [Backup and restore](/docs/operate/backup-restore).

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/export \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" > obleth-models.json

# Only some models: names that match no model are skipped
curl -s "http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/export?names=qwen3,flux-2" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" > two-models.json

# Preview without writing, then apply
curl -s -X POST "http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/import?dry_run=true" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data @obleth-models.json
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/import \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data @obleth-models.json
```

```yaml
format: obleth-models
version: 1
models:
  - model_name: glm-5-3
    aliases: [glm-5-3-mxfp4]
    upstream_model: zai-org/GLM-5.3-MXFP4
    api_base: https://inference.example.com/v1
    quantization: mxfp4
    context_window: 131072
    tags: [coding, "reasoning:3"]
    endpoints:
      - name: primary
        api_base: https://inference.example.com/v1
        priority: 100
        weight: 100
  # A sparse

chunks.title: Import from a provider
chunks.heading: Import from a provider
chunks.text:
Enter the provider's **API base URL** and an optional **API key**, then **Fetch models**. obleth reads `GET {base}/models` from the gateway, so the key never reaches your browser. A 404 usually means the base should gain or drop its `/v1`.

Every model the provider serves is listed. New ones are selected; ones you already have are hidden behind **Show N already imported** and can't be picked. Set the defaults for every model (type, context window, input and output cost per token), then change each row's name or type where you need to.

**Review import** shows each model as it would be created, with any problem for every model at once, such as an alias already taken. Confirm to create them.

Imported models point at the provider's base URL and ID and carry the key you gave. Like a model added by hand, each is created switched off and turns on when its first health check passes; the result says which came on and why the others stayed off. Run the import again later and only new models are offered.

chunks.title: Import from a provider
chunks.heading: Names and formats
chunks.text:
Each provider ID becomes a suggested name: lowercase, with anything outside `a-z 0-9 . -` turned into dashes. A trailing format token (`fp8`, `bf16`, `fp16`, `mxfp4`, `nvfp4`, `int8`, `int4`, `awq`, `gptq`, `gguf`) moves into the model's [quantization](/docs/models/model-registry#quantization), and the full name becomes an [alias](/docs/models/model-registry#aliases), so callers of the provider's spelling keep working:

| Provider ID | Name | Quantization | Alias |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Qwen3-8B-FP8` | `qwen3-8b` | `fp8` | `qwen3-8b-fp8` |
| `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8` | `qwen-qwen3-8b` | `fp8` | `qwen-qwen3-8b-fp8` |
| `fp8` | `fp8` | `unknown` | none |

The model's upstream model is the provider's ID, unchanged. Two selected models that end up with the same name are refused until you rename one.

A provider model counts as already imported when one of your models has its name (with or without the format suffix), or has the same base URL and upstream ID. That second check keeps a model you renamed after importing it from being offered again.

- The base URL must be `http` or `https`. A host that resolves to a link-local or cloud-metadata address is refused.
- The key is sent as a bearer token. A 401 or 403 is reported as a rejected key.
- The request times out after 5 seconds and doesn't follow redirects; enter the final URL instead.
- The answer can be the OpenAI `{"object": "list", "data": [...]}` shape or a bare array. Entries without an `id` are skipped, and the rest are

chunks.title: Import from a provider
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A base URL that answers `GET /models`, or an exported models file
  Models › Add model › From a provider
  Only new models; existing ones are never edited

chunks.title: Inference gateways
chunks.heading: Catalogs at `/v1/models/`
chunks.text: Some gateways serve their model catalog only at `/v1/models/`, with the trailing slash, and answer 404 at `/v1/models`. obleth's model validation and health checks retry with the slash, so such a gateway still validates and its catalog can be read. **Check connection** in Add model doesn't retry; type the upstream model instead. A gateway that refuses the catalog request outright leaves image and video models `unknown` rather than down; see [Health checks](/docs/models/model-health). Clients calling obleth can use either spelling: both return obleth's own registry.

chunks.title: Inference gateways
chunks.heading: Connect a model
chunks.text:
On **Models**, choose **Add model** › **Connect an endpoint** and enter the gateway's base URL as the **API base**, for example `http://my-inference-gateway.inference.svc:8080/v1`. **Check connection** lists the models the gateway serves. See [Register a model](/docs/models/model-registry).

The **Upstream model** is the ID the gateway routes on, sent in the request's `model` field. The model's **Name** is what clients call, so you can rename a model for clients without touching the gateway.

If the gateway reads a header to choose a pool, a routing strategy or a tenant, add it under **Upstream headers**; use the header names your gateway documents. If the gateway needs its own key, set **Upstream API key**. obleth never forwards a client's `Authorization` or `x-api-key` upstream; it sends the model's key as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`.

Upstream headers also go on obleth's own calls to the model, such as health checks and auto-tune, so a header that picks the backend picks the same one for them. See [Upstream headers](/docs/models/model-registry#upstream-headers).

To register many models at once, use [Import from a provider](/docs/models/import-models) with the gateway's base URL. A format suffix in a gateway's model IDs, such as `-FP8`, moves into the model's quantization and the full name stays as an alias.

chunks.title: Inference gateways
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A gateway or router with an OpenAI-compatible API
  Register each model with the gateway's URL as its API base
  Keys, tenants, fairshare, budgets and usage accounting

chunks.title: Inference gateways
chunks.heading: Size each model's pool
chunks.text:
Set each model's pool to about the number of requests the replicas behind the gateway serve at once for that model. See [Pool sizes](/docs/models/pool-sizes), or measure it with [Capacity auto-tune](/docs/models/capacity-autotune).

When an autoscaler changes the replicas behind the gateway, a fixed number goes stale. On Kubernetes, use the `discovered` mode with the `kubernetes` source, and point the model at a Service that selects the model-server pods, not the gateway's own pods. The `endpoints` source would count the gateway as a single replica.

chunks.title: Inference gateways
chunks.heading: Who does what
chunks.text:
An inference gateway sits between an API layer and several replicas of a model server and picks the replica for each request: the least loaded one, or the one with a matching prefix or KV cache. A Kubernetes Service in front of several model-server pods is the simplest form. obleth works in front of any of them, sending OpenAI-compatible requests to the gateway as the model's upstream.

| Concern | obleth | Inference gateway |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who may send, and at what priority | ✓ | |
| Per-tenant and per-key budgets and limits | ✓ | |
| Usage, cost and energy accounting | ✓ | |
| Response cache, boons, MCP tools | ✓ | |
| Which replica serves a request | | ✓ |
| Prefix- and KV-cache affinity | | ✓ |

obleth decides who sends and when; the gateway decides which replica serves it.

chunks.title: Inference gateways
chunks.heading: Without an inference gateway
chunks.text: An inference gateway is useful for replica-aware routing, not required. A model's API base can point straight at a single model server or at a hosted OpenAI-compatible provider. Several servers can be registered as the model's [endpoints](/docs/operate/reliability), and obleth fails over or balances between them itself.

chunks.title: Health checks
chunks.heading: Alerts
chunks.text:
Alerts go through the channels in **Settings › Alerts**; see [Alerting](/docs/operate/alerting). Each model sends one alert when it reaches its failure threshold and one when it recovers. Nothing is sent while alerts are off for the model, it is in maintenance, or it is off.

Each enabled [endpoint](/docs/operate/reliability) is probed on its own and gets its own state. Requests skip endpoints that are `unhealthy` or off; `degraded` and `unknown` endpoints stay in rotation. A `degraded` result lifts a stale `unhealthy`, but never lowers a confirmed `healthy`.

A model with no API base of its own, such as one [launched on Slurm](/docs/deployments/slurm-provisioning), takes its state from its endpoints, measured against its minimum replicas:

| Endpoints serving (answered the probe) | Model state |
| --- | --- |
| At least the minimum | `healthy` |
| Some, but fewer than the minimum | `degraded` |
| Every live endpoint `unknown` | `unknown` |
| None registered, or none reachable | `unhealthy` |

Recent traffic can settle such a model only while an endpoint is still serving. These probes run from the gateway, so a replica the provisioner promoted can still read `unhealthy` if the gateway can't reach its node.

| Environment variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_MODEL_HEALTH_ENABLED` | `true` | Run scheduled checks |
| `OBLETH_MODEL_HEALTH_INTERVAL_SECS` | `900` | Default check interval |
| `OBLETH_MODEL_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_SECS` | `30` | Timeout per check |
| `

chunks.title: Health checks
chunks.heading: Catalog checks for image and video models
chunks.text: An image or video model is healthy when the upstream catalog lists it. Because some servers mount their catalog only at `/v1/models/`, a 404 is retried once with the trailing slash. When the upstream answers the catalog with another 4xx, for example a gateway that doesn't serve `/models` or guards it differently from inference, the model is `unknown` rather than down: it stays routable and doesn't alert. No answer at all is `unhealthy`, a 5xx is `degraded`, and a catalog that answers without the model is `unhealthy`. Catalogs are cached per API base for 60 seconds.

chunks.title: Health checks
chunks.heading: Check a model
chunks.text:
On a model's page, **Check health now** runs a check at once; on a model that is off, **Check and turn on** runs one and turns the model on if it passes. The page's **Health** section sets the schedule, alerts, the failure threshold and a maintenance window, and lists recent checks. On **Models**, select rows to check several models together.

```bash
# One model
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/health/check \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# Every model that is on, has checks on and is not in maintenance
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/health \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

chunks.title: Health checks
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Every 900 seconds per model by default, and on demand
  One tiny real request, or nothing when the model served traffic recently
  A model's page › Health

chunks.title: Health checks
chunks.heading: States
chunks.text:
| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `healthy` | The model served a real request, or recent client traffic succeeded |
| `degraded` | Reachable but not confirmed: overloaded (408, 429, 5xx), or rejected by an endpoint while the catalog lists the model, which points at a wrong model type. Doesn't alert |
| `unhealthy` | The model is missing upstream, the key was rejected, or the upstream is unreachable. Counts toward the failure threshold |
| `unknown` | Nothing could be verified, such as a wildcard catalog. Never alerts |
| `disabled` | The model is off; no request is made |

A model reads `unhealthy` only once it has failed its **failure threshold** of checks in a row (2 by default), the same point at which the down alert goes out. A single failed check doesn't flip it.

chunks.title: Health checks
chunks.heading: What a check does
chunks.text:
A check uses the cheapest signal it can trust:

1. **Recent traffic.** A successful client request for the model within its check interval (at least 300 seconds) settles it as `healthy` without a probe. Recent errors are never trusted on their own; they fall through to a probe.
2. **A real request** to the endpoint the model's type serves.
3. **The upstream catalog** (`GET {api_base}/models`) for image and video models, where a real request would be a costly generation.

Probe tokens are recorded under an internal tenant with `request_type = health_probe`, so they never land on a client's bill and are hidden from the request log. Probes and catalog requests carry the model's [upstream headers](/docs/models/model-registry#upstream-headers).

chunks.title: Health checks
chunks.heading: What clears a failure
chunks.text:
- **A passing check.** The next scheduled or manual check that comes back `healthy` clears the failure and sends a recovery alert.
- **Fixing the configuration.** Changing a model's API base, upstream model, type or upstream headers resets its health: the state goes back to `unknown`, the failure count to zero, the alert state clears, and the next check runs within one worker pass. Check history is kept.
- **A maintenance window.** Until it ends, failed checks are still recorded but don't alert, and the model shows as in maintenance.

chunks.title: Health checks
chunks.heading: What the active probe sends
chunks.text:
| Model type | Probe |
| --- | --- |
| Chat | `POST {api_base}/chat/completions`, one `ping` message, `max_tokens: 1` |
| Embeddings | `POST {api_base}/embeddings`, `input: "ping"` |
| Speech | `POST {api_base}/audio/speech`, `input: "."`, `voice: "alloy"` |
| Transcription | `POST {api_base}/audio/transcriptions` with a 0.1-second silent WAV |
| Search | `GET {api_base}/search?q=ping&format=json`, one real search; no catalog check |
| Image, video, other | `GET {api_base}/models`, and the model must be listed |

A probe tries up to three times, backing off, on a 408, 429, 5xx or network error before it records a result.

Scheduled and bulk checks skip a [retired](/docs/models/model-lifecycle) model, whose backend is usually gone. A staged model is checked like an active one.

chunks.title: Model lifecycle
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The model's page › Lifecycle
  Staged, active, deprecated, retired
  Deprecation headers, then a `410` or the replacement

chunks.title: Model lifecycle
chunks.heading: Retire a model
chunks.text:
On the model's page, set **Lifecycle** › **Status** to **Deprecated**. Pick the **Replacement** (a model of the same type that is still served and listed), the **Retire on** date (midnight UTC that day) and, if you want, a **Note to callers** of up to 500 characters, such as where to ask. **What callers see** previews the headers or the error, and **Who calls it** lists the keys that used the model in the last 30 days, linked to their requests.

Choose **Save lifecycle**. The section saves on its own, not with the save bar, and applies within a few seconds. From then on the model is still served, with headers saying it is going away, and `auto` stops picking it.

On the retirement date the model retires itself: requests naming it are refused with `410 Gone`. To retire it at once, set **Retired** instead; the dashboard asks first. With **Once retired** › **Answer with the replacement** on, the replacement answers instead of the `410`.

Or through the Management API:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/status \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "status": "deprecated",
    "replacement": "new-model",
    "retire_at": "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z",
    "note": "Questions? Ask the platform team.",
    "redirect": false
  }'
```

The body sets the whole lifecycle: `status` (`staged`, `active`, `deprecated` or `retired`), `replacement`, `retire_at` (RFC 3339), `note` and `redirect`. `POST /api/v1/models`

chunks.title: Model lifecycle
chunks.heading: Stage a new model
chunks.text:
**Add model** has a **Start staged** switch, on by default, and a model launched from a [recipe](/docs/deployments/deployment-recipes) starts staged too. A staged model answers anyone who sends its name, but nothing advertises it: it is left out of `/v1/models` and `/model/info`, `GET /v1/models/<name>` returns `404`, and `auto` never picks it. Health checks and capacity discovery run as usual, so you can watch it work, and the Playground can call it.

When it is ready, open the model's page, set **Lifecycle** › **Status** to **Active** and choose **Save lifecycle**. Before a staged model goes live, the dashboard asks you to confirm and says whether `auto` may start sending it requests.

chunks.title: Model lifecycle
chunks.heading: What callers see
chunks.text:
| Status | Requests | `/v1/models`, `/model/info` | `auto` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Staged | Served as usual | Left out; `GET /v1/models/{id}` is `404` | Never picks it |
| Active | Served as usual | Listed | May pick it |
| Deprecated | Served, with lifecycle headers | Listed with `status`, and `replacement`, `retire_at` and `note` when set | Never picks it |
| Retired | `410`, or the replacement answers | Left out; `GET /v1/models/{id}` still answers, so a caller can find the replacement | Never picks it |

Every response from a deprecated model carries:

```text
x-obleth-model-status: deprecated
Deprecation: @1790812800
Sunset: Tue, 01 Dec 2026 00:00:00 GMT
Link: </v1/models/new-model>; rel="successor-version"
x-obleth-model-replacement: new-model
```

`Deprecation` (RFC 9745) is when the model was deprecated, `Sunset` (RFC 8594) is sent once a retirement date is set, and `Link` and `x-obleth-model-replacement` once a replacement is named. Client libraries and proxies that know the standard headers can warn without obleth-specific code.

A request to a retired model gets the same headers and this body:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "message": "The model `old-model` was retired on 2026-12-01. Use `new-model` instead. Questions? Ask the platform team.",
    "type": "invalid_request_error",
    "param": "model",
    "code": "model_retired",
    "replacement": "new-model",
    "retired_at": "2026-12-01T00:00:00+00:00"
  }
}
```

Refusals are written to the usage ledger with

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Add a model
chunks.text:
On **Models**, choose **Add model**, then **Connect an endpoint**. Enter the **API base** (usually ending in `/v1`) and an **API key** if the server needs one. **Check connection** lists what the server serves; pick one and the upstream model, name and type are filled in.

**Name** is what clients send as `model`. Check the **Type**, and add **Aliases** and a **Description** if you want them. **Start staged**, on by default, keeps it unlisted until you make it active; see [Model lifecycle](/docs/models/model-lifecycle).

**Concurrent requests** is the model's [pool size](/docs/models/pool-sizes); blank uses the default. Set the context window and the price, then choose **Create model**.

A new model starts switched off, and obleth checks its health right away. If the check passes, the model turns on; if not, it stays off, so a mistyped URL never takes traffic, and its page says why, with **Check and turn on**. See [Health checks](/docs/models/model-health).

The sheet's other tabs import [from a provider](/docs/models/import-models) or [from a file](/docs/models/import-models#import-a-file). To run a model on your own cluster, launch it from [Deployments](/docs/deployments/overview).

With the [Management API](/docs/reference/management-api), create the model switched off, then activate it:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model_name": "qwen3-8b",
    "upstrea

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Aliases
chunks.text:
An alias is another name that reaches the same model, so clients that pinned an old spelling keep working. Usage, allowlists, pools and budgets all use the model's own name.

A model's name can't be changed: to rename one, create it again with the old name as an alias. A model keeps at most 16 aliases, matched exactly. An alias can't be another model's name, alias or variant, or `auto`. On an API update, `aliases` replaces the list; `[]` removes them all. Registering Claude model IDs as aliases is how [Anthropic clients](/docs/clients/anthropic-messages-api) reach your models.

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Connection
chunks.text: **Connection** holds the **Upstream model** (the name the server itself serves), the **API base URL**, the **Upstream API key**, the request timeout and retries. The key is write-only. On an API update, omit `api_key` to keep it and send `""` to clear it. To spread a model over several servers, add **Endpoints**; see [Reliability and failover](/docs/operate/reliability).

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Export and import the registry
chunks.text: **Import or export** on Models writes models to an `obleth-models` manifest that you can keep in a repository, edit and apply back, on this gateway or another. See [Import a file](/docs/models/import-models#import-a-file).

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Find and change a model
chunks.text:
![The Models list: summary tiles above a table of models with health, load, requests, first-token time, price, context and tags](/dashboard/models.png)

Search the list by name, alias, upstream or router tag (press `/`), filter it by type, status and where the model runs, and sort it by load, requests, name or age. Select rows to check, turn on or off, export or delete several models at once.

Each model has a page at `/models/<name>`.

![A model's page: the section list, the Serving switch, tiles for load and requests, a request chart and where the model runs](/dashboard/model.png)

Below that, every setting is on one scrolling page, in sections from **General** to **Deployment**. **Find a setting** (`⌘K`) jumps to any field. Edits collect in the save bar, which lists what changed; **Save changes** saves them all at once. Endpoint changes apply as soon as you make them.

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: `GET /model/info`
chunks.text: `GET /v1/models` and `GET /model/info` list every enabled model from the registry, without calling any upstream, with its aliases, variants, tags, quantization and boons, including the helper model each boon calls. Staged and retired models are left out; see [Model lifecycle](/docs/models/model-lifecycle). A tenant sees only the models it may call. See [Model discovery](/docs/clients/openai-compatible-api#model-discovery).

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Limits and prices
chunks.text:
**Capacity** sets how many requests reach the model at once; see [Pool sizes](/docs/models/pool-sizes) and [Response cache](/docs/models/response-cache).

**Pricing** is edited per million tokens. Each request is billed at the price in force when it ran.

| Type | In the dashboard | API field (USD per unit) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chat | Input and output, per 1M tokens | `input_cost_per_token`, `output_cost_per_token` |
| Embeddings | Input, per 1M tokens | `input_cost_per_token` |
| Speech | Per 1M characters | `cost_per_character` |
| Transcription | Per audio second | `cost_per_audio_second` |
| Image | Per image | `cost_per_image` |
| Video | Per video, when the upstream accepts the job | `cost_per_video` |

**Capabilities** holds the context window. The [auto router](/docs/routing/auto-model-routing) skips a model whose window is smaller than the request needs, and the Anthropic Messages API clamps `max_tokens` to it.

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
An OpenAI-compatible server that already serves the model
  Models › Add model
  Off until its first health check passes; staged by default

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Quantization
chunks.text: **Quantization** records the format of the served weights, so re-quantizing is an edit, not a rename. It never affects routing. The values are `unknown` (the default), `none`, `fp16`, `bf16`, `fp8`, `nvfp4`, `mxfp4`, `int8`, `int4`, `awq`, `gptq` and `gguf`; anything else is refused.

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Rejected request fields
chunks.text:
Some servers crash or misbehave on a request field they don't support. **Rejected request fields** lists them, one top-level body key per line (case-sensitive, up to 32, never `model`). A request carrying one, at the top level or inside `extra_body`, gets a `400` in the OpenAI error shape (`invalid_request_error`, `param` naming the field, code `unsupported_parameter`) and never reaches the server; Request logs record it as rejected, with no tokens.

The check covers every route, Responses and Messages included. Aliases, variants and family members use the model's list, and fields that reasoning effort or boons add are not checked. On the API it is `rejected_request_fields`, on model create and update or `PUT /api/v1/models/{id}/rejected-request-fields`. Empty by default.

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Routing
chunks.text: For chat models, **Routing** sets how `model: auto` treats the model. **Eligible for auto** off keeps it reachable by name only. **Routing bias** multiplies its score, from `×0.1` to `×3.0`.

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Tags
chunks.text: Router tags say what the model is good at: `coding`, `general`, `reasoning`, `math`, `vision`, `long-context`, `fast`, `creative`, `writing`. A tag can carry a level, `tag:1` to `tag:3` (Basic, Strong, Best); a bare tag lets the router derive it from the model's cost. Unknown tags are dropped. See [Auto routing](/docs/routing/auto-model-routing).

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Upstream headers
chunks.text:
**Upstream headers** are added to every request obleth sends to the model: a routing hint an [inference gateway](/docs/models/inference-gateways) reads, or an organization header a provider requires. Write one `Name: value` per line. Your value wins over a client's header of the same name, and they also go on obleth's own calls to the model, such as health checks. Values are encrypted and write-only; the API returns only `upstream_header_names`.

On the API, `upstream_headers` is the model's whole set:

| Write | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Field omitted | Stored headers are left unchanged |
| `{}` | Every header is removed |
| `{"x-a": "1", "x-b": null}` | Exactly `x-a` and `x-b`: `x-a` set to `1`, `x-b` keeps its stored value, any other header is removed |

In the dashboard, a line with a name and no value keeps that header's stored value.

Names are stored in lowercase. Refused with `400`: invalid header names; `authorization` (use the API key), `host`, `content-length`, `content-type`, `accept-encoding` and hop-by-hop headers; more than 32 headers; a value over 4096 bytes or with control characters. Changing the headers resets the model's health state.

chunks.title: Register a model
chunks.heading: Variants
chunks.text: A [variant](/docs/models/model-variants) is a listed name that reaches the model with extra boons on, such as speculation.

chunks.title: Variants
chunks.heading: Add a variant

chunks.title: Variants
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The model's page › General › Variants
  The model's backend, pool, capacity and prices
  8 variants per model

A [boon](/docs/boons/overview) on a model acts for everyone who calls it. Some boons change what a caller gets: with [speculation](/docs/boons/speculation), a fast drafter may write the answer. A variant is a second name for the model with extra boons turned on, such as `my-model-spec` for `my-model` plus speculation. Callers who want the boon ask for the variant; callers who name the model get its own answer.

chunks.title: Variants
chunks.heading: Responses and usage
chunks.text:
A response served through a variant carries `x-obleth-model-variant: <name>`. When speculation shipped a draft, it also carries `x-obleth-drafted-by: <drafter>`.

The usage row records the variant in `model_variant`, while `model` stays the model's name, so per-model reports and the daily rollup are unchanged. The request's panel in Request logs shows **Variant**. Calls a boon makes for the request are their own rows, each linked to it by `parent_request_id`; see [Helper calls and billing](/docs/boons/overview#helper-calls-and-billing).

A variant name is matched exactly and is case-sensitive. It shares one namespace with every model's name, aliases and variants, and with [model families](/docs/models/reasoning-effort#model-families), so it can't be the model's own name, one of its aliases, another model's name or alias, another variant, or `auto`. Creating a model under a name that is already an alias or variant returns `400`. Boons must come from the [boon list](/docs/boons/overview#the-boons); an unknown one is refused. A variant that adds no boon beyond the model's own works like an alias, but is listed.

Variants are exported, imported and backed up with their model, and stored in `models.variants`.

chunks.title: Variants
chunks.heading: What a variant shares
chunks.text:
A request to a variant is served by its model's route, with the variant's boons added to the model's own. Everything else is the model's: backend and endpoints, pool and capacity, prices, health and [lifecycle](/docs/models/model-lifecycle). Two names never make two pools for one backend.

- **Discovery.** `GET /v1/models` lists each variant as its own entry, after its model, with `variant_of`, its `description` and the `boons` a request through it runs with. `/model/info` lists them under the model's `variants`.
- **Routing.** `auto` never picks a variant.
- **Allowlists.** A tenant allowed the model may call its variants, and a tenant can be allowed a variant alone by listing the variant's name.
- **Response cache.** A variant's cached answers are kept apart from its model's.
- **Verdicts.** `/v1/verdicts` treats a variant as another name for its model and runs no boons.

chunks.title: Pool sizes
chunks.heading: Choosing the Service
chunks.text:
With the `kubernetes` source, **Capacity** lists the Services it can see in the allowed namespaces, each with its ready count, so you pick one rather than type it. If the model's default Service exists, it reads "Using `<service>` in `<namespace>` · N ready", with **Change**. **Use default** clears the choice.

The default comes from `OBLETH_CAPACITY_DEFAULT_SERVICE`, a template with `{upstream_model}` and `{model_name}` placeholders. A model with no namespace is looked up in each allowed namespace in order. The list comes from `GET /api/v1/capacity/services`.

chunks.title: Pool sizes
chunks.heading: Fallback states
chunks.text:
| State | Pool size used |
| --- | --- |
| `discovered` | The value read on this pass |
| `stale` | The last value read, kept because the source has no answer: no replica serving, the Service gone, or the API server unreachable |
| `fallback` | **Fallback slots**, or the default pool size: nothing has been read yet, or the model can't be discovered as configured |

Each change of state is logged once. Gateway replicas can disagree for up to one interval after a change.

chunks.title: Pool sizes
chunks.heading: Follow the backend
chunks.text:
When an autoscaler adds replicas, or a node drains, a fixed number goes stale. In the **`discovered`** mode the pool follows the backend:

```
pool size = max(1, ceil(ready replicas × per-replica concurrency × headroom))
```

Each gateway replica re-reads the backend every interval and resizes the pool without cutting in-flight requests short.

Set `OBLETH_CAPACITY_DISCOVERY_ENABLED=true`, or `obleth.capacityDiscovery.enabled: true` in Helm. For the `kubernetes` source, also list the namespaces it may read (see [Turn on discovery](#turn-on-discovery)).

On the model's page, under **Capacity**, choose **Discovered**, then a **Capacity source**: `endpoints` or `kubernetes`.

Set **Per-replica concurrency**, the requests one replica serves at once (for example vLLM's `--max-num-seqs`), and **Headroom** (`1.0` is exactly the ready capacity). **Fallback slots** is the pool used while discovery has no answer. Save.

The section then shows the live count, for example "Live: 4 ready × 32 per replica = 128".

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/capacity-mode \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "capacity_mode": "discovered",
    "capacity_source": "kubernetes",
    "capacity_service": "my-model-serve",
    "capacity_namespace": "inference",
    "per_replica_max_in_flight": 32,
    "capacity_headroom": 1.0
  }'
```

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `capacity_mode` | `static` | `stati

chunks.title: Pool sizes
chunks.heading: Observe it
chunks.text:
`GET /api/v1/capacity/discovery` reports the answering replica's settings and, for each `discovered` model, its source, Service, ready replicas, per-replica value, derived and in-force pool size, in-flight counts, state and the reason for a `stale` or `fallback` state. The metric `obleth_capacity_discovery_models{state}` counts models by state. The **Deployments** page shows the same for [watched Kubernetes models](/docs/deployments/overview).

An autoscaler that scales on utilization or running requests still sees saturation at 100% of ready capacity. One that scales on queue depth at the backend only sees a queue if requests wait there: give that model a headroom above 1, such as `1.25`.

The derived value is the model's cluster-wide pool size, like a typed one. With shared slots (the default) every gateway replica draws from the same slots, so a backend with 4 ready replicas at 32 each gets at most 128 requests however the load balancer spreads them. When the slots are split (shared slots off, or Redis unavailable), each of 2 gateway replicas admits 64. See [Multiple gateway replicas](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine#multiple-gateway-replicas).

chunks.title: Pool sizes
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
32 requests per model (`OBLETH_DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT`)
  A model's page › Capacity
  The `discovered` mode, from endpoints or a Kubernetes Service

chunks.title: Pool sizes
chunks.heading: RBAC
chunks.text: With discovery on and at least one namespace listed, the chart renders a ServiceAccount for the gateway pods and, in each listed namespace, a Role granting only `get`, `list` and `watch` on `endpointslices` (`discovery.k8s.io`), with its RoleBinding. There is no ClusterRole and nothing on pods, Services or Secrets. The namespaces must exist, and whoever runs `helm` must be allowed to create Roles in them.

chunks.title: Pool sizes
chunks.heading: Set a model's pool
chunks.text:
Every model has its own fairshare pool: the number of requests obleth has in flight to it at once. Requests beyond that wait in the model's queue, and tenant and key weights decide who goes next. See [Fairshare engine](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine).

On a model's page, under **Capacity**, set **Max slots** to about the number of requests the model's backend serves at once without queuing, such as the sum of your servers' maximum concurrent sequences. Blank uses `OBLETH_DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (default `32`). To measure the number instead of guessing, run [Capacity auto-tune](/docs/models/capacity-autotune).

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/capacity \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"max_in_flight": 32}'
```

Send `{"max_in_flight": null}` to go back to the default. The pool size is cluster-wide: with several gateway replicas, they share the slots between them. **Admission weight** does not change a model's pool.

A steady queue (`obleth_queue_depth`) means the pool is smaller than the load.

`OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (default `4096`) caps the requests in flight across every pool together. It guards the gateway process, not any one backend, so keep it above the sum of the pools you expect to be busy at once; if the configured pools add up to more, the gateway logs a warning at start-up. `GET` and `PUT /api/v1/capacity` read and set it live, on the gateway replica that answers

chunks.title: Pool sizes
chunks.heading: Sources
chunks.text:
**`endpoints`** counts the model's own enabled, healthy [endpoints](/docs/operate/reliability): all of them under load balancing and sticky sessions, only the one in use under failover. A model with no endpoints counts its API base as one replica while it is healthy. An endpoint's own **Max in flight** wins over the model's per-replica value, and the values are added up: endpoints at 8, 2 and unset, with a per-replica value of 4, give 14. It needs nothing outside obleth.

**`kubernetes`** counts the ready endpoints of a Service, from its EndpointSlices. An endpoint counts when it is ready, serving and not terminating; nothing else is read. Which pods count is up to the Service's selector: point the model at a Service that selects only the model-server pods that take requests, not a gateway in front of them.

chunks.title: Pool sizes
chunks.heading: Turn on discovery
chunks.text:
| Environment variable | Helm value | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_CAPACITY_DISCOVERY_ENABLED` | `obleth.capacityDiscovery.enabled` | `false` | Run the discovery loop. Off, a `discovered` model uses its fallback |
| `OBLETH_CAPACITY_DISCOVERY_INTERVAL_SECS` | `obleth.capacityDiscovery.intervalSecs` | `15` | Seconds between reads |
| `OBLETH_CAPACITY_DISCOVERY_NAMESPACES` | `obleth.capacityDiscovery.namespaces` | empty | Namespaces the `kubernetes` source may read. Empty leaves it unavailable |
| `OBLETH_CAPACITY_DEFAULT_SERVICE` | `obleth.capacityDiscovery.defaultService` | empty | Service name template for models that name none |

```yaml
obleth:
  capacityDiscovery:
    enabled: true
    intervalSecs: 15
    namespaces:
      - inference
    defaultService: "{upstream_model}"
```

The chart ships this as `examples/values-capacity-discovery.yaml`. Docker Compose passes the switch and the interval through from `.env`; the `kubernetes` source needs the gateway to run in a pod.

chunks.title: Reasoning effort
chunks.heading: Ask for a level
chunks.text:
| API | Where effort is read |
| --- | --- |
| Chat completions | `reasoning_effort`, or `reasoning.effort` |
| Responses | `reasoning.effort` |
| Anthropic Messages | `output_config.effort`; else `thinking`: `disabled` is none, and an `enabled` budget under 4,096 tokens is low, under 16,384 medium, and 16,384 or more (or unset) high. `adaptive` names no level |

`minimal` reads as low, `xhigh` and `max` as high, and `off` and `disabled` as none. Any other value is refused with `400` by a mapped or unsupported model and by a family; a pass-through model gets it as sent. The Responses and Messages translations to chat have no field for effort, so on those APIs effort reaches a model only through a map or a family.

  
    curl
    Python
  
  

```bash
curl -si http://localhost:8088/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "acme",
    "reasoning_effort": "high",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Is 2^61 - 1 prime?"}]
  }'
```

  
  

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8088/v1", api_key="sk_...")
raw = client.chat.completions.with_raw_response.create(
    model="acme",
    reasoning_effort="high",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Is 2^61 - 1 prime?"}],
)
print(raw.headers.get("x-obleth-reasoning-effort"))  # the level served
reply = raw.parse()
```

chunks.title: Reasoning effort
chunks.heading: How a level is applied
chunks.text:
| `mode` | In the dashboard | What the model's server gets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `passthrough` (default) | **Pass through** | The request as the caller sent it, effort included |
| `mapped` | **Translate the four levels** | The caller's `reasoning_effort` and `reasoning` removed, and the level's fields merged in |
| `unsupported` | **This model has no effort control** | The caller's `reasoning_effort` and `reasoning` removed, so a server that would reject them never sees them |

A mapped model needs an action for every level:

- `{"send": {…}}` merges those fields into the request. Objects merge key by key and your value wins, so a caller's other `chat_template_kwargs` keys stay. `{"send": {}}` sends nothing, which leaves the server's own default.
- `{"use": "<level>"}` serves the request as another level, for a model that lacks this one, such as `"none": {"use": "low"}` on a model with no off switch. It must name a level that sends.
- `default_level` is the level served when the caller names none. Without it, such a request goes as it came.

chunks.title: Reasoning effort
chunks.heading: Keep members out of the listing
chunks.text:
A family stands for its members, but callers would still see `acme`, `acme-instruct` and `acme-think` in `/v1/models`. On each member's page, turn off **List in /v1/models** under **General** and save with the save bar. Or:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/models/$MODEL_ID/listing \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"listed": false}'
```

An unlisted model and its variants are left out of `/v1/models` and `/model/info` only. They still answer to every name and to `GET /v1/models/{id}`, stay `auto` candidates and can be family members. [Staging](/docs/models/model-lifecycle#stage-a-new-model) would also keep the model from `auto`.

chunks.title: Reasoning effort
chunks.heading: Model families
chunks.text:
A family is one name for several chat models, with the level picking which one answers: `acme-instruct` for none and `acme-think` for the rest, all called as `acme`. A request that names no level gets the family's default level.

On the Models page, open **Model families** › **Add family**. Enter the **Name** callers send, an optional **Description**, the model for each level under **Which model answers each level**, and **When a caller sets no effort**. The preview says where requests go. Or:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/model-families \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
