chunks.title: Management API
chunks.heading: Where keys are used
chunks.text:
`/usage/key-sources` and `/usage/key-rejections` take `since_ms` and `until_ms`
(default the last 24 hours, at most 31 days) and `tenant_id` or `key_id`.
`key_id` takes one key or up to 200 joined by commas (`key_id=a,b,c`), so one
call covers every key a person holds; a bad id, more than 200, or a
`key_id` that names no key (`key_id=`) is a `400`.
Key-rejections rows come newest `last_seen_ms` first: `limit` caps them
(default and most 10,000) and `per_key` caps any one key's rows (default
no cap), so one busy key can't push the others out. When rows were left
out, the response carries `x-obleth-truncated: true`; a caller that adds up
counts should narrow the query (`key_id`, `per_key`, a shorter window)
rather than trust a cut list. The read gives up after 10 seconds.
A key-sources row is one key, `network` (the IPv4 `/24` or IPv6 `/48`) and
`client_country`, with `requests`, `distinct_ips`, `last_seen_ms`,
`first_seen_ms` (the first time the key was ever seen from that country) and
`network_first_seen_ms` (as far back as client addresses are kept). At most
10,000 key-sources rows come back, with `x-obleth-truncated: true` when rows
were left out, and that read also gives up after 10 seconds. A
key-rejections row is one key, `reason`
(`disabled` or `ip_not_allowed`), `client_ip` and `client_country`, with
`count`, `first_seen_ms`, `last_seen_ms` and `sample_user_agent`. Both carry
`network_name`, the narrowest named network that holds the network or
address, or `null`. Requ

chunks.title: Postgres schema
chunks.heading: Migrations
chunks.text:
The gateway compiles the numbered files in `schema/postgres/` into its binary.
At start, under a Postgres advisory lock so replicas don't race, it runs each
file the `schema_migrations` table does not list, in order, and records it
there; a file and its record commit together. A database with no record (a new
one, or one last run by a gateway older than versioning, which re-ran every file
on each boot) runs every file once and then records them all. With
`OBLETH_SCHEMA_VERIFY_ONLY=true` the gateway changes nothing and refuses to
start while any file is unrecorded. A configuration backup covers
`fairshare_groups`, `tenants`, `api_keys`, `models`, `model_endpoints`,
`mcp_servers`, `model_families`, and `app_settings`.

| File | Adds |
| --- | --- |
| `0001_init.sql` | `fairshare_groups`, `tenants`, `api_keys`, `audit_log`, `models`, `model_health_checks`, `model_endpoints`, `managed_models`, `model_replicas`, `mcp_servers`, `app_settings` |
| `0002_tracing_flag.sql` | `tracing_enabled` on `tenants` and `api_keys` |
| `0003_guardrails_policy.sql` | `tenants.guardrails_policy` |
| `0005_managed_launcher_spec.sql` | `managed_models.launcher_spec` |
| `0006_recipes.sql` | `recipes` (`0004`, an earlier table it replaced, is retired) |
| `0007_replica_port_and_min_replicas.sql` | `model_replicas.port_base`, `managed_models.min_replicas` |
| `0008_managed_provision_error.sql` | `last_provision_error`, `last_provision_error_at` on `managed_models` |
| `0009_replica_cancel_requested.sql

chunks.title: Postgres schema
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Postgres holds configuration and the audit trail: tenants, keys, models,
endpoints, MCP servers, knowledge collections, Slurm specs, settings, and the
dashboard's login tables. Usage history lives in ClickHouse and hot state in
Redis; see [ClickHouse usage](/docs/reference/clickhouse-usage) and
[Redis layout](/docs/reference/redis-layout).

chunks.title: Prometheus metrics
chunks.heading: Example queries
chunks.text:
Client request rate by admission class:

```promql
sum by (admission) (rate(obleth_requests_total{admission!="boon"}[5m]))
```

P95 time to first token:

```promql
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(obleth_ttft_ms_bucket[5m])))
```

Response-cache hit rate:

```promql
sum(rate(obleth_cache_lookups_total{result="hit"}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(obleth_cache_lookups_total[5m]))
```

Upstream failures that reached clients:

```promql
sum(rate(obleth_upstream_attempts_total{outcome="exhausted"}[5m]))
```

Replicas in fairshare fallback:

```promql
sum(obleth_fairshare_shared_slots_mode{mode="fallback"}) > 0
```

Lost usage rows (alert on any increase):

```promql
increase(obleth_telemetry_rows_lost_total{outcome="dropped"}[15m]) > 0
```

chunks.title: Prometheus metrics
chunks.heading: Label values
chunks.text:
| Label | Values |
| --- | --- |
| `admission` | `fast`, `queued`, `rejected`, `boon` (a helper call made by a boon; always `2xx`) |
| `mode` | `shared`, `split`, `fallback` (shared slots on, Redis unreachable), `local` |
| `state` | `discovered`, `stale` (last value kept), `fallback` (static `max_in_flight` or default) |
| `outcome` (upstream) | `success`, `retry`, `conn_retry`, `timeout`, `failover`, `exhausted` |
| `result` (JWT) | `ok`, `unknown_issuer`, `bad_alg`, `unknown_kid`, `bad_signature`, `expired`, `not_yet_valid`, `bad_audience`, `bad_subject`, `malformed`, `not_provisioned`, `provision_failed` |
| `outcome` (knowledge) | `hit`, `miss`, `no_query`, `no_window`, `error` |
| `issuer_index` | Position in `OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS`, from 0 |

- **`boon` admission.** Exclude it to count client requests only:
  `obleth_requests_total{admission!="boon"}`.
- **Fairshare mode.** `split` enforces the configured limits divided by the
  live replica count; `local` is one live replica, or both
  `OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_SHARED_SLOTS` and `OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_REPLICA_AWARE` off. See
  [Multiple gateway replicas](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine#multiple-gateway-replicas).
- **Upstream outcomes.** `retry` has a configured retry left on the endpoint;
  `conn_retry` is the one extra attempt on a fresh connection after a
  connection-level failure; `failover` moves to the next endpoint;
  `exhausted` means the client got `502` or `504` and was not billed. See
  [Reliability](/docs/operate/rel

chunks.title: Prometheus metrics
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The gateway serves Prometheus text format at `/metrics` on the metrics listener
(`OBLETH_METRICS_LISTEN`, default `0.0.0.0:9091`). Every metric starts with
`obleth_`. Labels are low-cardinality: no tenant, key, model or collection is a
label. For per-tenant and per-model breakdowns, query the
[ClickHouse usage ledger](/docs/reference/clickhouse-usage).

Each gateway process exports its own values. With several replicas, `sum()`
across targets, except where the table says `max()`.

chunks.title: Prometheus metrics
chunks.heading: Scrape configuration
chunks.text:
```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: obleth
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["obleth:9091"]
```

The Compose `observability` profile ships this job (5 s interval) plus
Postgres, Redis, ClickHouse (`9363`) and HAProxy (`8404`). With the Prometheus
Operator, set `serviceMonitor.enabled: true` in the Helm chart; the
ServiceMonitor scrapes the `metrics` port every 5 s.

chunks.title: Redis layout
chunks.heading: Budget scripts
chunks.text:
Budget changes run as Lua scripts, so they are atomic across replicas.

| Script | Keys | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RESERVE` | bucket | Refills the bucket for the elapsed time, then reserves the estimate |
| `RESERVE_WITH_TERM` | bucket, term usage, term reserved | Checks committed plus reserved usage against the term cap, then reserves from the bucket and records the term reservation |
| `RECONCILE` | bucket | Applies estimate minus actual to the bucket |
| `TERM_USAGE_READ`, `TERM_USAGE_ADD` | term usage | Reads or adds to committed usage, resetting it when the period changes |
| `TERM_RECONCILE` | term usage, term reserved | Releases a reservation and commits the actual usage once |

The bucket refills at `tokens_per_minute / 60000` tokens per millisecond. An
estimate larger than the whole bucket is admitted when the bucket is full and
runs into debt down to `-capacity`. The term check runs first, so a request
refused for its term budget holds no bucket tokens.

| Condition | Status | Message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Per-minute bucket empty | `429` | `token budget exceeded` |
| Tenant term budget used up | `403` | `tenant term budget exhausted` |
| Key term budget used up | `403` | `api key term budget exhausted` |

A reservation that is never settled, for example after a crash, goes when its
10-minute key expires. All of a scope's reservations expire together, so brief
over-admission is possible, bounded by concurrency times the estimate. Commits
are always exact, and

chunks.title: Redis layout
chunks.heading: Eviction
chunks.text:
The bundled Helm Redis runs with `--maxmemory` (`redis.maxmemory`, default
`400mb`, under a 512Mi limit) and `--maxmemory-policy volatile-lru`, so only
keys with a TTL are evicted. Resolver entries, committed term usage, the
replica set, and the slot hashes are never evicted. When memory is full and
nothing is left to evict, Redis rejects writes, which the gateway treats as a
Redis failure under `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN`. The bundled Compose Redis sets no
memory limit. On your own Redis, use a `volatile-*` policy or `noeviction`: an
`allkeys-*` policy can evict resolver entries, which then return `401` until
the next re-warm.

chunks.title: Redis layout
chunks.heading: Invalidation channel
chunks.text:
Management API writes publish a target on `obleth:invalidate`. Each replica
drops the matching entry from its in-process cache (300-second TTL in front of
Redis).

| Payload | Drops |
| --- | --- |
| `*` | Every in-process entry |
| `model:<name>` | One model route |
| `mcp:<name>` | One MCP server |
| Anything else | The key with that hash |

After a resubscribe, a replica drops its whole in-process cache and re-warms
Redis, since messages sent while it was disconnected are lost.

chunks.heading: Key prefixes
chunks.text:

| `obleth:mcp:<name>` | String: resolved MCP server | None |
| `obleth:budget:<tenant_id>` | Hash: per-minute bucket `tokens`, `ts` (ms); absent when `tokens_per_minute` is 0 | 10 min, re-armed on every reserve and reconcile |

chunks.title: Redis layout
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Redis holds the data plane's hot state: resolver entries for keys, models, and
MCP servers, budget counters, shared fairshare slots, and a few caches.
Postgres stays the source of truth for configuration; see
[Postgres schema](/docs/reference/postgres-schema).

chunks.title: Redis layout
chunks.heading: Rebuilding from Postgres
chunks.text:
Resolver entries have no TTL, so the gateway keeps them in step with Postgres
four ways:

1. **Startup.** Each gateway pushes every key, model, and MCP server.
2. **Every write.** A Management API change updates or deletes the entry and
   publishes an invalidation. A delete whose eviction fails returns `502`.
3. **Re-warm.** Every `OBLETH_REDIS_REWARM_SECS` (300, at most 86400; `0` turns
   the timer off) and after every Redis reconnect, each gateway pushes a fresh
   snapshot and prunes stale entries.
4. **Resync.** `POST /api/v1/resync`, or **Reconcile cache** under
   Settings › Data and backups, runs the same push and prune on demand and
   returns counts per namespace.

The prune SCANs `obleth:key3:*`, `obleth:model:*`, and `obleth:mcp:*` and
deletes what the snapshot doesn't list, so a revoked key stops resolving. It
then re-reads Postgres and restores anything created during the pass. The
request path never reads Postgres: a key missing from Redis returns `401`
until the entry is written back.

chunks.title: Redis layout
chunks.heading: Requirements
chunks.text:
- **A password.** Redis holds API keys, so an open instance lets anyone who
  reaches it mint keys. Connect with
  `OBLETH_REDIS_URL=redis://:PASSWORD@host:6379`. The bundled Compose and Helm
  Redis always run with `--requirepass` (`REDIS_PASSWORD`, Helm
  `redis.password`).
- **One primary.** Redis Cluster and sharded keyspaces are not supported: the
  budget and slot scripts touch several keys in one call. A managed endpoint
  that fails over behind one address is fine.
- **Timeouts.** Each command waits at most `OBLETH_REDIS_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS`
  (250) and each connect `OBLETH_REDIS_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` (2000). A failed
  budget call follows `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN`; a failed key lookup returns `503`.

```bash
redis-cli -a "$REDIS_PASSWORD" --no-auth-warning --scan --pattern 'obleth:model:*'
```

chunks.title: Redis layout
chunks.heading: ResolvedKey
chunks.text:
Everything admission needs is in one JSON value, so the request path does no
relational lookup:

```json
{
  "key_id": "661f9500-...",
  "tenant_id": "550e8400-...",
  "tenant_name": "chatbot",
  "fairshare_group": "default",
  "group_weight": 100,
  "weight": 100,
  "tokens_per_minute": 50000,
  "max_in_flight": null,
  "disabled": false,
  "status": "active",
  "timezone": "UTC",
  "active_from": null,
  "active_until": null,
  "weekly_windows": null,
  "budget_tokens": null,
  "budget_cost_usd": null,
  "budget_period": null,
  "budget_started_at": null,
  "key_budget_tokens": null,
  "key_budget_cost_usd": null,
  "key_budget_period": null,
  "key_budget_started_at": null,
  "key_weight": 100,
  "key_max_in_flight": null,
  "end_user_fairshare": false,
  "background": false,
  "allowed_networks": [],
  "allowed_countries": [],
  "allowed_models": null,
  "internal": false,
  "tracing_enabled": false,
  "guardrails_policy": null,
  "compression_policy": null,
  "synthetic": false
}
```

`weight` and `max_in_flight` are the tenant's; `key_weight` and
`key_max_in_flight` are the key's share and cap inside each model's pool.
`end_user_fairshare` gives each end user the key names their own place in
those pools. `background` sends the key's requests to each model's background
pool.
`allowed_networks` and `allowed_countries` list the networks and countries the
key may be used from; both empty means anywhere. Entries moved from
`obleth:key:` to `obleth:key2:` in v2.7.0 with `allo

chunks.title: Redis layout
chunks.heading: Shared fairshare slots
chunks.text:
With `OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_SHARED_SLOTS` on (the default) and more than one replica
live, every fairshare limit is a set of cluster-wide slots. See
[Multiple gateway replicas](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine#multiple-gateway-replicas).

- **Replica set** (`obleth:gateway:replicas`): one member per process, its host
  name plus a random suffix, scored by heartbeat expiry on the Redis clock.
  Each replica heartbeats every `OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_REPLICA_HEARTBEAT_SECS` (5);
  a member expires after `OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_REPLICA_TTL_SECS` (15, at least
  twice the interval).
- **Totals** (`obleth:fairshare:slots`): `g` for every pool together,
  `p|<pool>`, `t|<pool>|<tenant>`, and `k|<pool>|<key>`, plus wait markers
  `w|<pool>` and `w` (global) holding the Redis time until which a replica
  waits, and `wa|<pool>`, until which a request there has waited too long for
  slots to be held ([session affinity](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine#session-affinity)).
- **Holdings** (`obleth:fairshare:held:<instance>`): the same count fields for
  one replica. Every script applies a holdings change to the totals too, so the
  totals are always their sum. Counts at zero are deleted.
- **Held slots** ([session affinity](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine#session-affinity)):
  each `obleth:fairshare:hold:<id>` holds the count fields of one slot kept for
  a session's next step, plus `h|<pool>`, which the totals also count, so a
  held slot still counts against every limit. `<id>` is the pool id, `

chunks.title: Auto routing
chunks.heading: Conversations
chunks.text:
By default each request is routed afresh. The classifier reads the newest user message, so a conversation that opens with small talk and moves on to code is routed as code from that turn on.

A follow-up with no topic of its own, such as "make it shorter" or "thanks", classifies as `general` alone. The user message before it then decides, up to three user messages back, so the follow-up keeps the conversation's topic. Those messages were classified when they were sent, so the answer usually comes from the cache.

Tool results are not user messages: every step of an agent's tool loop is classified on the request that started it. Spare capacity is scored on every request, so two turns on the same topic can still go to different models when one is busy. Without a classifier, the heuristics read the whole conversation.

chunks.title: Auto routing
chunks.heading: How a model is chosen
chunks.text:
The router works on the live model list, in three stages.

1. **Filter.** Models that cannot serve the request are dropped: disabled, [staged, deprecated or retired](/docs/models/model-lifecycle), unhealthy, not eligible for auto, outside the tenant's model list, too small a context window, or missing a capability it needs (tools, a JSON schema, images). A matching [boon](/docs/boons/overview) can stand in for vision or schema support.
2. **Tier (optional).** With difficulty tiering on, models too weak for the request's difficulty on its topics are dropped. This stage narrows the field but never empties it.
3. **Score.** Each survivor is scored on spare capacity, this request's estimated cost, and tag fit, then multiplied by its route bias.

At temperature `0` the top score wins, ties broken by name. Above `0`, the pick is sampled from the scores, spreading traffic across near-equal models.

chunks.title: Auto routing
chunks.heading: Keep a conversation on its model

chunks.title: Auto routing
chunks.heading: Long system prompts
chunks.text: The classifier also reads the system text. A client whose system message is mostly its own instructions (tool descriptions, display formats, an agent's rules) can have those decide the topic: a short brainstorming request behind a long tool preamble classifies as `coding`. Such a client sends `x-obleth-classify-system: <bytes>`, and the classifier reads only that many bytes at the end of the system text, where a client usually puts what the person wrote; `0` reads none of it. Anything that isn't a number is ignored, and the whole system text is read as before. [Simulating a decision](#simulating-a-decision) takes the same value as `classify_system`.

chunks.title: Auto routing
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
`"model": "auto"`
  Chat completions, Responses, Messages and Verdicts
  Settings › Routing, and the Playground's Router tab

chunks.title: Auto routing
chunks.heading: Per-model controls
chunks.text:
On a model's page, under **Routing**:

- **Eligible for auto** off keeps the model out of `auto`. Clients can still call it by name.
- **Route bias** multiplies the model's score (0.1 to 3.0, `1.0` neutral), to prefer or avoid a model without retagging or repricing it. A small bias such as `1.05` breaks a price tie.

```
spare     = 1 − in_flight / cap        # cap: the model's max in flight, or default_soft_cap (8)
cost      = 1 for the cheapest estimate of this request, 0 for the dearest
base      = capacity_weight × spare + cost_weight × cost
score     = tag_weight × tag_match + (1 − tag_weight) × base    # base alone when the request has no tags
final     = score × route_bias
```

The cost estimate uses the model's prices, the prompt estimate, and its observed average answer length (500 tokens until it has answered). `tag_match` is the share of the request's tags the model carries. Weights are clamped to 0 to 1 and `temperature` to 0 to 2.

Request difficulty comes from the `x-obleth-effort` header, else the classifier, else heuristics: a pasted stack trace is 3; phrases such as "root cause", or a prompt over 8,000 characters or 32,000 estimated tokens, are 2; anything else is 1.

A model's level on a tag follows `tier_source`: `hybrid` (default) derives it from price rank among the models with that tag unless the tag declares one; `derived` always uses price rank; `declared` uses declared levels, and a bare tag is 1.

Each classification reads one user message and the sy

chunks.title: Auto routing
chunks.heading: Send a request
chunks.text:
```bash
curl http://localhost:8088/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "auto", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a Python function that parses ISO-8601 durations."}]}'
```

The gateway picks a registered `chat` model before admission. The request is then queued, billed and logged under the model it picked. Other request types (embeddings, audio, images) must name a model.

With difficulty tiering on, send `x-obleth-effort: low`, `medium` or `high` to set the request's difficulty yourself.

If no model can serve the request, it fails with 503 `no model is available to satisfy the auto request`.

chunks.title: Auto routing
chunks.heading: Simulating a decision
chunks.text:
`POST /api/v1/router/simulate` runs the same code as the data plane against the live fleet and returns the decision without dispatching anything:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/router/simulate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prompt": "Prove the AM-GM inequality", "classify": true}'
```

Every body field is optional and overrides a live input: `prompt` or `messages`, `max_tokens`, `tenant_id`, `effort`, the capability flags, any weight, `busyness` (in-flight counts per model) and `uniform` (a fixed random draw). `classify: true` uses the live classifier instead of the heuristics, and reads a `messages` conversation turn by turn as a real request is read. The response lists the pick, the tags and difficulty with their source, every scored candidate, and each dropped model with its filter.

A traced request also records an `auto_route` span explaining the decision it served.

chunks.title: Auto routing
chunks.heading: Tags and difficulty
chunks.text:
Each model can carry tags from a fixed list, set in the **Routing** section of its page:

```
coding · general · reasoning · math · vision · long-context · fast · creative · writing
```

`creative` is fiction and verse. `writing` is any prose to draft or edit: emails, letters, essays, posts, and rewrites for tone, length or grammar.

A tag can carry a strength from 1 to 3, such as `coding:3`, for difficulty tiering.

A request's tags and difficulty come from the **classifier**, when one is set, or else from keyword heuristics. The heuristics find only `coding`, `math`, `vision`, `long-context` and `writing`.

The classifier is a small, fast chat model that you register like any other. It answers through [verdicts](/docs/clients/verdicts): one yes/no question per tag that the candidate models carry, plus a three-level difficulty score, each read from the first token's probabilities. The questions share a prompt prefix, so with prefix caching they cost about as much as one. A tag applies above p(yes) 0.5, at most three per request. `coding` and `writing` are never applied together: "write a SQL query" says yes to both, so only the stronger of the two is kept.

A classifier failure routes cheaper, never more expensive: unanswered tags are not applied, unanswered difficulty is 1, and with no answers the heuristics are used. A slow or missing classifier never blocks a request. Pick a model that answers directly, not a reasoning model. To build one, see [Training a classifier](/doc

chunks.title: Auto routing
chunks.heading: Try a prompt in the Playground
chunks.text:
The Playground's **Router** tab shows where a prompt would go without sending it, and how each candidate scored.

![The Playground Router tab: a coding prompt routed to qwen3-coder-30b, the classify, filter, score and pick stages, each candidate's score broken into capacity, cost and tag, and the router weight sliders](/dashboard/router.png)

The weight sliders change only the simulation, with live and draft scores side by side, until you choose **Apply to gateway…**. See [Playground](/docs/dashboard/playground#router).

chunks.title: Auto routing
chunks.heading: Tune it in Settings
chunks.text:
**Settings › Routing** shows readiness findings in its header (listed at the end of this page), then sets the classifier (on or off, its model and timeout), the [default model for Anthropic clients](/docs/clients/anthropic-messages-api), the default model for [verdicts](/docs/clients/verdicts), whether [conversations keep their model](#keep-a-conversation-on-its-model), and the weights, from a profile or by hand:

| Profile | Capacity | Cost | Tag | Tiering |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Balanced (default) | 0.6 | 0.4 | 0.5 | off |
| Best answer | 0.4 | 0.05 | 0.9 | on |
| Cost saver | 0.5 | 0.9 | 0.4 | off |

Changing any value makes the profile **Custom**. Changes reach every gateway within 15 seconds.

The same settings are `GET` and `PUT /api/v1/settings/auto-router`. A `PUT` changes only the fields it sends:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/auto-router \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"classifier_enabled": true, "classifier_model": "qwen3-0.6b", "classifier_timeout_ms": 250}'
```

`GET /api/v1/router/readiness` returns the readiness findings.

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Billing and traces
chunks.text:
Harm classifications are helper calls billed to the tenant as request type `guardrails_boon`. The pattern scanners make no model call. With tracing on, scans record `boon:guardrails_input` and `boon:guardrails_output` spans. See [Observability](/docs/operate/observability).

Gateway-owned probe keys are never scanned.

A `log_only` policy with output scanners also monitors streamed responses. The gateway copies each chunk to a decoder as it forwards it, so the client's stream is never delayed or changed, and scans once the stream ends.

- Server-sent events are reassembled across chunk boundaries, so a match split across chunks or tokens is still found.
- Content and reasoning deltas are collected separately, so interleaving can neither create nor hide a match.
- Responses driven by the [gateway tool loop](/docs/boons/tool-loop) are monitored across all their turns.
- Monitoring stops at 512 KiB of response body, or at an event that is not valid JSON. The gateway then logs a warning with the request id and the reason, and raises no alert for that response.

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Tenant. On when the tenant has a policy
  A tenant's page › Guardrails
  Nothing, except a guard-model call for the harm scanner

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Paths a block or redact policy refuses
chunks.text:
A policy that blocks or redacts refuses, with 400, requests it cannot enforce:

| Policy | Refused | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input | Completion `prompt` given as token ids | Token ids cannot be scanned |
| Input | A POST to a path the gateway does not recognise, such as `/tokenize` | Its body is not a format the scanners read |
| Output | `/v1/completions`, audio transcription and translation, unrecognised paths | Output scanners read chat responses only |

Endpoints that return no text (embeddings, images, speech, rerank, moderations, video jobs) are served. Use `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses` or `/v1/messages` for text. Under an input policy, embedding, rerank and moderation inputs go through every input scanner, so indexing a document that trips one returns 400. A `log_only` policy refuses nothing.

Output scanners read every choice of an answer (`n` above 1), with its content, reasoning, refusal, legacy `text` and tool-call arguments. A redacted answer loses its log-probabilities, since they spell the text out again. An answer the gateway cannot read is refused with `502 the response could not be checked against the content policy` instead of passed on.

Output scanning that blocks or redacts needs the whole answer, so the gateway asks the backend for a non-streaming response and replays it as a stream to a client that asked for one. It also skips the [response cache](/docs/models/response-cache) for that request.

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Scanners and actions
chunks.text:
| Scanner | How it works | Catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `prompt_injection` | Patterns, in the gateway | Jailbreak and instruction-override attempts |
| `pii` | Patterns, in the gateway | Social security, email, phone and card numbers |
| `ban_keywords` | Your word list, in the gateway | Whole words from the list, any case |
| `harm` | One yes/no question to the guard model | Harmful content |

What happens on a match:

- **`block`** refuses with 400. On input, `request blocked by content policy` is returned before admission, so nothing reaches the model and nothing is billed. On output, `response blocked by content policy`; the answer was already generated, so the request is billed its real usage.
- **`redact`** masks the matches and lets the request continue. Only `pii` and `ban_keywords` can be redacted; `prompt_injection` and `harm` still block.
- **`log_only`** changes nothing and raises an alert, keyed `guardrails_input_<tenant_id>` or `guardrails_output_<tenant_id>` (with `_harm_` for a harm verdict). See [Alerting](/docs/operate/alerting).

The `x-obleth-boons: off` header turns off boons only. It does not skip a tenant's guardrails.

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: Turn on guardrails for a tenant
chunks.text:
On **Tenants**, open the tenant and go to **Guardrails**.

**FERPA / personal info** redacts personal information both ways. **Prompt-injection defense** blocks injection attempts before they reach the model. **Monitor only** raises an alert when personal information appears and never blocks. Or choose the action and scanners yourself.

The harmful-content scanner asks a model you choose. Its backend must return logprobs.

The policy applies to every key of the tenant from the next request, whatever model it calls. Clients change nothing.

Through the Management API, `PATCH /api/v1/tenants/{id}/guardrails` sets the policy, and `{"policy": null}` removes it:

```bash
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID/guardrails \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"policy": {"action": "redact", "input_scanners": ["pii", "prompt_injection"],
       "output_scanners": ["pii"], "guard_model": null, "ban_keywords": [], "fail_open": true}}'
```

| Field | Values |
| --- | --- |
| `action` | `block`, `redact` or `log_only` |
| `input_scanners` | Any of `prompt_injection`, `pii`, `ban_keywords`, `harm` |
| `output_scanners` | Any of `pii`, `ban_keywords`, `harm` |
| `guard_model` | The model for `harm`; required when `harm` is used |
| `ban_keywords` | The tenant's word list for `ban_keywords` |
| `fail_open` | `true` (default) passes content through when a scanner fails; `false` refuses with 503 |

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: What is scanned
chunks.text:
Input scanners run on every request from the tenant's keys, on every path:

- In `messages`, every message except the model's own turns and tool output: `user`, `system`, `developer`, and messages with no role. A content part's text is read whatever the part's type is called, or with no type.
- The text fields of other requests: `prompt` (completions, image generation), `input` (embeddings, moderations, speech), and `query` and `documents` (rerank).
- The text fields of multipart forms, such as the prompt of an image edit or a transcription. A redaction is written back into the forwarded form.
- `POST /v1/verdicts`: the state and every question, before admission.

`/v1/responses` and `/v1/messages` are translated to chat and scanned as chat. Spellings with extra or trailing slashes are handled like their `/v1` forms.

Not scanned: uploaded files (audio, images, video reference frames), token-id inputs, and tool output and assistant turns in `messages`. A request with nothing to scan is passed through without a guard-model call.

For a tenant with an input policy, the [auto router's classifier](/docs/routing/auto-model-routing#tags-and-difficulty) is not called, because it would read the prompt before the scan.

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.heading: When a scanner fails
chunks.text:
The `harm` scanner reads p(unsafe) from the guard model's first token and flags content above 0.5. A reply that puts almost no probability on either answer, or no reply at all, is a scanner error, and `fail_open` decides:

- `fail_open: true` (default) passes the content through unchanged.
- `fail_open: false` refuses with `503 content policy scanner unavailable`.

This changed in v2.0.0. Earlier versions counted any guard-model reply that did not start with UNSAFE as safe, so a policy with `fail_open: false` let requests through when the guard model did not answer. It now blocks them. Check that your guard model's backend returns logprobs before upgrading a fail-closed policy.

chunks.title: Training a classifier
chunks.heading: Adapt it to your own task
chunks.text:
Only the task definition changes. A task supplies:

1. **The questions**: your own booleans, choices and scores, such as inclusion criteria or severity levels.
2. **The rendering**: the exact strings production will send.
3. **The corpus**: text from your domain.
4. **The probe set**: a handful of inputs with certain answers, for stage 0 and the discrimination check.

The teacher audit, the soft-label ensemble, the loss and the checks carry over unchanged.

If you use your own operational data instead of public corpora, confirm that its data classification permits it, remove identifiers, and get consent where the text came from people. Distillation copies what is in the corpus into a model you keep.

chunks.title: Training a classifier
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Two or three good judge models behind the gateway
  A sub-1B model that answers in one token
  Training runs in your own tooling; the gateway serves the teachers and the result

Much judgment work is classification: is this ticket urgent, does this abstract meet the criteria, which model should serve this request. A small model asked cold is an unreliable judge. Distillation closes the gap: large **teacher** models label text through [`POST /v1/verdicts`](/docs/clients/verdicts), and a small **student** learns to reproduce their probabilities.

The running example is the [auto router's classifier](/docs/routing/auto-model-routing#tags-and-difficulty): one yes/no question per routing tag (nine) plus a three-level difficulty score. The same recipe works for any verdicts task.

chunks.title: Training a classifier
chunks.heading: Stage 0: audit the teachers
chunks.text:
Do not skip this stage. A large model is not automatically a good judge.

Send a handful of inputs whose answer is not in doubt through `/v1/verdicts`, and compare p(yes) on categories that fit with categories that do not. From one fleet, on the routing task:

| Model | p(yes) when it fits | When it does not | Margin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `glm-5-3` | 0.994 | 0.116 | **0.878** |
| `gemma4-31b-it` | 0.700 | 0.000 | **0.700** |
| `qwen3-235b-a22b-instruct-2507` | 0.750 | 0.171 | **0.579** |
| `gpt-oss-120b` | 0.275 | 0.142 | 0.133 |
| `llama4-maverick-17b` | 0.009 | 0.047 | −0.038 |

Size predicts little. Use three teachers from the top band if you can; with two, one odd judgment moves a label by half its range.

Prefer instruction-tuned models to reasoning models. A verdict reads the first token, and a reasoning model's judgment lives in the thinking it skips: `gpt-oss-120b` answered "no" at p=0.89 to "is this math?" on a grade-school math problem.

chunks.title: Training a classifier
chunks.heading: Stage 1: generate soft labels
chunks.text:
Stream prompts from a corpus and ask each teacher every question in one `/v1/verdicts` call. The router shows the classifier one user message at a time, so label single user messages, short follow-ups included. The routing example used four openly licensed datasets: `allenai/WildChat-1M` (real traffic), `HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k` (variety), `ise-uiuc/Magicoder-OSS-Instruct-75K` (coding) and `openai/gsm8k` (math).

- **Keep the probabilities, not the top answer.** A label of `p(coding) = 0.62` teaches the student to be unsure where the teachers were, which makes its confidence worth thresholding on.
- **Filter per question, not per input.** Teachers often agree on eight questions and split on the ninth. Dropping the whole input throws away eight good labels.
- **Check the averages per source.** Math prompts should score high on `math`, code prompts on `coding`; a flat table means the teachers are not discriminating. One poor teacher pushed rejections to 83% of inputs; two audited teachers, to about 14%.

Each input costs one prefill plus one output token per question per teacher, because the questions share a prompt prefix on one pinned backend replica. Run labeling under its own tenant at weight `1`: it uses capacity nobody else wants and loses every contended slot to interactive traffic. See [Priority boost](/docs/sharing/priority-boost).

chunks.title: Training a classifier
chunks.heading: Stage 2: distill
chunks.text:
Train the student on the KL divergence between its distribution over the answer labels and the teachers'. That is the quantity the gateway reads at inference, so training and serving optimize the same number.

- **Train on the exact production prompt.** Render training examples exactly as the gateway sends them (see [Verdicts](/docs/clients/verdicts#how-it-works)), and pin your renderer to that format with a test, so a prompt change without new training data fails the build.
- **Ship a plain chat template.** A template that opens a `<think>` block puts a thinking token, not an answer, first. Use plain ChatML for a one-token judge.
- **Reward mass on the labels.** Confidence is discounted by the probability that falls outside the answer labels. A stock Qwen3-0.6B puts about 4e-11 of its first-token mass on the labels; an extra loss term pulls that toward 1 within a few dozen steps.

A full fine-tune of a 0.6B model over about 100,000 inputs takes a few hours on one accelerator.

chunks.title: Training a classifier
chunks.heading: Stage 3: evaluate and deploy
chunks.text:
Measure, in order: **discrimination** (the p(yes) margin, as in stage 0; below 0.5 the model is unusable), **agreement** with the teachers on held-out inputs, and **calibration** (expected calibration error, Brier score).

Serve the student like any other chat model and register it:

```bash
vllm serve runs/model-v1 --served-model-name my-judge --max-model-len 2048
```

For routing, point the classifier at it:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/auto-router \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"classifier_enabled": true, "classifier_model": "my-judge"}'
```

Evaluate the served model, not only the checkpoint. [Simulate](/docs/routing/auto-model-routing#simulating-a-decision) with `"classify": true` compares decisions without dispatching anything. Keep the previous classifier registered until the new one has served real traffic for a day; switching back is one `PUT`.

Watch `classifier_timeout_ms` after switching. A timeout silently falls back to the keyword heuristics, visible as `tag_source: "heuristic"` in a simulate response. Warm classifications of nine questions took 125 to 160 ms on one fleet, so the default 250 ms can be tight for the first call to a cold replica.

chunks.title: Training a classifier
chunks.heading: When it is worth doing
chunks.text:
Distill when a judgment is high-volume, narrow and repeated. Run it a hundred times and you can prompt a large model; a hundred thousand times, train a small one. You need no labeled data: the teachers generate the labels.

Models asked cold fail in measurable ways. One 30B model answered yes to every category (p(yes) 0.84 to 0.98, including `vision` for text-only prompts), and from a lettered list put about 0.7 on whichever option came first. A student learns from thousands of confident "no" examples, which prompting cannot supply.

chunks.title: Accounts and sign-in
chunks.heading: Add OIDC sign-in
chunks.text:
OIDC signs people in to Chat. It doesn't change how Chat reaches the gateway: by default Chat still signs its own token for each person, so the gateway doesn't need to trust your provider (see [Connect the gateway](/docs/run-chat/connect-gateway)). Any provider with an OIDC discovery document works. [Sign-in setups](/docs/run-chat/sign-in-setups) has complete settings for passwords only, Globus, CILogon and Keycloak.

Local sign-in stays available alongside it unless you turn it off. Set all three of issuer, client ID and secret, or none of them:

```bash
OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_ISSUER=https://idp.example.edu/realms/research
OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=obleth-chat
OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=…
OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_ALLOW_SIGNUP=false
```

Register `<OBLETH_CHAT_ORIGIN>/api/auth/oidc/callback` as the exact redirect URI.

Identity is keyed by issuer and subject. Chat never links accounts by email address. To connect an existing account to an identity-provider user, link the subject in **People**. With `OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_ALLOW_SIGNUP=true`, anyone who can sign in to that issuer gets a standard account on first sign-in.

A sign-in through the provider lasts until its ID token expires, and at most `OBLETH_CHAT_SESSION_HOURS`. Check your provider's ID-token lifetime: Keycloak's default is 5 minutes, which signs people out of Chat every 5 minutes. Raise it for Chat's client, or [forward provider tokens](/docs/run-chat/forward-tokens), where Chat refreshes them instead.

Accounts created at sig

chunks.title: Accounts and sign-in
chunks.heading: Add people
chunks.text:
There is no public registration. In **Settings › Administration › People**, create an account and give it one of:

- **An invitation link.** A one-use, time-limited link you copy and send to the person; they choose their own password. Chat sends no email.
- **A temporary password.** The person must change it before they can chat.

From the same list you can promote and demote administrators, disable an account, send a recovery link, revoke a person's sessions and link an OIDC identity. The last enabled administrator can't be demoted or disabled.

**Settings › Administration › Groups** holds groups for model access and sharing; see [Models, groups and limits](/docs/run-chat/models-and-limits).

chunks.title: Accounts and sign-in
chunks.heading: Map identity-provider groups
chunks.text:
Chat can put people into its own groups from a claim in their ID token:

```bash
OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_GROUP_CLAIM=groups
OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_GROUP_MAP={"research-staff":["<chat group UUID>"]}
OBLETH_CHAT_DEFAULT_GROUP_IDS=<chat group UUID>
```

The map turns claim values into Chat group UUIDs, and Chat reconciles only the memberships the mapping created; ones you add by hand stay. `OBLETH_CHAT_DEFAULT_GROUP_IDS` adds every new local or OIDC account to those groups. No mapping grants the administrator role.

chunks.title: Accounts and sign-in
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Settings › Administration › People
  Username and password
  OIDC
  None, unless OIDC allows it

chunks.title: Accounts and sign-in
chunks.heading: Sessions
chunks.text:
Sessions are opaque HttpOnly cookies, stored hashed in Postgres and valid for `OBLETH_CHAT_SESSION_HOURS` (12 by default). People see and revoke their own sessions in **Settings › Personal › Security**. Changing a password revokes older sessions, and disabling an account ends its access on every replica. Ending a session also ends the personal API tokens and workspace preview access made in it. A response that's streaming rechecks its session every 15 seconds.

Passwords are hashed with Argon2id and must be at least 12 characters.

chunks.title: Accounts and sign-in
chunks.heading: Sign-in throttling
chunks.text:
Limits are shared across replicas:

- Each client address gets `OBLETH_CHAT_LOGIN_RATE_PER_MINUTE` (300) sign-in, password-change and activation requests a minute. OIDC redirects have their own budget of the same size.
- Each account gets 10 password attempts a minute per client. A correct password refunds its own attempt.
- 50 failures a minute on one account stop only the clients that are failing on it. A client with no failures on that account in the last 10 minutes counts against a separate limit of 50 a minute, so failures from other addresses can't lock someone out, and rotating addresses still adds at most 50 guesses a minute.
- A refused client stays refused until it has been quiet for 10 minutes since its last counted attempt. Chat logs when an account reaches either limit.

Behind a reverse proxy, every client looks like the proxy until you trust it; see [Reverse proxies](/docs/run-chat/reverse-proxies).

Authorization code with PKCE, state and nonce, ID-token signature, issuer and audience, and a one-use transaction bound to the browser and stored in Postgres. Sessions are capped by the ID token's expiry and by `OBLETH_CHAT_SESSION_HOURS`. Chat keeps no refresh tokens and signing out ends only the Chat session, except in [forward mode](/docs/run-chat/forward-tokens), where Chat keeps and refreshes them and revokes them at sign-out. Linking an identity revokes the account's pending invitation and recovery links.

Role, account, model, group and limit changes appear

chunks.title: Branding
chunks.heading: A banner
chunks.text:
A banner is one line at the top of every page, for an announcement or a note such as that Chat is in development. An administrator sets it in **Settings › Administration › System**, not in `site.config.js`, so it changes without a restart. People see a change the next time they load Chat.

| Setting | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Text | Up to 200 characters on one line. The top bar shows what fits, and the rest when someone points at it. Blank shows no banner |
| Link | Optional text and a web or `mailto:` address, shown after the text. It opens in a new tab |
| Style | **Notice** is quiet; **Warning** is amber |
| Show it on the sign-in page | Also shows it as a strip above the sign-in page, to anyone who opens Chat |
| Let people close it | Adds a close button. A closed banner stays closed in that browser until its text or link changes |

Changes appear in **Activity** as settings changes.

chunks.title: Branding
chunks.heading: Change the branding
chunks.text:
Start from the file the image ships, so you keep every setting and its comment:

    ```bash
    mkdir -p branding/assets
    docker run --rm --entrypoint cat <chat-image> /app/branding/site.config.js > branding/site.config.js
    ```

  
  
    Change the name, text, logo and links. Put your images in `branding/assets` and refer to them as `./assets/custom/<file>`.
  
  
    Mount the file at `/app/branding/site.config.js` and the images at `/app/branding/assets/custom`, as shown below. Later edits need only a page reload.
  

  
    Kubernetes
    Compose
  
  

```bash
kubectl -n obleth-chat create configmap chat-branding \
  --from-file=site.config.js=branding/site.config.js \
  --from-file=branding/assets/
```

```yaml
# In the Deployment's pod spec
volumes:
  - name: branding
    configMap: { name: chat-branding }
containers:
  - name: chat
    volumeMounts:
      - { name: branding, mountPath: /app/branding/site.config.js, subPath: site.config.js, readOnly: true }
      - { name: branding, mountPath: /app/branding/assets/custom, readOnly: true }
```

A `subPath` mount doesn't pick up ConfigMap changes, so restart the Deployment after updating it.

  
  

```yaml
# Under the obleth-chat service
volumes:
  - ./branding/site.config.js:/app/branding/site.config.js:ro
  - ./branding/assets:/app/branding/assets/custom:ro
```

chunks.title: Branding
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
site.config.js
  On the next page load
  Obleth Chat, with the Obleth mark

Chat reads its branding from `site.config.js`, which it serves next to the web app at `/site.config.js`. Every visitor can read the file, so never put a secret in it.

chunks.title: Branding
chunks.heading: What you can set
chunks.text:
| Setting | Default | What it changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `siteName` | `Obleth Chat` | The name beside the logo, the browser title and the sign-in footer. A `\n` stacks a long name beside the logo, such as `'Research\nComputing'`; elsewhere it reads as one line |
| `siteSubtitle` | empty | A small line under the name |
| `assistantName` | `Assistant` | The name on the model's replies |
| `description` | A sentence about Chat | The page's meta description |
| `logo.light`, `logo.dark`, `logo.alt` | The Obleth mark | The logo on light and dark themes. One path covers both; two empty paths give a text-only brand |
| `favicon.light`, `favicon.dark` | The Obleth mark | The browser tab icon. Empty paths use a neutral chat icon |
| `icons.greeting`, `icons.assistant`, `icons.loading` | `chat` | Built-in icons by name, such as `book` or `bolt`. `''` hides one |

chunks.title: Connect the gateway
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The gateway URL and a signing key
  Chat as a trusted JWT issuer
  obleth gateway only
  5 minutes
  None

Chat works only with the obleth gateway. It has no setting for an API key or another provider, and every request carries a per-person token, so pointing `OBLETH_CHAT_GATEWAY_URL` at an OpenAI-compatible server, LiteLLM or vLLM doesn't work. Put those behind the gateway as model backends instead; see [Inference gateways](/docs/models/inference-gateways).

Chat never holds a gateway API key. By default it signs a five-minute RS256 token for each request, whose subject is the person's Chat account ID, and only Chat's server sends it. The gateway checks the token against Chat's public keys and accounts for the request under that identity, so every person has their own usage, budget and fairshare position. See [Identity tokens](/docs/clients/identity-tokens) for the gateway side.

Because the gateway trusts Chat, not your identity provider, Chat and the gateway don't need the same identity provider. Chat can use passwords or any OIDC provider; see [Sign-in setups](/docs/run-chat/sign-in-setups) for examples. To send each person's own identity-provider token instead, see [Forward provider tokens](/docs/run-chat/forward-tokens).

chunks.title: Connect the gateway
chunks.heading: Set it up
chunks.text:
[`setup.sh`](/docs/run-chat/install) makes the signing key, configures Chat and prints the gateway entry, so with it only the last two steps are left: trust Chat in the gateway and check it.

  
    Generate a dedicated RSA key outside source control:

    ```bash
    umask 077
    openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 \
      -out /secure/path/obleth-chat-signing.pem
    ```

  
  
    Set the gateway's origin (without `/v1`) and the key file. Both are needed, or neither, unless you [forward provider tokens](/docs/run-chat/forward-tokens).

    ```bash
    OBLETH_CHAT_GATEWAY_URL=http://obleth-gateway:8080
    OBLETH_CHAT_GATEWAY_SIGNING_KEY_FILE=/secure/path/obleth-chat-signing.pem
    OBLETH_CHAT_GATEWAY_ISSUER=https://chat.example.edu
    OBLETH_CHAT_GATEWAY_AUDIENCE=obleth
    ```

    The issuer defaults to `OBLETH_CHAT_ORIGIN` and the audience to `obleth`. Restart Chat; it publishes its public key at `/.well-known/jwks.json`.

  
  
    **Merge** this entry into the gateway's existing `OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS` array (Helm: `obleth.jwtIssuers`), keeping any other issuers:

    ```json
    {
      "issuer": "https://chat.example.edu",
      "jwks_url": "http://obleth-chat:8085/.well-known/jwks.json",
      "audience": "obleth",
      "algorithms": ["RS256"],
      "subject_claim": "sub",
      "identity_claims": ["username"],
      "tenant": "chat-users",
      "jit_provision": true
    }
    ```

    Pick an existing tenant that has the models, budgets

chunks.title: Connect the gateway
chunks.heading: What Chat sends
chunks.text:
- **Discovery**: `GET /v1/models`, live, filtered by the models each person may use.
- **Generation**: `POST /v1/chat/completions` with the stored history, streaming with usage chunks. Chat records `x-obleth-session-id` and `x-obleth-request-id` with each reply, so you can find its trace in the gateway's request logs.
- **Effort**: the thinking effort as `reasoning_effort`. With **Auto**, Chat sends `model: "auto"` and tells the router how hard the request is: None and Low send `x-obleth-effort: low`, High sends `high`, and Medium leaves the router to judge.
- **Embeddings**: for [Knowledge](/docs/run-chat/enable-knowledge), `POST /v1/embeddings` with the embedding model.
- **Identity**: only the token in `Authorization`. Chat sends no `x-obleth-end-user` header or `user` field, because each person already has their own identity key.

Stopping a response cancels the upstream request. Chat follows no redirects from the gateway, so a bearer token can't be sent somewhere unexpected.

To show administrators a link to the gateway's dashboard, set `OBLETH_CHAT_ADMIN_GATEWAY_URL` to its public URL.

Every Chat replica must use the same signing key and issuer. Chat publishes one key at a time; staged rotation with two keys isn't implemented yet. Without `OBLETH_CHAT_SECRET_KEY_FILE`, saved [connection](/docs/chat/connections) tokens are encrypted with a key derived from the signing key, so replacing it makes them unreadable and people enter them again. Set a secret key first and thos

chunks.title: Decisions
chunks.heading: Another endpoint
chunks.text:
Enter the address that takes `POST` requests in the verdicts format. An address with no path, or one ending in `/v1`, gets `/v1/verdicts` added, so another obleth gateway's base URL works as it is. Any other path is used as given.

- **Key.** Sent as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. Chat encrypts it with `OBLETH_CHAT_SECRET_KEY_FILE`, so saving one needs that file. Leave the field blank to keep the saved key. If the secret key changes, Chat can't read the saved key and says so rather than asking without it.
- **Redirects** aren't followed, so the key goes only to the address you entered.
- People's own gateway tokens never go to another endpoint.

chunks.title: Decisions
chunks.heading: Choose where to ask
chunks.text:
The **Decisions** card shows where questions go now.
  
  
    **This gateway**, **Another endpoint** with its URL and key, or **Off**.
  
  
    **Check** asks a sample question with the values in the form, saved or not, and says which model answered and how long it took. **Save** applies them on every replica.
  

| Endpoint | Who asks | Whose usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| This gateway | The person the question is for, with their gateway identity | That person's, under their limits |
| Another endpoint | Chat, with the key you enter | The key's |
| Off | Nobody | None |

chunks.title: Decisions
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Settings › Administration › System › Decisions
  The gateway, as each person
  Verdicts, `POST /v1/verdicts`
  Research checks

Chat asks these questions in the [verdicts](/docs/clients/verdicts) format: a state, typed questions, and a probability for every answer. Any service that accepts that request can answer, so the gateway is one choice among several. When decisions are off or an endpoint fails, the feature that asked goes on without an answer.

chunks.title: Decisions
chunks.heading: The model
chunks.text: Leave **Model** blank to let the endpoint choose. On obleth that's the model under **Settings › Routing › Verdicts**, or `auto` when none is set. The model must return token probabilities (`logprobs`): self-hosted servers such as vLLM, SGLang and llama.cpp do, and many hosted APIs don't.

chunks.title: Decisions
chunks.heading: What uses decisions
chunks.text:
| Feature | What it asks | Turn it off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Run checks](/docs/chat/research#run-checks) | Whether a finished run really tested its idea | Untick **Check research runs** |
| [Placement checks](/docs/chat/research#placement-checks) | Whether a new experiment builds on its parent, or is another option of the round under the baseline | Untick **Check where new experiments go** |
| [Report checks](/docs/chat/research#report-checks) | Whether comparisons and causes in a research reply follow from its runs | Untick **Check research reports** |
| [Paper sections](/docs/chat/research#papers) | Which section of a paper answers what research is looking for | Untick **Pick sections of papers** |
| [Memory checks](/docs/chat/memory#what-chat-remembers) | Whether each memory Chat would add or change lasts beyond the chat it came from | Untick **Check memories before they are kept** |
| [Cluster changes](/docs/run-chat/enable-connections#changes-a-decision-may-allow) | Whether a job submission, a new file or a move on a cluster was asked for, stays within the request, keeps existing data and is easy to undo, so it can run without the Allow card | Untick **Let decisions allow changes the person asked for** |

The placement and report checks act only on a no the answer is at least 50% sure of. A memory is kept only on a yes over 50%; one the model leaves unanswered is dropped, and when no answer comes back at all the chat is read again later. An endpoint that doesn't send

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Auto mode
chunks.text: By default a tool that may change something waits for the person's **Allow**. A person can switch a chat to **Auto mode**, where every tool runs without asking; research chats start that way so long runs don't stall. Calls still carry that person's own token. Set `OBLETH_CHAT_AUTO_MODE=off` to remove the switch for everyone; chats already in Auto mode then ask again.

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Bring job output back
chunks.text:
slurmrestd can't serve files, so the model sees a job's state and exit code but not what it printed. With **Bring job output back** ticked on the cluster, it can read that too. The option appears when Chat has [object storage](/docs/run-chat/enable-knowledge) (`OBLETH_CHAT_S3_*`).

- **How it works.** Chat gives each job it submits a link that can upload one object to that storage, valid for 7 days. The job runs the person's script unchanged and, as it ends, uploads the last 1 MiB of its output file with `curl`. It also does this when it is cancelled or runs out of time, and keeps the script's exit code. The model reads it with **Job output**.
- **What the cluster needs.** The compute nodes must reach the storage endpoint and have `curl`. Check with `srun -t 1 curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' <endpoint>`: any HTTP code means they can.
- **Output files.** Chat follows `--output` patterns with `%j`, `%x`, `%u`, `%A`, `%a`, `%N` and `%%`. A job with any other pattern runs as before, without sending its output.
- **Retention.** Chat keeps each job's output for 30 days, and removes it sooner when the cluster or the person is removed.

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Changes a decision may allow
chunks.text:
Every change a cluster tool makes waits for **Allow**, unless a [decision](/docs/run-chat/decisions) can vouch for it first. Only changes that add something are put to one: a Slurm job submission, writing a new file, and moving a file. The decision answers four questions from the person's own messages and the card the person would have seen: did they ask for this action, does it stay within what they asked, does it leave existing data as it is, and could they undo it. A sure yes to all four (over 70% each) runs the call without the card, and the step shows **allowed by a decision** with the answers kept in the reply's activity. A doubt on any question, an unanswered one, or no answer at all shows the card as before.

Trashing, overwriting, cancelling a job, Kubernetes apply and delete, device actions and the tools of MCP servers always ask. The judge never sees what the model read from files, pages or tool results, so text found there cannot talk it into an action, and the model is told that text from files on a cluster is data, not instructions. Turn it off with **Let decisions allow changes the person asked for** in Admin › System › Decisions.

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Choose what people can add
chunks.text:
Connections are on whenever Chat is connected to the gateway and has `OBLETH_CHAT_SECRET_KEY_FILE` or a gateway signing key. `OBLETH_CHAT_CONNECTIONS` narrows them:

| Value | People can add | Pages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `all` (default) | MCP servers, Slurm clusters, Kubernetes clusters and devices | **Settings › MCP servers**, **Compute › Clusters** and **Compute › Devices** |
| `mcp` | MCP servers only | **Settings › MCP servers** |
| `off` | Nothing | Neither. The composer has no **Tools** button |

Restart Chat after changing it. Connections saved under a wider setting are kept but hidden, and their tools aren't offered.

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Devices
chunks.text: A device is a person's own board, reached through their browser over Web Serial; Chat's pods never talk to it. Each call is written to the `device_calls` table (migration `073`), the browser tab showing the chat carries it out and posts the result, and the reply goes on. Nothing is set up on the server beyond `all`, and there is nothing to share: a device can't be shared with everyone. Firmware for flashing comes from the chat's workspace, so flashing needs [workspaces](/docs/run-chat/enable-workspaces).

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Network access
chunks.text:
- Chat's own pods must reach each server. Under a NetworkPolicy, allow egress to slurmrestd, the Kubernetes API servers and MCP servers.
- People's own connections must use `https` and public addresses. Chat resolves the host itself and refuses loopback, private and link-local ranges. An administrator's own connections are exempt, as shared ones are, since an administrator could share the same address. `OBLETH_CHAT_CONNECTIONS_ALLOW_PRIVATE=true` lifts the rule for everyone, for development only.
- Shared connections, added by administrators, may use `http` and internal addresses.

- Tokens are encrypted at rest with XChaCha20-Poly1305, under `OBLETH_CHAT_SECRET_KEY_FILE` when it's set and otherwise under a key derived from the gateway signing key. With both set, Chat moves tokens to the secret key at startup and every five minutes, so the signing key can later be replaced or removed. Without a secret key, replacing the signing key makes saved tokens unreadable, and people enter them again. Adding the secret key is one-way: a configuration without it can't read the moved tokens.
- A person's token for a shared connection is bound to both the connection and their account, so it can't be decrypted for anyone else.
- Removing a shared connection deletes everyone's tokens for it. Removing your own token takes that connection out of your chats.
- Creating, changing and removing shared connections is recorded in **Settings › Administration › Activity**.
- Each account can have up t

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A secret key or the gateway signing key
  On by default; OBLETH_CHAT_CONNECTIONS
  Each person's own token

Connections give the model tools from MCP servers, Slurm clusters, Kubernetes clusters and [devices](/docs/chat/devices) plugged into people's computers. What people see is in [Connections](/docs/chat/connections). This page covers what you set up as the operator.

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Reach files on the cluster
chunks.text:
slurmrestd submits jobs and reads their state, but it cannot show a file. With **Reach files on the cluster** ticked, the model can list, find, read, search and measure each person's own files on the cluster, write and move files, and move files to a trash directory, as that person.

- **How it works.** The first files call in a while submits a small job (1 CPU, 1 GB) as the person, with their own Slurm token. The job runs a Python program that Chat ships inside the batch script. It connects out to Chat, asks for the chat's file operations one at a time, carries each out under the directories the cluster allows, and posts the result. It exits once idle for 20 minutes, at its time limit, or when Chat ends the session; the next call starts a new one. Waiting costs nothing: the job holds one request to Chat at a time, up to 50 seconds, and Chat wakes it through a Postgres notification the moment a call is filed. Nothing on the cluster listens, and no account of Chat's own reads anyone's files. A job whose account turns out not to be the person's ends the session at once.
- **Settings.** The **partition** and **QoS** for the session job: pick a small one that starts a 1-CPU job within seconds, so the first call is quick. The **session length** is the job's time limit (8 hours by default). The **directories the model may reach** are absolute paths or `~`, separated by commas, with `$USER` standing for the Slurm user; `~` alone by default, `~,/scratch/$USER` for a scratch space (`~

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Secrets
chunks.text: People can save named values under **Settings › Secrets**: a device's console password, a key a tool needs. A value is sealed with the same key as connection tokens and opens only for its owner's own browser, through `GET /api/secrets/{name}/value`, when a device tool they allowed needs it; the model is told the names, never a value. Secrets come with connections and need nothing of their own. Migration `074` adds the table; each person can keep up to 50.

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Share a Kubernetes cluster
chunks.text:
In **Compute › Clusters**, choose **Add a cluster**, then **Kubernetes cluster**. Enter the API server URL and, for a private CA, the certificate from `certificate-authority-data` (base64-decoded). Tick **Share with everyone**.
  
  
    Each person needs their own token: a service account per person, or a token your identity provider issues. Bind it to what they may do.

    ```bash
    kubectl create namespace alice
    kubectl -n alice create serviceaccount alice
    kubectl -n alice create rolebinding alice-edit --clusterrole=edit --serviceaccount=alice:alice
    kubectl -n alice create token alice --duration=720h
    ```

  
  
    Each person chooses **Add your token** and pastes it, with a default namespace if they like. Chat checks it with a SelfSubjectReview and shows whom it acts as.

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Share a Slurm cluster
chunks.text:
slurmrestd must run with `rest_auth/jwt`. Chat uses the newest REST API version the server offers, from v0.0.40 to v0.0.45. For a newer slurmrestd, enter its version, such as `v0.0.46`, in **REST API version** on the cluster; Chat then uses only that one.

Chat never lists every job on the cluster. A person's running, pending and recently ended jobs come from the accounting endpoints (`/slurmdb/…/jobs`, filtered by their user name), so slurmrestd must serve them as well as the scheduler's; the queue's size comes from `/diag`. Chat reads at most 32 MiB of any one answer.

  
    In **Compute › Clusters**, choose **Add a cluster**, then **Slurm cluster**. Enter the slurmrestd URL without `/slurm/v0.0.x`, and tick **Share with everyone**.
  
  
    Each person chooses **Add your token**, enters their Slurm user name and a JWT. Chat checks it against slurmrestd before saving it.

    ```bash
    # On a login node, as yourself
    scontrol token lifespan=2592000
    # Paste the part after SLURM_JWT=
    ```

    Jobs then run as that Slurm user.

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Share an MCP server
chunks.text:
In **Settings › MCP servers**, choose **Add MCP server** and enter its URL. Shared servers may use `http` and internal addresses.
  
  
    Tick **Share with everyone**. To have each person use their own token, also tick **Each person adds their own token**.
  
  
    Enter a token if the server needs one to list its tools. With personal tokens, this token is used only for that. Chat connects once, lists the tools and keeps the list until you choose **Refresh tools**.
  

People then see the server under **Shared with everyone**, with **Add your token** when it needs theirs.

chunks.title: Enable connections and clusters
chunks.heading: Tokens belong to people
chunks.text:
A call to a connection always carries one person's token, so the server's own permissions decide what that person may do:

- **Someone's own connection** uses the token they entered.
- **A shared Slurm or Kubernetes cluster** never has a token of its own. The administrator stores its address; each person adds their own token, and until they do, the cluster stays out of their chats.
- **A shared MCP server** uses the administrator's token for everyone, unless it's set to **Each person adds their own token**. Then it works like a shared cluster. Use that setting for any server whose tokens are personal, such as one that submits jobs as the caller.

Tokens are checked when they're saved, encrypted, and never shown again.

chunks.title: Enable Knowledge
chunks.heading: Choose the embedding model
chunks.text:
An administrator chooses the embedding model and its prefixes in **Settings › Administration › System › Knowledge search**. The list shows the embedding models the gateway offers. `OBLETH_CHAT_EMBEDDING_MODEL` sets the default model.

Each prefix comes from the first of these that is set:

1. The administrator's choice in Settings.
2. `OBLETH_CHAT_EMBEDDING_QUERY_PREFIX` or `OBLETH_CHAT_EMBEDDING_DOCUMENT_PREFIX`, while the default model is in use. They never carry over to another model.
3. The model's own prefixes, for the models in the table below.

Any other model gets no prefix. Choosing a model in Settings fills in its prefixes, so check them against the model's documentation only when it isn't in the table.

Vectors from different models, or the same model with different prefixes, can't be compared. When the model or a prefix changes, Chat indexes every document and saved item again, on its own, with the new settings. Until that finishes, search finds only what has been redone, and a large library takes a while and uses the gateway's embedding capacity. Switching back indexes everything again too. Chat asks for confirmation before it starts, and the card shows how much is left.

The same happens when the defaults change in the environment and no administrator has chosen otherwise.

Chat recognises these by a part of the model's name in the gateway:

| Model | Name contains | Search prefix | Passage prefix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-Embedding | `qwen3-embedding`

chunks.title: Enable Knowledge
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
An S3 bucket, pgvector, an embedding model
  OBLETH_CHAT_S3_ENDPOINT
  2 GiB, 2,000 documents

Document files go to an S3-compatible bucket. Passages and vectors stay in Chat's Postgres database, so pgvector must be installed there (see [Install Chat](/docs/run-chat/install#prepare-the-database)). The same bucket also holds the files people attach to chats and the images models generate; see [Where files are kept](#where-files-are-kept).

chunks.title: Enable Knowledge
chunks.heading: Set it up
chunks.text:
Any S3-compatible store works: AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, MinIO, Garage. Create an access key that can read, write and delete objects in that bucket only.
  
  
    Register an embedding model in the gateway and make sure Chat's tenant may use it. The default is `qwen3-embedding-8b`; any embedding model works. Chat stores 1,024 dimensions: it keeps the first 1,024 of a longer vector and renormalizes them, which suits models trained to be truncated, such as Qwen3-Embedding, and pads a shorter one with zeros, which doesn't change its distances.

    Most embedding models expect a prefix before searches and before passages. Chat knows the prefixes for common models and uses them on its own; for any other model, set them (see [Choose the embedding model](#choose-the-embedding-model)).
  
  

    ```bash
    OBLETH_CHAT_S3_ENDPOINT=https://<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com
    OBLETH_CHAT_S3_BUCKET=obleth-chat
    OBLETH_CHAT_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=…
    OBLETH_CHAT_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=…
    OBLETH_CHAT_EMBEDDING_MODEL=qwen3-embedding-8b
    ```

    Restart Chat. **Library** appears in the sidebar for everyone, with Saved, Collections and Generated, and answers get a Save button. Without these settings Library is hidden.

  

Opening a document's original file, for example from a citation, sends the person's browser straight to the bucket on a 5-minute signed link. People's browsers must therefore reach `OBLETH_CHAT_S3_ENDPOINT` and trust its certificate. With a bucket on a private netwo

chunks.title: Enable Knowledge
chunks.heading: Settings
chunks.text:
| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_S3_ENDPOINT` | unset | Turns Knowledge on. Chat uses path-style addresses |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_S3_BUCKET` | unset | The bucket |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `OBLETH_CHAT_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | unset | The bucket's credentials |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_S3_REGION` | `auto` | Signing region. `auto` suits R2; set the real region for S3 |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_EMBEDDING_MODEL` | `qwen3-embedding-8b` | Default gateway embedding model. An administrator can choose another in Settings |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_EMBEDDING_QUERY_PREFIX` | Qwen3-Embedding's instruction | Default text put before each search. Empty for none |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_EMBEDDING_DOCUMENT_PREFIX` | empty | Default text put before each passage and saved item |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_KNOWLEDGE_USER_MB` | `2048` | Storage per person, in MiB |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_PDFTOTEXT`, `OBLETH_CHAT_PDFTOHTML`, `OBLETH_CHAT_UNZIP` | on `PATH` | Paths to the extraction tools, if they're elsewhere |

chunks.title: Enable Knowledge
chunks.heading: Where files are kept
chunks.text:
With a bucket configured, Chat stores these files there:

| Files | Stored under |
| --- | --- |
| Knowledge documents | `knowledge/<user>/<document>` |
| Chat attachments | `attachments/<user>/<file>` |
| Generated images | `images/<user>/<image>` |

Without a bucket, attachments and generated images are kept in Postgres. Turning the bucket on later needs no other step: a background worker moves existing files into it one at a time, and files stay readable throughout. Each replica logs `moving files kept in Postgres into object storage` when it starts moving them.

Attachments and generated images are served through Chat, never through a link to the bucket, so people's browsers don't need to reach the bucket to open them. Deleting a file, a chat or an account deletes the stored files shortly afterwards. An upload whose chat or file was never saved is deleted after 15 minutes.

Moving files out of Postgres frees their space for new rows, but the database files don't shrink. To give the space back to the disk, run this once the move is done, in a quiet period:

```sql
VACUUM FULL attachments, generated_images;
```

`VACUUM FULL` rewrites both tables and blocks reads and writes on them while it runs.

chunks.title: Enable workspaces
chunks.heading: Add previews
chunks.text:
A workspace's apps open in its **Preview** tab, served at `<id>.<domain>`. Without a preview domain everything else works: workspaces, the terminal, files, code and the browser.

Create a wildcard DNS record and a wildcard certificate for the domain, route it to Chat through your ingress, and set `OBLETH_CHAT_PREVIEW_DOMAIN`. The domain must not contain Chat's own origin.

Only Chat's own page can open a preview, and preview access lasts as long as the sign-in it came from: signing out, a revoked session, a disabled account or lost workspace access ends it within seconds. The preview cookie lasts an hour, renewed while the person is signed in.

```bash
OBLETH_CHAT_PREVIEW_DOMAIN=sbx.example.edu
```

chunks.title: Enable workspaces
chunks.heading: Keep workspaces in their own namespace
chunks.text: `deploy/k8s-workspaces.yaml` creates an `obleth-sandboxes` namespace with the same Role for Chat's ServiceAccount, a ResourceQuota and default-deny NetworkPolicies. Apply it after `deploy/k8s.yaml`, then set `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_NAMESPACE=obleth-sandboxes`.

chunks.title: Enable workspaces
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Kubernetes
  Pods, exec and volumes in its namespace
  Administrators only
  gVisor

Chat starts each person's workspace as a pod and a volume, runs commands in it through the Kubernetes API and proxies its preview. With `deploy/k8s.yaml` from the [Kubernetes install](/docs/run-chat/install), there is nothing more to set up. The manifest gives Chat a ServiceAccount and a Role for pods, exec and volumes in its own namespace, plus NetworkPolicies so that only Chat reaches those pods and they reach only DNS and public HTTP and HTTPS addresses. The namespace enforces Pod Security `restricted`, so the API server refuses privileged, root or host-network pods there.

NetworkPolicies only take effect if your cluster's network plugin enforces them. Calico, Cilium and k3s's built-in policy controller do; Flannel on its own doesn't, and some managed clusters need policy enforcement turned on. Without it, workspace pods can reach anything the cluster network can.

Administrators see **Compute › Workspaces**, a chat can get a workspace, and projects get a **Research** tab. Chat checks its permissions when it starts; **Settings › Administration › System** shows whether workspaces are on and, if they are off, why.

To leave workspaces out, set `OBLETH_CHAT_WORKSPACES=off`. Outside a cluster, Chat reaches the API server with `OBLETH_CHAT_KUBE_API`, `OBLETH_CHAT_KUBE_TOKEN_FILE` and `OBLETH_CHAT_KUBE_CA_FILE` and a namespace from `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_NAMESPACE`, for local development.

Worksp

chunks.title: Enable workspaces
chunks.heading: Run workspaces under gVisor
chunks.text:
gVisor runs each pod against its own user-space kernel, so code in a workspace never talks to the node's kernel directly. It is set up per node.

  
    Install `runsc` and `containerd-shim-runsc-v1` and add the `runsc` runtime to containerd, as in [gVisor's containerd guide](https://gvisor.dev/docs/user_guide/containerd/quick_start/). Label those nodes, for example `gvisor=installed`.
  
  

    ```yaml
    apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RuntimeClass
    metadata:
      name: gvisor
    handler: runsc
    scheduling:
      nodeSelector:
        gvisor: installed
    ```

  
  
    Set `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_RUNTIME_CLASS=gvisor` and restart Chat. Workspace and browser pods then start only on the labelled nodes. Their volumes must be able to attach there, so pick a StorageClass that reaches those nodes (`OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_STORAGE_CLASS`).

chunks.title: Enable workspaces
chunks.heading: Serve the images from your own registry
chunks.text:
A workspace or browser pod must be ready within three minutes, and a node pulls the image the first time it runs one. The workspace image is about 1 GB, so where pulls from `ghcr.io` are slow, a first start on a node can run out of time and say *the workspace pod was not ready after three minutes*. Copying the images to a registry on your network makes each start fast without anything else changing.

Copy both images with every release, keeping their digests, so the copy is the same image you would have pulled:

```bash
for img in workspace browser; do
  skopeo copy --all --preserve-digests \
```
