    docker://ghcr.io/thediymaker/obleth-chat/$img:vX.Y.Z \
    docker://registry.example.internal/obleth-chat/$img:vX.Y.Z
done
```

`--all` copies every architecture; without it the multi-architecture digest changes. Then point Chat at the copies, pinned by the same digest:

```bash
OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_IMAGE=registry.example.internal/obleth-chat/workspace:vX.Y.Z@sha256:…
OBLETH_CHAT_BROWSER_IMAGE=registry.example.internal/obleth-chat/browser:vX.Y.Z@sha256:…
```

`skopeo inspect --raw docker://ghcr.io/thediymaker/obleth-chat/workspace:vX.Y.Z | sha256sum` gives the digest. If an admission policy limits which images run in the workspace namespace, allow the new address too. An image you build yourself goes to your registry the same way.

chunks.title: Enable workspaces
chunks.heading: Settings
chunks.text:
| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_WORKSPACES` | `auto` | `off` turns workspaces and the browser off |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_ACCESS` | `admins` | `admins` or `everyone` |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_NAMESPACE` | Chat's namespace | Where workspace and browser pods run |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_IMAGE` | this release's `workspace` image | The workspace image; pin it by digest in production |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_SLOTS` | `8` | Most workspace and browser pods running at once |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_RUNTIME_CLASS` | unset | RuntimeClass for workspace and browser pods, such as `gvisor` |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_STORAGE_CLASS` | cluster default | StorageClass for each person's volume |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_STORAGE` | `10Gi` | Volume size, and the disk cap Chat enforces |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_CPU` | `2` | CPU limit per pod |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_MEMORY` | `4Gi` | Memory limit per pod |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_IDLE_MINUTES` | `60` | Stop an idle pod; its files are kept |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_RETENTION_MINUTES` | `10080` | Delete a volume this long after its last use (7 days) |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_PREVIEW_DOMAIN` | unset | Wildcard domain for previews; unset, workspaces run without previews |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_PREVIEW_HOST_SUFFIX` | unset | Added to each preview's name (`<id>-dev.<domain>` with `-dev`), so a test Chat can share the domain and wildcard certificate; route names ending in the suffix to it |

Each person has one pod and one volume. Each chat wi

chunks.title: Enable workspaces
chunks.heading: The browser
chunks.text:
With workspaces on, each person also gets a [browser](/docs/chat/browser): a headless Chromium in a second pod with a small volume for its profile, in the same namespace and under the same access rule (`OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_ACCESS`). Browser pods carry the workspace labels, so the same NetworkPolicies apply: only Chat connects (to DevTools on port 9222), and they reach only public HTTP and HTTPS addresses.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_BROWSER` | `on` | `off` leaves the browser out |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_BROWSER_IMAGE` | this release's `browser` image | The browser image, from `deploy/browser/Dockerfile`; pin it by digest in production |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_BROWSER_MEMORY` | `1Gi` | Memory limit per browser |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_BROWSER_CPU` | `1` | CPU limit per browser |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_BROWSER_STORAGE` | `1Gi` | Profile volume size |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_BROWSER_IDLE_MINUTES` | `15` | Stop an idle browser; its sign-ins are kept |

A browser's profile volume is deleted after the workspace retention (`OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_RETENTION_MINUTES`) without use.

chunks.title: Chat environment variables
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Chat reads its configuration from the environment at startup; it doesn't read `.env` itself (Compose passes it with `--env-file`). A setting set to an empty value is the same as one left unset, except the two embedding prefixes, where empty means no prefix. `.env.example` in the repository lists the common ones with comments and marks those `deploy/compose.yaml` does not pass: the branding and secret-key files it does not mount, workspaces and the browser, which need Kubernetes, and the embedding prefixes, which Compose cannot leave unset (choose them in Settings › Knowledge there).

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_DATABASE_URL` | required | Postgres URL for a database Chat owns |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_ORIGIN` | `http://localhost:8085` | The exact URL people open. Must be HTTPS unless it's loopback |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_LISTEN` | `127.0.0.1:8085` | Address and port to listen on |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_UI_URL` | none | The interface server (the `chat-ui` image), which Chat sends every page request to. Without it Chat serves only its API |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_BRANDING_DIR` | `branding` | Folder with `site.config.js` and `assets/`. The image sets `/app/branding` |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_DB_CONNECTIONS` | `20` | Postgres connections per replica, 2 to 200 |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_MAX_STREAMS` | `128` | Concurrent responses per replica, 1 to 4096 |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_SESSION_HOURS` | `12` | Session lifetime, 1 to 168; up to 8760 in forward mode, where password sessions stay capped at 168 |

chunks.title: Features and what they need
chunks.heading: At a glance
chunks.text:
| Feature | Needs | Turn it on | While it's off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Conversations, history, presets | Postgres | Always on | — |
| Answers from models | The obleth gateway | [Connect the gateway](/docs/run-chat/connect-gateway) | The composer says no models are available |
| Single sign-on | An OIDC provider | `OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_ISSUER` and client, see [Accounts](/docs/run-chat/accounts) | Username and password only |
| Projects and groups | Postgres | Always on | — |
| Library: Saved, Collections, Generated | An S3 bucket, pgvector, an embedding model in the gateway | [Enable Knowledge](/docs/run-chat/enable-knowledge) | **Library** leaves the sidebar, and answers have no Save button |
| Documents in a message: PDF, Word, PowerPoint, Excel | `pdftotext` (poppler) and `unzip` where Chat runs (the published image has both) | Always on | — |
| Searching a document too long to read whole | Knowledge | Comes with Knowledge | A document whose text is over 75 KB is refused with a message that names the limit |
| Files in object storage | An S3 bucket | The same bucket settings as Knowledge, see [Where files are kept](/docs/run-chat/enable-knowledge#where-files-are-kept) | Attachments and generated images are kept in Postgres |
| MCP servers | A secret key or the gateway signing key | On by default; `OBLETH_CHAT_CONNECTIONS` | With `off`, **Settings › MCP servers** and the composer's **Tools** button are hidden |
| Slurm and Kubernetes clusters | A secret key or the gateway

chunks.title: Features and what they need
chunks.heading: Check what's on
chunks.text:
`/api/capabilities` lists each feature as configured or not; the web app reads it when it starts, and hides what is not set up:

```bash
curl -s https://chat.example.edu/api/capabilities | jq .features
```

```json
{
  …
  "connections": true,
  "clusters": true,
  "knowledge": false,
  "workspaces": false
}
```

`workspaces` is per person: it's true only for a signed-in account allowed to use them (`OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_ACCESS`), so the unauthenticated `curl` above always shows `false`.

chunks.title: Features and what they need
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Chat, projects, groups, accounts
  Library, workspaces, clusters
  Environment variables, then restart

Chat starts with conversations, projects and accounts. Everything that needs more infrastructure stays off until you configure it, and its pages and buttons are hidden rather than shown empty.

chunks.title: Features and what they need
chunks.heading: Turn a feature off again
chunks.text:
Remove its variables and restart Chat. The data stays in Postgres and the bucket. Turn the feature back on and it's there again.

- **Knowledge.** Collections, saved items and their files are kept.
- **Object storage.** Attachments and generated images already in the bucket can't be opened while it's off, and Chat answers 503 for them. Keep the bucket settings while any files are in it.
- **Workspaces.** Volumes stay in the sandbox namespace. Chat doesn't delete any while workspaces are off, and its retention cleanup (`OBLETH_CHAT_SANDBOX_RETENTION_MINUTES`) resumes once they're back on.
- **Clusters.** Saved clusters and people's tokens are kept but hidden, and the model is offered no cluster tools.
- **All connections.** With `OBLETH_CHAT_CONNECTIONS=off`, the connections API answers 503 and no tools are offered. Saved servers and tokens stay encrypted in Postgres.

- Knowledge embeds every document and saved item through the gateway, so it needs the gateway as well as the bucket.
- Connections encrypt tokens with `OBLETH_CHAT_SECRET_KEY_FILE`, or without it with a key derived from the gateway signing key. With neither there are no connections, whatever `OBLETH_CHAT_CONNECTIONS` says. See [Enable connections and clusters](/docs/run-chat/enable-connections).
- Research runs experiments in workspace pods. Slurm runs for research aren't wired up yet.

chunks.title: Forward provider tokens
chunks.heading: Check your identity provider
chunks.text:
The gateway accepts a bearer token as a JWT only when it's a signed compact JWT (it starts with `eyJ`) with a `kid` header, an asymmetric signature and `iss`, `aud` and `exp` claims. Anything else is read as an API key and refused with `401 invalid api key`. **Globus Auth issues opaque access tokens, so forward mode can't work with Globus; use sign mode.**

Decode one access token from your provider and check two things:

```bash
cut -d. -f2 <<<"$ACCESS_TOKEN" | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d 2>/dev/null; echo
```

- `iss` is the provider's issuer URL, exactly as its discovery document gives it.
- `aud` contains the audience you'll put in the gateway's issuer entry, such as `obleth`. Chat asks for no audience when it signs people in, so the provider must add it by configuration. Keycloak's default is `account`.

chunks.title: Forward provider tokens
chunks.heading: Choose a mode
chunks.text:
| | Sign (default) | Forward |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The gateway trusts | Chat | Your identity provider, and Chat for password accounts |
| Same identity provider for Chat and gateway | Not needed | Needed |
| Identity-provider requirements | None; OIDC is optional | JWT access tokens with the gateway's audience, and refresh tokens |
| How long a provider sign-in lasts | Until the ID token expires, at most `OBLETH_CHAT_SESSION_HOURS` | While the provider keeps the grant, up to `OBLETH_CHAT_SESSION_HOURS` |
| Password accounts | Work | Work while the signing key is set |
| Same gateway identity as direct API use | No | Yes, with tokens from the same provider |

Use sign mode, described in [Connect the gateway](/docs/run-chat/connect-gateway), unless you need the last row.

chunks.title: Forward provider tokens
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
An OIDC provider that issues JWT access tokens
  `OBLETH_CHAT_GATEWAY_AUTH=forward`
  Your identity provider
  Globus Auth

In forward mode, Chat sends the access token your identity provider issued to the signed-in person, unchanged, in the gateway's `Authorization` header. The gateway verifies it against the provider, so Chat holds no key that can act as anyone. A person then has the same gateway identity in Chat as when they call the gateway with a token from the same provider, from a script or a notebook.

chunks.title: Forward provider tokens
chunks.heading: Set it up
chunks.text:
Register `<OBLETH_CHAT_ORIGIN>/api/auth/oidc/callback` as the redirect URI, as for any [OIDC sign-in](/docs/run-chat/accounts#add-oidc-sign-in). Then:

    - Add the gateway's audience to access tokens. In Keycloak, add an **Audience** mapper to the client with **Included Custom Audience** `obleth` and **Add to access token** on.
    - Allow refresh tokens for the `offline_access` scope. In Keycloak the `offline_access` role comes with the realm's default roles; users imported without those roles are refused with "Offline tokens not allowed for the user or client".
  
  
    Merge an entry for the provider into `OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS` (Helm: `obleth.jwtIssuers`). Keep Chat's entry if password accounts should keep working:

    ```json
    {
      "issuer": "https://idp.example.edu/realms/research",
      "jwks_url": "https://idp.example.edu/realms/research/protocol/openid-connect/certs",
      "audience": "obleth",
      "algorithms": ["RS256"],
      "subject_claim": "sub",
      "identity_claims": ["preferred_username"],
      "tenant": "chat-users",
      "jit_provision": true
    }
    ```

    Take `jwks_url` from the provider's discovery document. The gateway logs `jwks loaded issuer=…` for it at startup. See [Identity tokens](/docs/clients/identity-tokens) for every field.
  
  
    ```bash
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_ISSUER=https://idp.example.edu/realms/research
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=obleth-chat
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=…
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_SCOPES="openid

chunks.title: Forward provider tokens
chunks.heading: What changes for people
chunks.text:
- **Signing in again.** Turning forward mode on ends the provider sign-ins made before it: those people see **Sign in again to continue**. Password sessions carry on.
- **A new gateway identity.** Usage, budgets and fairshare history stay with each person's old identity key, which is under Chat's issuer. Switching back to sign mode moves people to that old key again.
- **Sign-in lifetime.** Chat refreshes the access token shortly before it expires. When the provider refuses a refresh, Chat ends that sign-in. Signing out, revoking a session or disabling an account revokes the refresh token at the provider when its discovery document lists a revocation endpoint.
- **Password accounts.** They get Chat's signed token while `OBLETH_CHAT_GATEWAY_SIGNING_KEY_FILE` is set. Without it, they see **This account can't use the models here. Sign in with single sign-on instead.** Someone linked to the provider never gets Chat's token.
- **Where the token goes.** Only to the gateway. MCP servers, workspaces, previews and the browser never see it.

- **Sign-in fails with "Identity provider sign-in failed"** and Chat logs `OIDC authorization code exchange failed`: the provider refused Chat's token request. In forward mode this is usually a refused `offline_access`; see step 1.
- **Replies fail with "Gateway rejected the Chat identity. Check its trusted issuer configuration."**: the gateway refused the provider's token, despite the message's wording. Check `obleth_jwt_verify_total` by `result`

chunks.title: Install Chat
chunks.heading: Check it
chunks.text:
- `/healthz` answers when the process is up.
- `/readyz` also checks the database; use it for readiness probes.
- `/api/admin/health`, signed in as an administrator, returns the replica's version, the database pool, active streams, whether workspaces are on and the address Chat sees for you.

chunks.title: Install Chat
chunks.heading: Limits
chunks.text:
- **Workspaces and the browser run only on Kubernetes.** Chat starts them as pods; with Docker, Chat runs without them.
- **Previews need a wildcard DNS name and certificate.** A preview is an app the model wrote. Served from Chat's own address, it could call Chat as the person signed in, so each app gets an address of its own, such as `a1b2c3.sbx.example.edu`. That takes a wildcard DNS record and a wildcard certificate for the preview domain. Without them, workspaces, the terminal, files, code and the browser all work; only the **Preview** tab is missing. See [Add previews](/docs/run-chat/enable-workspaces#add-previews).

chunks.title: Install Chat
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Docker or Podman, or Kubernetes
  About ten minutes
  8085

Chat is one Rust binary that serves the web app and its API. PostgreSQL with pgvector holds everything: accounts, sessions, conversations, files and Knowledge passages. You can run several replicas against one database; they share sessions, limits and running responses through it.

Accounts and conversations work without a gateway. Models and generation show as unavailable until the [gateway trusts Chat](/docs/run-chat/connect-gateway).

chunks.title: Install Chat
chunks.heading: Set it up
chunks.text:
Get the latest release, then run `setup.sh` for Docker or Kubernetes. It asks for anything it needs, makes the passwords and Chat's signing key, starts Chat and prints the administrator password and what's left to do. Run it again after you pull a new release; it keeps the passwords and keys it made.

```bash
git clone --branch v1.0.0 https://github.com/thediymaker/obleth-chat.git
cd obleth-chat
```

  
    Docker
    Kubernetes
  
  

```bash
./setup.sh docker
```

It asks for two things:

- **The address people open Chat at.** `http://localhost:8085` if only you will use it on this machine.
- **The gateway's URL, as the Chat container reaches it.** A gateway on the same host is `http://host.docker.internal:<port>`.

It writes `.env` with generated passwords, puts the signing key in `.local/`, and starts Chat and PostgreSQL 17 with pgvector through Docker Compose or Podman Compose. Chat listens on `127.0.0.1:8085`, and PostgreSQL publishes no port. For any address other than this machine, put your HTTPS reverse proxy in front of Chat, with response buffering off and long read timeouts: replies stream.

  
  

```bash
./setup.sh kubernetes
```

It needs `kubectl` with access to the cluster, and asks for:

- **The namespace**, `obleth-chat` unless you choose another.
- **The address people open Chat at**, through your ingress.
- **The gateway's URL inside the cluster**, such as `http://obleth-gateway.obleth.svc.cluster.local:8080`.

It creates the namespace and Secrets and app

chunks.title: Install Chat
chunks.heading: Set it up by hand
chunks.text:
`setup.sh` only fills in files from the repository, so you can do the same steps yourself, for example to keep the manifests in your own GitOps repository.

Give Chat its own database and a role that owns it, separate from the gateway's database. The role doesn't need to be a superuser, but pgvector must be installed on the server and the extension created in Chat's database by a superuser:

```sql
CREATE ROLE obleth_chat LOGIN PASSWORD '…' NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE;
CREATE DATABASE obleth_chat OWNER obleth_chat;
\connect obleth_chat
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
```

Chat runs its migrations at startup.

With CloudNativePG, have the operator create the extension when it creates the database:

```yaml
bootstrap:
  initdb:
    database: obleth_chat
    owner: obleth_chat
    postInitApplicationSQL:
      - CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector
```

The operator's `<cluster>-app` Secret has a ready-made connection string under the key `uri`. Use it as `OBLETH_CHAT_DATABASE_URL`; the host in it (`<cluster>-rw.<namespace>`) resolves from Chat's namespace.

`deploy/compose.yaml` runs Chat, its interface server and PostgreSQL 17 with pgvector. Set these in `.env`:

- `OBLETH_CHAT_POSTGRES_ADMIN_PASSWORD` and `OBLETH_CHAT_POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, 64 hex characters each.
- `OBLETH_CHAT_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD`, at least 12 characters.
- `OBLETH_CHAT_ORIGIN` and `OBLETH_CHAT_GATEWAY_URL`.
- `OBLETH_CHAT_GATEWAY_SIGNING_KEY_FILE`, the absolute path of an RSA key ([Connect the

chunks.title: Install Chat
chunks.heading: Sign in the first time
chunks.text:
Open your address and sign in as `admin` with the password `setup.sh` printed. It's also in `.env` or in Secret `obleth-chat-env`, as `OBLETH_CHAT_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD`. Chat creates this account only when it has no users.
  
  
    Change it in **Settings › Personal › Security**.
  
  
    Invite accounts in **Settings › Administration › People**. See [Accounts and sign-in](/docs/run-chat/accounts).
  

Chat needs HTTPS for any address other than this machine. Terminate TLS at your ingress or reverse proxy, and use the exact URL people open as the address. Behind a proxy, also see [Reverse proxies](/docs/run-chat/reverse-proxies).

chunks.title: Install Chat
chunks.heading: Trust Chat in the gateway
chunks.text: `setup.sh` prints an entry for the gateway's issuers. Add it to `OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS` (Helm: `obleth.jwtIssuers`), keeping any other issuers, and restart the gateway. The model picker then lists the gateway's models. [Connect the gateway](/docs/run-chat/connect-gateway) explains each field and how to choose the tenant.

chunks.title: Models, groups and limits
chunks.heading: A better suited model, offered once
chunks.text: When a chat on a provisional or blocked model first reaches for a cluster or workspace tool, Chat offers the best certified model the person can use, with its score, in a card at the end of the reply. Switching uses that model for the chat from the next message; keeping the model, or choosing not to be asked again, is one click. People can turn the offers off under Settings › Appearance (**Suggest a better suited model**). No offer appears when no certified model is available to them, and the card never changes a chat by itself.

chunks.title: Models, groups and limits
chunks.heading: Changes through connections
chunks.text:
Every change a connection tool makes waits for **Allow** unless a [decision](/docs/run-chat/decisions) can vouch for it, and only a model trusted to that degree gets that shortcut. **Changes through connections** on each model is one of:

- **Decide from certification** (the default): the model is **certified** when its certification score is 90% or more, and **provisional** otherwise or until a score is recorded.
- **Certified**: a change it proposes may run on a decision's say-so; the rest ask.
- **Provisional**: every change asks the person, whatever a decision would say.
- **Blocked**: the model is offered only the tools that read, and is told a change needs a certified model the person can switch to.

Chats on `auto` count as provisional, since the model is picked after the tools are offered. Scores come from the certification suite in the Chat repository (`evals/certify`): `publish.py` sends each model's result (score, cases passed and total, suite, date) to `PUT /api/admin/model-certification/{model}`, and the model editor shows it. `DELETE` on the same address clears a score.

chunks.title: Models, groups and limits
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Settings › Administration › Models
  Settings › Administration › Usage & limits
  Daily at 00:00 UTC

chunks.title: Models, groups and limits
chunks.heading: Publish models
chunks.text:
**Settings › Administration › Models** lists the gateway's chat models. For each one you can set:

- **Display name, description and tags**, and its **order** in the picker
- **Enabled**: whether it's published at all
- **Visibility**: everyone, administrators only, or chosen groups
- **Generation defaults**: system instructions, thinking effort, temperature, top P and output token limit. An output limit of 0, the default, sends none, so the model's own applies; a set limit can be up to 262,144 tokens
- **Worker**: whether the model can run [worker agents](/docs/chat/agents)
- **Changes through connections**: how far the model is trusted with changes on clusters and other connections (see below)
- **Locked parameters**: defaults people can't override

One model can be the **default** for new chats. A model the gateway newly reports is visible to everyone until you give it a profile that restricts it. A model the gateway no longer serves stays listed as unavailable.

Chat checks visibility both when listing models and when generating, so a hidden model can't be requested directly. The gateway's own tenant allowlist still applies on top. **Auto** has no Chat profile: people's own preferences apply to it, and the gateway chooses only among its Auto-eligible models.

![Settings › Administration › Models: each model's tags, who it's visible to, how many settings people can adjust, and Configure model](/chat/admin-models.png)

chunks.title: Models, groups and limits
chunks.heading: Set allowances
chunks.text:
**Settings › Administration › Usage & limits** shows requests and tokens per person and sets:

| Limit | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concurrent responses | 12 per person | Responses one person can have running at once, across their chats; worker agents a reply starts are not counted. Each chat runs one at a time |
| Daily requests | Unlimited | Generation attempts per day, including follow-up suggestions |
| Daily tokens | Unlimited | Reported tokens per day, plus the output budget reserved for running responses |

Set site-wide limits and override them for one person. Limits are enforced in Postgres transactions, so they hold across every replica.

Token admission checks the reported totals so far plus the output budget each running response has reserved. A response with no output limit reserves an estimate of 8,192 tokens until its usage is reported. Each worker agent is charged on its own record under its worker model. It's an operational allowance, not an exact billing ceiling. A response that ends without a reported total, because it was stopped, failed or expired, is charged an estimate: about four bytes per token of context and saved output, with output capped at its reserved budget. Usage reports show only reported counts, and missing usage is marked incomplete.

Follow-up suggestions use at most 256 output tokens and are charged their whole budget. They yield to new responses and never take the last free stream slot. Token counts in imported conversatio

chunks.title: Models, groups and limits
chunks.heading: Use groups
chunks.text: Groups in **Settings › Administration › Groups** do two jobs: they decide model visibility, and people use them to [share projects and collections](/docs/chat/projects). Add members by hand, or map them from your identity provider (see [Accounts and sign-in](/docs/run-chat/accounts#map-identity-provider-groups)).

chunks.title: Models, groups and limits
chunks.heading: Which settings win
chunks.text: From weakest to strongest: the model's defaults, then the person's own preferences (**Settings › Personal › Conversation defaults** and saved presets), then the chat's or request's settings. A locked parameter always uses your value.

chunks.title: Models, groups and limits
chunks.heading: Worker models
chunks.text: Tick **Worker** on the models that do worker agents' legwork: fast, inexpensive models that call tools well. When at least one worker model is visible to a person, their chats offer the `delegate` tool, and the main model picks among the worker models they can see, the first in the picker's order by default. Visibility applies to worker models as to any other.

chunks.title: Operate Chat
chunks.heading: Alerts
chunks.text: `deploy/prometheus-alerts.yaml` has sample rules. `OblethChatDown` fires for each scraped Chat process that stops answering, and `OblethChatMissing` when Prometheus finds none to scrape, so they fit the single static target in `deploy/prometheus.yaml` as well as its Kubernetes pod-discovery job. `OblethChatBackupStale` is in `deploy/prometheus-alerts-backup.yaml`: load it only where a backup job writes the status files (below), or it fires two hours after install.

chunks.title: Operate Chat
chunks.heading: Backups
chunks.text:
Back up Chat's Postgres database: it holds everything except files in your bucket and workspace files, which are on Kubernetes volumes that Chat deletes 7 days after their last use. With a bucket configured, it holds Knowledge documents, chat attachments and generated images, so back it up as well (see [Where files are kept](/docs/run-chat/enable-knowledge#where-files-are-kept)).

To have Chat report your backups, point `OBLETH_CHAT_BACKUP_STATUS_DIR` at a directory where your backup job writes two files after each success:

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `lastSuccess` | Unix seconds of the last successful backup |
| `bytes` | Its size in bytes |

Chat reads them at each scrape and exports `obleth_chat_backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds` and `obleth_chat_backup_bytes`. A missing or non-integer file leaves that gauge out.

chunks.title: Operate Chat
chunks.heading: Capacity
chunks.text:
| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_MAX_STREAMS` | `128` | Responses one replica streams at once (1 to 4096) |
| `OBLETH_CHAT_DB_CONNECTIONS` | `20` | Postgres connections per replica (2 to 200) |

No database transaction stays open while Chat waits for tokens, so a replica with 128 streams needs far fewer than 128 connections.

Large requests are bounded per replica, whatever the number of people: uploads must declare their size, are refused before reading when they are too large, and read their body only after sign-in. A replica holds at most 256 MiB of uploads and of files on their way into workspaces at once, and runs one history import at a time from upload to save. Per-person limits are in [Models, groups and limits](/docs/run-chat/models-and-limits).

chunks.title: Operate Chat
chunks.heading: Health checks
chunks.text:
| Path | Answers when |
| --- | --- |
| `/healthz` | The process is up. Use it for liveness |
| `/readyz` | The process is up and the database answers. Use it for readiness and startup |

Every replica is the same. Postgres holds sessions, limits, running responses, approvals and the document queue, so a replica can stop at any time and another takes over. Stop, sign-out and a graceful shutdown save the partial output of running responses.

chunks.title: Operate Chat
chunks.heading: Metrics
chunks.text: `/metrics` is Prometheus text: HTTP requests by route and outcome, active streams, time to first token, generation outcomes and duration, and reported token counters. Labels are bounded: no usernames, conversation IDs, prompt text or arbitrary model names. Scrape it from your internal network only; `deploy/prometheus.yaml` is a sample scrape configuration. Set `OBLETH_CHAT_METRICS_TOKEN` and `/metrics` answers only requests with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; others get `401`.

chunks.title: Operate Chat
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
/healthz, /readyz
  /metrics
  All in Postgres

chunks.title: Operate Chat
chunks.heading: Reply ratings
chunks.text:
**Settings › Administration › Feedback › Reply ratings** shows how people rate replies, over the last 7, 30 or 90 days: thumbs up and down per model with the share up, the reasons given for thumbs down, and the 50 latest comments with their model, rating, reasons and date. **Download CSV** saves the per-model table.

It never shows which conversation or reply a rating came from, or who gave it. Bear in mind that a comment can still name its writer in its own words, and that a model with only a handful of ratings narrows down who rated it. A rating is deleted with its reply, its chat or its person.

chunks.title: Operate Chat
chunks.heading: Sent feedback
chunks.text:
The **Feedback** button in the sidebar opens a form for a problem, an idea or anything else, up to 4,000 characters. **Settings › Administration › Feedback › Sent feedback** lists what people sent, newest first, with the page they were on, Chat's version and the date. Filter it by open or done and by kind, and **Mark done** what you've dealt with.

A sender is named only when they ticked **You can contact me about this**; otherwise it shows as anonymous. Feedback stays in Chat, and a person can send up to 20 a day. When a person is deleted, what they sent stays, without their name.

The **Feedback button** setting there sets how the button shows for everyone:

| Setting | What people see |
| --- | --- |
| Highlighted | A **Send feedback** card at the bottom of the sidebar, for a site in development or a new release |
| In the sidebar | A plain **Feedback** item above **Settings** (the default) |
| Off | No button; the form can't be sent |

chunks.title: Operate Chat
chunks.heading: Upgrades
chunks.text:
Chat applies new database migrations at startup. Take a backup before you upgrade, then roll out the new image. Responses running on a replica that stops are saved and marked interrupted; people can regenerate them.

The repository's suites cover local auth and revocation, last-admin concurrency, OIDC against a local RSA issuer, group and model access, locked defaults, concurrent leases and quotas, reconnect persistence, gateway identity and streaming, thinking, cancellation, safe Markdown, private files and imports, and Knowledge. Run them with:

```bash
npm test
cargo check --all-targets
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://… TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://… cargo test --all-targets
```

Use a disposable Postgres server; the Rust tests create isolated databases. `scripts/run-load-fixture.py` runs a load smoke test against a deterministic local gateway.

chunks.title: Reverse proxies
chunks.heading: Check it
chunks.text: Signed in as an administrator, open `/api/admin/health`. Its `client` field shows the connecting peer, whether Chat trusts it, the forwarded chain and the address Chat used for your own request. Check that the address is yours, not the proxy's: if it is the proxy's, everyone behind it shares one sign-in limit.

chunks.title: Reverse proxies
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
OBLETH_CHAT_TRUSTED_PROXY
  `/api/admin/health`, field `client`
  Chat uses the TCP peer

Sign-in limits are kept per client address. Behind a reverse proxy, Chat sees the proxy as the peer, so every person shares one limit until you trust the proxy.

chunks.title: Reverse proxies
chunks.heading: Request sizes
chunks.text:
Most requests are small, but two aren't. Allow them on the proxy, or set the limit to at least these for Chat's routes:

| Request | Largest body | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /api/attachments` | A little over `OBLETH_CHAT_MAX_FILE_MB`, about 51 MB by default | The web app sends a file's own bytes. A client that sends JSON with base64 needs 4/3 of the limit plus 1 MB |
| `POST /api/conversations/import` | 200 MB | A chat-history export. Saving a large one can take a minute or more before Chat answers, and an import waits for another one running on the same replica to finish |

nginx refuses bodies over 1 MB by default: set `client_max_body_size 200m;` for Chat (or more, if `OBLETH_CHAT_MAX_FILE_MB` is over 200), and a `proxy_read_timeout` of a few minutes or more. HAProxy sets no body limit; check that its client and server timeouts allow an import to finish.

chunks.title: Reverse proxies
chunks.heading: Streaming through a proxy
chunks.text:
Replies stream as server-sent events, and a workspace's terminal and previews use WebSockets. On the proxy:

- Turn off response buffering for Chat, or replies arrive in bursts.
- Allow long read timeouts. A response can run for 9 minutes, and a workspace turn much longer.
- Pass WebSocket upgrades, for the terminal and for dev servers' hot reload.

chunks.title: Reverse proxies
chunks.heading: Trust your proxy
chunks.text:
Set `OBLETH_CHAT_TRUSTED_PROXY` to your proxies' addresses or CIDR ranges, comma-separated. `loopback` covers `127.0.0.0/8` and `::1`, for a proxy on the same host.

Chat then reads `X-Forwarded-For`, but only from trusted peers. It walks the header from the nearest hop and stops at the first untrusted or malformed entry.

A trusted address can claim to be any client. Trust only your proxies, never a range that also holds clients, such as a whole LAN. The proxy must replace or append to `X-Forwarded-For`, not pass a client's value through unchecked.

| Deployment | Setting | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Binary behind nginx or Caddy on the same host | `loopback` | nginx: `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;`. Caddy sets the header by default |
| Compose, with a proxy on the host | The Compose network's gateway, such as `172.18.0.1` | Docker forwards the published port from its bridge, so Chat sees the bridge gateway, not loopback. `docker network inspect` shows it |
| Compose, with a proxy container | That container's address, or a subnet holding only the proxy | Publish Chat only to the proxy network or to loopback |
| Kubernetes ingress | The ingress controller's pod addresses, or the pod CIDR when a NetworkPolicy admits only trusted pods | The controller must see the real client. A load balancer that source-NATs, such as k3s ServiceLB with `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster`, hides it |
| Kubernetes proxy with host networking | The node addresses the

chunks.title: Sign-in setups
chunks.heading: Check how long a sign-in lasts
chunks.text:
After signing in through the provider, open **Settings › Personal › Security**: each session shows when it expires. In the default mode that's the provider's ID-token expiry, capped at `OBLETH_CHAT_SESSION_HOURS`. If it's shorter than you want people to stay signed in, raise the ID-token lifetime at the provider if it lets you; Chat can't extend it.

Chat keys provider accounts by issuer and subject. Changing the issuer, such as moving from Keycloak to Globus, gives everyone new, unlinked identities; link existing accounts in **People** before you switch, or turn sign-up on and let new accounts appear. The gateway keys Chat's tokens by Chat account ID, so a person keeps their gateway identity and usage as long as they keep their Chat account.

chunks.title: Sign-in setups
chunks.heading: CILogon
chunks.text:
Request a client at [cilogon.org/oauth2/register](https://cilogon.org/oauth2/register) with the redirect URI `https://chat.example.edu/api/auth/oidc/callback` and the scopes you need, at least `openid` and `profile`. CILogon approves clients by hand.
  
  
    ```bash
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_ISSUER=https://cilogon.org
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=cilogon:/client_id/…
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=…
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_SCOPES=openid profile email org.cilogon.userinfo
    ```

    Ask only for scopes your client was approved for. CILogon lets people sign in through many institutions and public providers, so keep sign-up off and link each person in **People**, unless everyone who can sign in through CILogon may use Chat.
  
  
    As with Globus, sign in once and [check when the session ends](#check-how-long-a-sign-in-lasts).
  

With `org.cilogon.userinfo`, CILogon can send `isMemberOf`, which you can map to Chat groups with `OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_GROUP_CLAIM=isMemberOf`; see [Map identity-provider groups](/docs/run-chat/accounts#map-identity-provider-groups).

chunks.title: Sign-in setups
chunks.heading: Globus
chunks.text:
In [Globus › Settings › Developers](https://app.globus.org/settings/developers), register an app that runs on a web server. Set the redirect URI to `https://chat.example.edu/api/auth/oidc/callback`, then create a client secret.

    To let in only your institution, turn on **Required Identity** and pick your institution's identity provider. Without it, anyone with a Globus account, including Google and ORCID sign-ins, can reach Chat. With it, people must have a linked identity from your institution, though they may sign in through another one.
  
  
    ```bash
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_ISSUER=https://auth.globus.org
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=<the app's client ID>
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=…
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_ALLOW_SIGNUP=true
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_PROVIDER_USERNAMES=true
    ```

    Leave `OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_ALLOW_SIGNUP` unset if you'd rather create accounts yourself and link each Globus identity in **People**. With provider usernames on, accounts are named after the Globus username, such as `jdoe@example.edu`; leave them off if your institution reuses usernames (see [Accounts and sign-in](/docs/run-chat/accounts#add-oidc-sign-in)).
  
  
    A Chat sign-in lasts until the ID token from Globus expires, at most `OBLETH_CHAT_SESSION_HOURS`. Sign in once and [check when the session ends](#check-how-long-a-sign-in-lasts).
  

Globus ID tokens carry no group claim, so put people into groups with `OBLETH_CHAT_DEFAULT_GROUP_IDS` or by hand.

chunks.title: Sign-in setups
chunks.heading: Keycloak with LDAP or AD
chunks.text:
Keycloak brokers your directory: add it under **User federation** in your realm, and Chat sees ordinary Keycloak users.

  
    In the realm, create an OpenID Connect client `obleth-chat` with **Client authentication** on and the standard flow only. Set **Valid redirect URIs** to `https://chat.example.edu/api/auth/oidc/callback` and copy the secret from **Credentials**.
  
  
    Keycloak's ID tokens follow the access token lifespan, 5 minutes by default, which would sign people out of Chat every 5 minutes. In the client's **Advanced › Advanced settings**, set **Access Token Lifespan** to how long a Chat sign-in should last, such as 12 hours. Or [forward tokens](/docs/run-chat/forward-tokens), where Chat refreshes them and the lifespan can stay short.
  
  
    To map directory groups to Chat groups, add a **Group Membership** mapper to the client's dedicated scope with the token claim name `groups`, **Full group path** off and **Add to ID token** on.
  
  
    ```bash
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_ISSUER=https://idp.example.edu/realms/research
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=obleth-chat
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=…
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_ALLOW_SIGNUP=true
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_PROVIDER_USERNAMES=true
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_GROUP_CLAIM=groups
    OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_GROUP_MAP={"hpc-users":["<chat group UUID>"]}
    ```
  

Sign-up is safe to turn on here, since only your directory's users can sign in to the realm.

chunks.title: Sign-in setups
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The same in every setup
  Not needed
  Kept alongside OIDC unless you turn them off

However people sign in, Chat signs its own token for each person when it calls the gateway, so the gateway trusts Chat, not your identity provider. Each person, local or OIDC, gets their own gateway identity, usage and budget. The gateway entry from [Connect the gateway](/docs/run-chat/connect-gateway#set-it-up) is the same in every setup.

| Setup | People sign in with | Who creates accounts | Can [forward tokens](/docs/run-chat/forward-tokens) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Passwords only | A Chat username and password | An administrator | No |
| Globus | Their institution, through Globus | Globus sign-in, or an administrator | No: Globus access tokens are opaque |
| CILogon | Their institution, through CILogon | CILogon sign-in, or an administrator | Only if CILogon issues JWT access tokens for your client |
| Keycloak with LDAP or AD | Their directory account | Keycloak sign-in, or an administrator | Yes |

Every example adds to the gateway settings Chat already has:

```bash
OBLETH_CHAT_ORIGIN=https://chat.example.edu
OBLETH_CHAT_GATEWAY_URL=http://obleth-gateway:8080
OBLETH_CHAT_GATEWAY_SIGNING_KEY_FILE=/secure/path/obleth-chat-signing.pem
```

chunks.title: Sign-in setups
chunks.heading: Passwords only
chunks.text:
Set no `OBLETH_CHAT_OIDC_*` variable. The first administrator comes from the bootstrap settings:

```bash
OBLETH_CHAT_BOOTSTRAP_USERNAME=admin
OBLETH_CHAT_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD=…
```

Sign in as that administrator, [create everyone else](/docs/run-chat/accounts#add-people) in **Settings › Administration › People**, then remove the bootstrap password. Sessions last `OBLETH_CHAT_SESSION_HOURS`.

chunks.title: Sign-in setups
chunks.heading: Provider only, no passwords
chunks.text: Any of the provider setups can turn local sign-in off. Link the administrators' provider identities with **Link single sign-on** in **People** first, then set `OBLETH_CHAT_PASSWORD_SIGN_IN=false` and remove `OBLETH_CHAT_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD`. Without a working provider, nobody can then sign in, so keep a way to reach the database or turn passwords back on.

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: In the response
chunks.text:
A chat or text completion that had energy measured also carries `energy_wh` and `co2_g` in its `usage`: in the JSON body, or in the usage chunk of a stream that asks for one with `stream_options.include_usage`.

```json
"usage": {"prompt_tokens": 412, "completion_tokens": 230, "total_tokens": 642, "energy_wh": 0.21, "co2_g": 0.08}
```

An answer that ran the gateway's tools (image generation, web search, MCP) or a [speculation](/docs/boons/speculation) draft carries the energy measured for the whole request. The values are read as the answer ends, a moment before the request settles, so they can differ from the stored figures in the last digits. A request with nothing measured, a cache hit, and every request while energy accounting is off answer exactly as before, without the fields.

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: Limits of both
chunks.text:
The figures are a lower bound for showback and sustainability reporting, not a metered bill:

- Idle power is not attributed to anyone. Per model, a model's power while it serves nothing is charged to nobody. Per node, a request only ever pays for its own slot.
- Per node, every node is charged at the cluster average, busy or not.
- Time spent waiting for a slot is free.
- Helper calls (vision, tool loops, drafts) record zero; their hardware time falls inside the main request's serving time.

A request that fails upstream still records energy for the time it was served, even when it is not billed.

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: Management API
chunks.text:
| Method | Path | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/settings/energy` | Current settings |
| `PUT` | `/api/v1/settings/energy` | Update the settings; applies live |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/settings/energy/test` | Run the power queries once, without saving |

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/energy \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"enabled": true, "prometheus_url": "http://prometheus:9090",
       "model_power_query": "sum by (model) (model_power_watts)", "model_power_label": "model",
       "model_requests_query": "sum by (model) (requests_running)",
       "power_query": "ipmi_dcmi_power_consumption_watts", "poll_interval_secs": 30,
       "energy_cost_per_kwh": 0.12, "carbon_g_per_kwh": 400, "pue": 1.2}'
```

An empty `model_power_query` or `power_query` turns that source off, and an empty `model_requests_query` counts only the gateway's own requests. The test call takes `prometheus_url` and any of `power_query`, `model_power_query`, `model_power_label` and `model_requests_query`. It returns `cluster_watts` and `node_count` for the per-node query (zero when not given) and, for the per-model query, `models` with `total_watts`, `series`, `matched` (each `model`, `series`, `watts`), `unmatched_series`, and `requests_in_progress` when a requests query is given. A model's slot count is `energy_slots_per_node` on the model create and update calls.

Energy accounting never delays

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A Prometheus that scrapes device or node power
  Settings › Energy
  Models you run yourself. Off by default

The gateway reads power in one of two ways, and you can use both:

- **Power per model.** A query returns watts for each model. Each model's power is split between the requests it is serving at that moment, across every gateway replica. Nothing needs setting on the models, and the numbers follow your deployments as they scale.
- **Power per node.** A query returns watts for each node. Each model declares how many requests saturate a node, and a request is charged one of those slots at the average node's power. Use this when your metrics cannot be tied to a model.

A model that matches a series of the per-model query is charged from it. Any other model falls back to its per-node slot share, and a model with neither records zero.

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: Power per model
chunks.text:
While a request is being served, it is charged its model's power divided by the number of requests that model is serving across the cluster:

```
energy_wh = ∫ model_watts(t) / in_flight(t) dt × PUE     (from admission to completion)
```

`in_flight` counts the model's admitted requests on every gateway replica. With [shared fairshare slots](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine) the gateway reads it from the cluster-wide counts every 2 seconds. Without them, each replica assumes the others carry as many requests as it does. `model_watts` is the latest reading of the series, and a new reading applies from the moment it arrives.

If other clients send requests to the same model servers, the gateway cannot see them, and its own requests would be charged for theirs. Add a **Requests per model** query that returns how many requests each model's servers are handling, with the same label as the power query. `in_flight` is then the larger of the gateway's count and the servers' count, read at each poll.

For example, a model drawing 1,000 W serves request A alone for one hour, then A and B together for an hour, then B alone for an hour. A and B are each charged 1,500 Wh. Together they account for all 3,000 Wh the model drew.

Several models can share one series, such as two routes to the same server pool. Their requests then split that power between them.

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: Power per model
chunks.text:
The query returns one series per model, named by a label (`model` unless you set **Model label**). A series matches a model when the label carries the model's name, its capacity Service, or its upstream model, checked in that order. Series that share a label value are summed.

On Kubernetes, the simplest source is a device exporter that labels each device with the pod using it, such as NVIDIA DCGM. Map the pod to a model with `label_replace`:

```
sum by (model) (
  label_replace(
    DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE{namespace="llm"},
    "model", "$1", "pod", "vllm-(.+)-[a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]{5}"
  )
)
```

With only node power, give each pod its share of the node by the accelerators it requested, using kube-state-metrics. This charges a model for the whole node, including CPUs, memory and fans, in proportion to its accelerators:

```
sum by (model) (
  label_replace(
    sum by (namespace, pod, node) (
      kube_pod_container_resource_requests{namespace="llm", resource="nvidia_com_gpu"}
    )
    / on (node) group_left ()
      max by (node) (kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="nvidia_com_gpu"})
    * on (node) group_left ()
      max by (node) (node_power_watts),
    "model", "$1", "pod", "vllm-(.+)-[a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]{5}"
  )
)
```

Replace `node_power_watts` with your per-node gauge, relabelled so that its node label is `node`. If your pods carry a label naming the model, allow it in kube-state-metrics (`--metric-labels-allowlist=pods=[your-label]`) and join on `kube_pod_labels` i

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: Power per node
chunks.text:
A request is charged its serving time's share of one slot, at the average power per node:

```
serving_ms     = total_ms − queue_wait_ms
watts_per_slot = cluster_watts / node_count / energy_slots_per_node × PUE
energy_wh      = watts_per_slot × serving_ms / 3,600,000
```

`cluster_watts` is `sum()` of your query and `node_count` is `count()` of it. For example, 44,800 W across 64 nodes is 700 W per node. At 8 slots per node and a PUE of 1.2 that is 105 W per slot, so a request served for 2.4 s is charged 0.07 Wh.

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: Power per node
chunks.text:
Any exporter with a power gauge works:

| Exporter | Example query |
| --- | --- |
| Intel Gaudi (Habana) | `habana_device_power_watts` |
| NVIDIA DCGM | `DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE` |
| IPMI (whole node) | `ipmi_dcmi_power_consumption_watts` |

With a per-device metric, either aggregate it per node (`sum by (node) (...)`) or declare slots per device instead of per node. The arithmetic only needs `cluster_watts / node_count` to mean the power of the unit you counted slots against. Use label selectors to scope a mixed cluster, such as `ipmi_dcmi_power_consumption_watts{cluster="prod"}`.

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: Requests per model
chunks.text:
Most model servers export a gauge of the requests they are running. For vLLM, relabel its served model name to the label your power query uses:

```
sum by (model) (
  label_replace(vllm:num_requests_running, "model", "$1", "model_name", "(.+)")
)
```

Leave it empty when this gateway is the only client of its model servers.

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: Turn it on
chunks.text:
In **Settings › Energy**, enter the Prometheus URL and a **Power per model** query, a **Power per node** query, or both. Choose **Test the queries**. It runs them once and shows the total power, which of your models match a per-model series, which series match no model, and the node count. A failure shows the Prometheus error as it came back.

Enter the cost of a kWh, your grid's grams of CO₂ per kWh (`0` leaves CO₂ out), and your data centre's PUE (default `1.0`, IT power only). The poll interval defaults to 60 seconds. With per-model power, 15 to 30 seconds follows scaling more closely.

Turn on **Energy** and save. The gateway picks the settings up without a restart.

On each self-hosted model that has no per-model series, set **Energy slots per node**: how many of its requests one node serves at once when fully loaded, that is replicas per node × concurrent sequences per replica. Two server instances per node with 4 sequences each is `8`. `0`, the default, leaves the model out. A model with a per-model series ignores this field.

The Prometheus URL must be reachable from the gateway process. In the Compose stack that is `http://prometheus:9090`, not `localhost:9090`, which inside the gateway container is the gateway itself. The URL is checked against the gateway's outbound address policy when you test and when you save.

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: What each request records
chunks.text:
Three values are stored on each request's usage row, next to its cost:

| Field | Unit | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `energy_wh` | watt-hours | Energy attributed to the request |
| `energy_cost_usd` | USD | That energy at your rate per kWh |
| `co2_g` | grams | That energy at your grid's carbon intensity |

They are computed once, when the request completes. Changing a rate, PUE, query or slot count later changes only future requests; history is never rewritten or backfilled.

chunks.title: Energy and carbon
chunks.heading: Where the numbers appear
chunks.text:
- **Overview**: an energy tile with kWh and CO₂ for the window.
- **Reports**: energy, CO₂ and power cost for the period, an Energy column in the breakdown, and Energy (kWh), CO₂ and energy cost columns in the export.
- **Request logs**: a request's panel shows its Wh and grams of CO₂.
- **Responses**: a chat or text completion's `usage` also carries `energy_wh` and `co2_g` when energy was measured for it, in the JSON body or, streamed, in the usage chunk a client asks for with `stream_options.include_usage`. They are read as the answer ends, a moment before the request settles, so they can differ from the stored figures in the last digits. Requests with nothing measured and cache hits have neither field.
- **Management API and ClickHouse**: energy sums beside `cost_usd` in usage queries and the daily rollup. See [ClickHouse usage](/docs/reference/clickhouse-usage).

chunks.title: How fairshare works
chunks.heading: Background work uses a background pool
chunks.text:
Requests from [batches](/docs/clients/batches), and every request from a key with [background priority](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys#background-priority), take slots in a second pool per model, the background pool, which shares the model's slots with the interactive pool. A background request starts only when no interactive request is waiting for that model on any gateway replica, and while background work holds less than `OBLETH_BATCH_MAX_SHARE` (default `0.75`) of the model's slots and of the global ceiling. A slot that frees while an interactive request waits goes to it, even if a background request asked first.

So background work fills capacity nobody else is using, and an interactive arrival always finds at least the remaining quarter of the slots free. Running background requests are never cut short. Batch owners and background keys split the background pool by the same group, tenant and key weights, and background requests don't count against any tenant's or key's max in flight. The Fairshare page shows the pool as `<model> (background)`, at the size background work may fill: a model with 32 slots shows a background pool of 24 at the default share, and fair shares in it are split from those 24. The pool's page says how many of the model's slots stay free for interactive requests. Needs attention and the overview's below-share count leave background pools out, since background work waits whenever its share is full.

chunks.title: How fairshare works
chunks.heading: Each model has its own pool
chunks.text:
A pool is the number of requests the gateway lets reach a model's backend at once. Its size is the model's max in flight, or `OBLETH_DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (default `32`) when the model has none. A model in the `discovered` capacity mode sizes its pool from the backend's ready replicas instead; see [Pool sizes](/docs/models/pool-sizes).

Pools are independent. A full pool never delays a model with free slots, and a tenant's use of one model costs it no priority on another. `OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` (default `4096`) is a safety ceiling across all pools together; keep it above the sum of your pool sizes so the pools do the limiting.

chunks.title: How fairshare works
chunks.heading: Limits hold across replicas
chunks.text:
With more than one gateway replica, every limit above (pool sizes, the global ceiling, tenant and key caps) holds for the fleet as a whole. A model with 20 slots behind three gateways admits 20 requests in total, on whichever gateways they reach. The slots are counted in Redis (`OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_SHARED_SLOTS`, on by default). With a single replica there is no Redis call on the request path.

If Redis stops answering, each gateway falls back to its share of each limit (the configured value divided by the number of live gateways, rounded up) and returns to shared slots when Redis recovers. It never admits without a limit.

chunks.title: How fairshare works
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
One pool of slots per model
  Group, then tenant, then key, by weight
  Requests queue for up to 60 s, then get a 503
  Limits hold for the whole fleet

chunks.title: How fairshare works
chunks.heading: Queued requests time out
chunks.text:
A request that waits `OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS` (default `60`) without getting a slot leaves the queue with a 503 and a `Retry-After` header:

```http
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
Retry-After: 5
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":{"message":"timed out waiting for model capacity","type":"obleth_gateway_error"}}
```

Clients should wait and retry. The OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs already retry on 503 and respect `Retry-After`.

Queuing covers contention. A request is refused at once only when it crosses a limit you set:

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `429 token budget exceeded` | The tenant's token rate is used up. See [Budgets and rate limits](/docs/sharing/quotas-and-rate-limits) |
| `403 tenant term budget exhausted` | The tenant's spend or token budget for the period is used up |
| `403 api key term budget exhausted` | The key's own budget for the period is used up |
| `403 model not permitted for tenant` | The model is not on the tenant's model list |
| `403` | The key is disabled, the tenant is suspended or archived, or the tenant is outside its access hours. The message says which |
| `503 scheduler unavailable` | The scheduler could not be reached; the gateway also raises an alert |

chunks.title: How fairshare works
chunks.heading: Read the Fairshare page
chunks.text:
**Fairshare** opens on every model pool, fullest first, with the number of requests running and waiting, the busiest pool, and each group's use against the share its weight guarantees.

![The Fairshare page: running and waiting tiles, model pools sorted by how full they are with one pool full and 56 requests waiting, and a Groups panel with each group's use against its share](/dashboard/fairshare.png)

A pool is **Busy** above 80% and **Full** at 100%. A pool whose model has nowhere to send a request (no API base, no enabled endpoint, or a watched backend with no ready replica) reads **No servers**, and its slots are left out of the totals. Clients read the same numbers for the models they may use from [`GET /v1/load`](/docs/clients/model-load). Open a pool (or follow a **Full** item from the Overview) to see who holds its slots:

![One model pool: every slot taken, three tenants each running their fair share with requests waiting, and the keys in the pool with their weights and caps](/dashboard/fairshare-pool.png)

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Fair share | The slots a tenant gets when every active tenant in the pool is busy: its group's share, split by tenant weight. Drawn as a tick on each bar |
| Above share | Slots a tenant holds beyond its fair share, borrowed while nobody else needed them |
| Next in line | A tenant waiting while below its fair share. These tenants get freed slots first, in the order shown |
| At share | A tenant with requests waiting that already

chunks.title: How fairshare works
chunks.heading: When a pool is full, requests queue
chunks.text:
A request that finds its model's pool full waits in that pool's queue instead of failing. When a running request finishes, the scheduler hands its slot to the waiter that is furthest below its fair share. The client sees a slower response, not an error.

A waiter whose client has disconnected is dropped from the queue and charged nothing. Requests already running are never cut short to make room.

chunks.title: How fairshare works
chunks.heading: When requests wait too long
chunks.text:
A pool that queues most of the time is too small for the traffic it gets.

- Raise the model's max in flight, if the backend can serve more at once. [Capacity auto-tune](/docs/models/capacity-autotune) finds the backend's limit.
- Add backend replicas. Adding gateway replicas does not add backend capacity.
- Check weights: one high-weight tenant can hold most of a busy pool.
- Keep `OBLETH_GLOBAL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` above the sum of your pool sizes. The gateway logs a warning at start when it is not.

Every request is recorded with an `admission` class (`fast`, `queued` or `rejected`) and `queue_wait_ms`. Admission timeouts are `rejected` rows with status 503; budget refusals are `rejected` rows with 429 or 403.

```sql
SELECT tenant_id, admission, count() AS requests, avg(queue_wait_ms) AS avg_wait_ms
FROM usage
WHERE ts_ms > toUnixTimestamp(now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR) * 1000
GROUP BY tenant_id, admission
ORDER BY requests DESC
```

In the dashboard, the bar on each row of **Request logs** splits a request's time into waiting for a slot, time to first token, and the rest.

chunks.title: How fairshare works
chunks.heading: Who gets the next slot
chunks.text:
Slots are divided in three steps, each by weight:

1. **Groups.** Each pool's slots are split between the active [fairshare groups](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys#fairshare-groups) by group weight.
2. **Tenants.** A group's share is split between its active tenants by tenant weight.
3. **Keys.** A tenant's share is split between its keys by key weight, so one busy key cannot take all of its tenant's slots.

Only tenants that are running or waiting on the pool count. A share is a claim when the pool is contended, not a reservation: slots a quiet group or tenant leaves unused are lent to whoever is waiting, and are returned as those borrowed requests finish.

Fairness is measured in tokens, not requests. Each request is charged its estimated token count when it is admitted, so a tenant sending long prompts uses up its share faster than one sending short ones.

A tenant or key can also carry a max in flight: a hard cap on how many of its requests run at once in each model's pool. Requests over the cap wait like any other. Set weights and caps on the tenant's page and in the key's panel; see [Tenants and keys](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys). To change a weight during an incident, see [Priority boost](/docs/sharing/priority-boost).

The scheduling algorithm, the scores it keeps and how shares are computed are in [Fairshare engine](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine).

chunks.title: Where keys work
chunks.heading: Limit a key to certain countries
chunks.text:
A key can also list **allowed countries**: two-letter codes such as `US` or `CA`, up to 50. Type them under **Allowed countries** in the key's panel or the new-key sheet, separated by commas or spaces; each code shows the country's name as you type. Through the API, send `allowed_countries` where you send `allowed_networks`:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/keys/$KEY_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "nightly-eval", "allowed_networks": ["10.20.0.0/16"], "allowed_countries": ["US"]}'
```

Codes are stored upper-case and each once. `XX` (the edge's "unknown") and anything that isn't two letters is refused with `400`, naming the entry. A `PUT` that leaves `allowed_countries` out keeps the list; send `[]` to clear it. **Replace…** and backups keep it.

How the two lists combine:

| Allowed networks | Allowed countries | A request is allowed when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| empty | empty | always |
| listed | empty | its client address is in one of the networks |
| empty | listed | its client country is listed |
| listed | listed | either one matches |

An unknown country never matches, so a request with no country is allowed only by its network. A request whose address is unknown but whose country is listed is allowed: the country alone is enough. A refusal names the country when the key lists any:

```json
{"error": {"code": "ip_not_allowed", "message": "This API key can't be used from 192.0.2.

chunks.title: Where keys work
chunks.heading: Limit a key to certain networks
chunks.text:
On **API keys**, open the key. A new key can be limited when you make it, in the new-key sheet.

Under **Allowed networks**, put one CIDR range or single address per line, up to 64. Leave it empty to allow any network.

The change reaches every gateway replica on the key's next request, like turning a key off. The keys list shows **Only 10.0.0.0/8** or **Only 2 networks** for a limited key.

The same through the Management API, when you make a key or edit one:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID/keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "nightly-eval", "allowed_networks": ["10.20.0.0/16", "198.51.100.7"]}'
```

A single address is stored as `/32` (or `/128` for IPv6). A `PUT /api/v1/keys/{id}` that leaves `allowed_networks` out keeps the list; send `[]` to allow any network again. **Replace…** and backups keep the list.

A request from anywhere else is refused before it reaches a model, on every data-plane endpoint:

```json
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden

{"error": {"code": "ip_not_allowed", "message": "This API key can't be used from 192.0.2.9. Its owner limited it to certain networks."}}
```

chunks.title: Where keys work
chunks.heading: Name your networks
chunks.text:
Private addresses have no country, so reports can't say where `10.20.5.0/24` is. **Settings › Networks** names your own networks, such as a campus, a VPN or a cluster's pods. Each named network has a name and one or more ranges, one address or range per line in the editor, and reports show the name for addresses inside it. Names only describe; they change no check.

An address takes the name of the **narrowest range** that holds it, whichever network that range is in. With the networks below, `198.51.100.20` is in both Campus (`198.51.100.0/22`) and HPC cluster (`198.51.100.0/24`), and is named HPC cluster; `198.51.102.9` is named Campus.

Tick **Ours** for your organization's own networks. The gateway changes no check because of it: it tells operators, and apps built on obleth, that use from these networks is expected. A key's allowed networks show the named networks as chips, yours first: pressing one allows all of its ranges and pressing it again removes them, hovering shows its ranges, and the box below holds only the addresses and ranges no whole named network covers. Key summaries name whole networks, such as "Only Campus, VPN and 2 more".

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/settings/networks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"networks": [
        {"name": "Campus", "ranges": ["198.51.100.0/22", "2001:db8::/48"], "ours": true},
        {"name": "Campus VPN", "ranges": ["203.0.113.0/25"], "ours":

chunks.title: Where keys work
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Allowed networks and countries in a key's panel
  Every data-plane request with that key
  Your proxies sending `X-Forwarded-For`
  Address, network, country and User-Agent per request

chunks.title: Where keys work
chunks.heading: See refused requests
chunks.text:
A request with a turned-off key, or from outside a key's networks and countries, is recorded with its address, country and User-Agent. `GET /api/v1/usage/key-rejections` takes the same parameters and lists them per key, reason (`disabled` or `ip_not_allowed`), address and country, with a count, the first and last time, and the latest User-Agent. Rows come newest first, at most 10,000: pass `limit` for fewer, `per_key` to cap any one key, and several keys in `key_id` joined by commas (at most 200) to see all of one person's keys in one call. When rows were left out, the response carries the header `x-obleth-truncated: true`. A `key_id` with no key in it is refused rather than read as every key.

Only real keys are recorded. A key that doesn't exist, or a mistyped one, is refused as an unknown key and leaves no row, so made-up keys can't fill the table or show up against anyone.

Refusals never turn a key off. Anyone holding a leaked key could otherwise get it switched off for its owner, so the gateway only records them: tell the owner, and they can rotate the key.

A key you turned off that keeps getting requests is still configured somewhere: a forgotten job, or a copy of the key you didn't expect. The address and User-Agent say where to look.

Refusals go to the ClickHouse table `key_rejections`, at most one row per key, address and reason every 10 seconds, with a count, so a client retrying in a loop doesn't fill the table. Writing them never slows the request. `key_country

chunks.title: Where keys work
chunks.heading: See where a key is used
chunks.text:
The **Key access** tab of **Reports** shows this for every key, with your network names, and the refused requests below it. The rest of this section is the API behind it.

Every usage row records `client_ip`, its network (`client_network`, the IPv4 `/24` or IPv6 `/48`), `client_country` and `user_agent`, and the request log (`GET /api/v1/usage/logs`) returns them for each request. `GET /api/v1/usage/key-sources` sums them per key:

```bash
curl "http://localhost:9180/api/v1/usage/key-sources?key_id=$KEY_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

```json
[{"key_id": "…", "key_name": "nightly-eval", "tenant_id": "…", "tenant_name": "genomics-lab",
  "network": "198.51.100.0/24", "client_country": "US", "requests": 412, "distinct_ips": 1,
  "last_seen_ms": 1794636531362, "first_seen_ms": 1793000000000, "network_first_seen_ms": 1794500000000}]
```

Each row is one key, network and country in the window, with `network_name` when one of your [named networks](#name-your-networks) holds it. `first_seen_ms` is the first time the key was ever seen from that country, kept after usage rows are pruned; `network_first_seen_ms` goes back as far as addresses are kept. A country or network first seen inside the window is new for that key. Filter with `tenant_id` or `key_id`, and set the window with `since_ms` and `until_ms` (default the last 24 hours, at most 31 days).

chunks.title: Where keys work
chunks.heading: Where the client address comes from
chunks.text:
When the connecting peer is a trusted proxy, the client comes from `X-Forwarded-For`. When the peer isn't a trusted proxy, the client is the peer.

**List your proxies.** With `OBLETH_TRUSTED_PROXIES` set, the gateway reads `X-Forwarded-For` from the right past every entry that is one of your proxies, and the first other address is the client. A request that passed a tunnel and then a load balancer (Cloudflare, then `cloudflared`, then HAProxy) is recorded at the client's address, not the tunnel's. Anything a client wrote to the left of that address is ignored, so a client can't claim an address by sending the header itself.

**The default** trusts every private and loopback range and takes only the **rightmost** entry, the one the nearest proxy added. It can't walk further: a client on a private network would look like a proxy, and could write any address and have its own skipped.

| Variable | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_TRUSTED_PROXIES` | the private and loopback ranges | Comma-separated CIDRs of your proxies, whose `X-Forwarded-For` is believed. `none` trusts no proxy |
| `OBLETH_CLIENT_ADDRESS_HEADER` | unset | A header a trusted proxy sets to exactly the client's address, such as `CF-Connecting-IP` or `X-Real-IP`. It wins over `X-Forwarded-For` when present |
| `OBLETH_CLIENT_COUNTRY_HEADER` | `cf-ipcountry` | Header a trusted proxy names the client's two-letter country in. Used only when the client address is public, and matches a key's allow

chunks.title: One key, many people
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A chatbot or other app with one key and many users
  The key's panel › Per-user fairshare
  `x-obleth-end-user`, or the request's `user`
  An administrator, one key at a time

A key's requests wait in the order they arrive. When an app sends everyone's requests through one key, a person with a long backlog holds up everyone else on that key. With per-user fairshare on, each person the app names waits in line on their own, as if they held their own key.

chunks.title: One key, many people
chunks.heading: See it working
chunks.text:
On **Fairshare**, each person appears in the key rows as the key's name and the person, such as `chatbot · user-4821`. The request ledger records the person in the `end_user` column of the ClickHouse `usage` table.

The setting has its own route, because `PUT /api/v1/keys/{id}` replaces every field and would otherwise turn it off whenever a key is edited without it.

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/keys/$KEY_ID/end-user-fairshare \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"end_user_fairshare": true}'
```

It returns 204, and the key's `end_user_fairshare` field shows the current value. **Replace…** keeps it, and backups carry it.

The gateway derives a queue id from the key and the person, so a person keeps their place across requests and gateway replicas, and people behind two different keys never share one. Like a key, a person's place is forgotten once they have nothing running or waiting. For people who need their own caps and budgets, use [identity tokens](/docs/clients/identity-tokens) instead: each person then gets a key of their own.

chunks.title: One key, many people
chunks.heading: Turn it on
chunks.text:
On **Tenants**, add a tenant for the app and set its weight: its share of each busy model against the other tenants. See [How fairshare works](/docs/sharing/how-fairshare-works).

Open the key on **API keys**, turn on **Per-user fairshare**, and save.

Send a stable id for the person on every request, in the `x-obleth-end-user` header or the request's `user` field. On `/v1/messages`, Anthropic's `metadata.user_id` works too. The header wins when both are sent.

  
    curl
    Python
  
  

```bash
curl https://gateway.example.com/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-obleth-end-user: user-4821" \
  -d '{"model": "qwen3-8b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}'
```

  
  

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://gateway.example.com/v1", api_key=OBLETH_KEY)
client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3-8b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
    user="user-4821",
)
```

chunks.title: One key, many people
chunks.heading: What changes
chunks.text:
- Each person gets their own place in the queue inside the key's tenant. The key's **Weight** and **Max in flight** apply to each person: a max in flight of 2 lets each person run two requests at a time in each model's pool.
- The tenant's weight, limits and budget still cover the whole app, and the key's budget, usage and cost stay on the key.
- A request that names no one shares the key's own place, as before.
- The header is not sent to the model's backend. The `user` field is passed on unchanged.

Ids are compared exactly after surrounding spaces are trimmed, and only the first 128 characters count.

Turn it on only for an app you trust to name people honestly. A caller that sends a new name on each request would otherwise jump ahead of the tenant's other keys.

chunks.title: Priority boost
chunks.heading: Boost a tenant from the Fairshare page
chunks.text:
On **Fairshare**, open the model pool that is queuing. Tenants waiting below their share are listed first as **Next in line**.

Choose the tenant. Its panel shows its weight, its cap on this model, and its keys.

Enter the new weight. The preview shows the tenant's new fair share in each pool and names the tenants that give up slots. A tenant's weight only moves slots inside its own group.

You can also change the weight under **Fairshare group and weight** on the tenant's page. To move slots between groups, change group weights on **Fairshare › Groups & weights**, which previews every group's new share before you save.

chunks.title: Priority boost
chunks.heading: Boost through the API
chunks.text:
```bash
# A tenant
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID/weight \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"weight": 1000}'

# A group
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/fairshare/groups/teaching/weight \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"weight": 400}'
```

A key's weight is set with `PUT /api/v1/keys/{id}`, which replaces all of the key's fields, so send its name, budget and cap along with the new weight. See [Tenants and keys](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys).

chunks.title: Priority boost
chunks.heading: During an incident
chunks.text:
A batch job is filling a model that an interactive service also uses. Raise the service's weight and lower the job's:

```bash
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$SERVICE_ID/weight \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"weight": 1000}'

curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$BATCH_ID/weight \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"weight": 10}'
```
