Requests already running finish; the next freed slots go to the service. If the job should never hold more than a few slots, also give it an in-flight cap on the model from the tenant's panel. Put the weights back when the incident is over.

For work that should only ever use spare capacity, such as labeling runs or benchmarks, give the tenant weight `1`. It loses every contended decision but still uses slots nobody else wants.

chunks.title: Priority boost
chunks.heading: Finding past changes
chunks.text:
Every weight change is in the audit log as `update_weight` (tenant), `update_fairshare_group_weight` (group) or `update_key` (key), with who made it. On **Audit**, filter by kind or search for the tenant's name. See [Audit log](/docs/dashboard/audit-log).

The change is written to Postgres and the audit log, the tenant's keys are re-pushed to Redis, and an invalidation on Redis pub/sub evicts them from every gateway's in-process cache. A group weight change re-pushes only the keys of tenants in that group. The scheduler reads the new weight on its next decision; no gateway restarts.

chunks.title: Priority boost
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A tenant, key or group weight
  On the next admission decision, on every replica
  Only pools that are full and queuing

chunks.title: Priority boost
chunks.heading: What a weight does
chunks.text:
Weights are ratios. In a full pool, a tenant with weight 400 gets twice the slots of a tenant with weight 200 in the same group. Weight does nothing while a pool has free slots, because every request is admitted at once. It does not change a tenant's token rate, budget or in-flight cap; see [Budgets and rate limits](/docs/sharing/quotas-and-rate-limits).

There are three levels of weight:

| Weight | Splits | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Group | Each pool between groups | `100` |
| Tenant | A group's share between its tenants | `100` |
| Key | A tenant's share between its keys | `100` |

Raising a tenant's weight raises all of its keys together. Raising one key's weight moves share toward that key inside its tenant. See [How fairshare works](/docs/sharing/how-fairshare-works).

chunks.title: Budgets and rate limits
chunks.heading: Access hours
chunks.text:
Access hours limit when a tenant may send traffic: a start date, an end date, weekly windows, or any mix, in the tenant's time zone. Outside them, requests are refused with 403 and a message saying why (not active yet, expired, or outside its scheduled window).

On the tenant's page, drag across the week grid. Through the API, windows are a day (`0` is Sunday) and start and end minutes from local midnight:

```bash
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID/schedule \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"timezone": "America/Phoenix", "active_until": "2026-12-20T00:00:00Z",
       "weekly_windows": [{"day": 1, "start_min": 1080, "end_min": 1440}]}'
```

chunks.title: Budgets and rate limits
chunks.heading: Budgets
chunks.text:
A budget is a cumulative cap over a period: a token cap, a dollar cap (from each model's prices), or both.

| Period | Resets |
| --- | --- |
| `monthly` | At the start of each calendar month, in the tenant's time zone |
| `term` | When you change the budget's start date |
| `lifetime` | Never. The default |

A tenant over its budget gets `403 tenant term budget exhausted`; a key over its own gets `403 api key term budget exhausted`. The key's budget is checked first.

```bash
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID/budget \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"budget_tokens": 50000000, "budget_cost_usd": 250, "budget_period": "monthly"}'
```

`null` clears a cap. Key budgets use the same three fields on the key; see [Tenants and keys](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys#keys). `GET /api/v1/budgets/usage` lists every capped tenant and key with its use in the current period, when the period started and when it resets.

chunks.title: Budgets and rate limits
chunks.heading: How the limits combine
chunks.text:
| Check | When it runs | Over the limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access hours, status, model list | Before admission | 403 |
| Pool size, tenant and key in-flight caps | Fairshare admission | Waits; 503 with `Retry-After` after the admission timeout |
| Key budget | After admission | `403 api key term budget exhausted` |
| Token rate | After admission | `429 token budget exceeded` |
| Tenant budget | After admission | `403 tenant term budget exhausted` |

A request refused by a budget or the token rate gives its slot back at once and never reaches the backend.

What happens follows `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN` (default `true`). Fail open admits the request without a reservation and raises a `redis_budget_reserve_failed_open` or `redis_key_budget_reserve_failed_open` alert. With `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN=false`, the request is refused with `503 budget check failed` (or `key budget check failed`) and the matching `*_failed_closed` alert is raised. Choose fail closed when overspending matters more than availability. See [Reliability](/docs/operate/reliability).

Committed budget usage in Redis has no expiry, so memory pressure cannot evict it and reset a budget mid-period.

Before admission the gateway estimates input tokens at about four characters per token, plus a small overhead per message. The output estimate is the request's `max_tokens` or `max_completion_tokens`, capped at 8192; without either, it is the input estimate clamped to between 512 and 8192. The same estimate is the request's wei

chunks.title: Budgets and rate limits
chunks.heading: In-flight caps
chunks.text:
A tenant's max in flight caps how many of its requests run at once in each model's pool. A key's max in flight does the same for one key. With several gateway replicas, the caps hold across all of them together.

Caps do not refuse requests. A request over its tenant's or key's cap waits in the queue like any other, and times out with a 503 after `OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS`; see [How fairshare works](/docs/sharing/how-fairshare-works#queued-requests-time-out). Use a cap to keep a batch job from filling a model even when nobody else is waiting.

chunks.title: Budgets and rate limits
chunks.heading: Model lists
chunks.text:
A model list limits a tenant to the models you name. Requests for any other model get `403 model not permitted for tenant`, `GET /v1/models` lists only the permitted ones, and `auto` routing picks only among them. An empty list permits every model.

```bash
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID/allowlist \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"allowed_models": ["llama-3.3-70b-instruct", "bge-m3"]}'
```

chunks.title: Budgets and rate limits
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Tokens per minute, per tenant
  In-flight caps per tenant and key, in each model's pool
  Token or dollar budgets per period, per tenant and key
  On the tenant's page, or in the key's panel

chunks.title: Budgets and rate limits
chunks.heading: Reserved, then reconciled
chunks.text:
Budgets are enforced in Redis, so they hold across every gateway replica.

1. **At admission**, the request's estimated tokens and cost are reserved against the cap. Concurrent requests count each other's reservations, so together they cannot pass the cap.
2. **At completion**, the reservation is released and the real usage is committed, once.
3. A reservation that never settles, for example after a crash, expires after 10 minutes.

A request that fails upstream without usage is not billed; a 502 or 504 after retries refunds its reservation. Calls the gateway makes on a request's behalf (vision, structured output, tool loops, speculative drafts, image generation) count against the same tenant and key budgets.

The gateway raises an alert when a tenant reaches 80% of a cap (`term_budget_warn:<tenant_id>`) and when it is used up (`term_budget_exhausted:<tenant_id>`), and the same per key. See [Alerting](/docs/operate/alerting).

chunks.title: Budgets and rate limits
chunks.heading: Set limits on a tenant
chunks.text:
On **Tenants**, open the tenant. **Limits right now** shows what is in force, with **Change** beside each line.

**Limits** holds the token rate and in-flight cap, **Access hours** the weekly grid and dates, **Budget** the spend and token caps, and **Models** the model list.

The save bar lists what changed. The gateway applies it on the next request, on every replica.

A key's own cap and budget are in its panel on **API keys**. Keys have no token rate of their own; they share their tenant's.

chunks.title: Budgets and rate limits
chunks.heading: Token rate
chunks.text:
The token rate (`tokens_per_minute`) is a token bucket per tenant. The bucket holds up to one minute's worth, so an idle tenant can burst that many tokens at once, and then refills at the set rate. A request that would overdraw it is refused with `429 token budget exceeded`. `0`, the default, means no rate limit.

Each request is charged its estimate when admitted and corrected to the real count when it finishes, so an estimate that ran high is refunded.

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID/quota \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tokens_per_minute": 2000000, "max_in_flight": 10}'
```

The quota call sets both fields at once: send `"max_in_flight": null` for no cap.

chunks.title: Tenants and keys
chunks.heading: Add a tenant and a key
chunks.text:
On **Tenants**, choose **Add tenant**. Give it a name, and optionally a fairshare group and weight.

On the tenant's page, choose **New key** (or use **New key** on **API keys** and pick the tenant). The secret is shown once, in a banner with **Copy** and **Copy as `OPENAI_API_KEY=…`**. The gateway keeps only a hash of it.

Clients send the key as `Authorization: Bearer sk_…` or as `x-api-key: sk_…`, the header Anthropic SDKs use. See [OpenAI-compatible API](/docs/clients/openai-compatible-api).

The same through the Management API:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "genomics-lab", "fairshare_group": "research", "weight": 200}'

curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID/keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "variant-pipeline"}'
# {"key": {...}, "secret": "sk_..."}
```

chunks.title: Tenants and keys
chunks.heading: Background priority
chunks.text:
Turn on **Background priority** in a key's panel for traffic that can wait, such as a nightly job or an evaluation run sent through one key. Its requests to a model run in that model's [background pool](/docs/sharing/how-fairshare-works#background-work-uses-a-background-pool), the one batches use:

- Nothing new starts for the key while an interactive request is waiting for that model.
- It never holds more than `OBLETH_BATCH_MAX_SHARE` (default `0.75`) of a model's slots.
- A request waits up to an hour for a slot instead of returning a 503 after `OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS`, so give the client a long enough timeout. A client that disconnects leaves the queue as usual.

Everything else about the key stays the same: streaming, budgets, usage and its tenant. The keys list marks the key **Background**. Only operators can set it, with its own route, so `PUT /api/v1/keys/{id}` never turns it off. **Replace…** and backups keep it.

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/keys/$KEY_ID/background \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"background": true}'
```

chunks.title: Tenants and keys
chunks.heading: Fairshare groups
chunks.text:
A group is a set of tenants that share one weight: a department, or all teaching tenants against all research tenants. Each pool is split between active groups by group weight first, then between each group's tenants. Every tenant is in the `default` group until you move it.

Change group weights on **Fairshare › Groups & weights**, which previews every group's new share before you save. Change a tenant's group on its page. Through the API:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/fairshare/groups \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "research", "weight": 300}'

curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT_ID/group \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"fairshare_group": "research"}'
```

Groups apply under the default `hierarchical` algorithm. With `OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_ALGORITHM=weighted`, all tenants compete directly and groups are ignored.

chunks.title: Tenants and keys
chunks.heading: Keys
chunks.text:
Give each person, application or pipeline its own key. All of a tenant's keys share its limits, budget and model list, and each key can also carry:

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weight | `100` | Its share of the tenant's slots against the tenant's other keys |
| Max in flight | none | A cap on its running requests, applied in each model's pool |
| Budget | none | Its own spend or token cap per period, checked before the tenant's |
| Per-user fairshare | off | For a key an app shares among many people: each person it names waits in line on their own. See [One key, many people](/docs/sharing/one-key-many-people) |
| Background priority | off | Its requests use only spare capacity. See [Background priority](#background-priority) |
| Allowed networks | any | Where it may be used from; requests from anywhere else are refused. See [Where keys work](/docs/sharing/key-networks) |

**API keys** shows every key with its tenant, status, last use, 30-day requests and spend, budget for the current period, and weight. Tiles count keys used today, near a budget, and unused for 30 days.

![The API keys page: tiles for keys used today, near a budget and unused for 30 days, above a list of keys with tenant, status, last use, requests, spend, budget this period and weight](/dashboard/keys.png)

Open a key for its 30-day use, its settings with a save bar, and **Replace…**, **Move…** and **Delete…**. **Replace…** makes a new key with the same settings; the old one ke

chunks.title: Tenants and keys
chunks.heading: Move keys to another tenant
chunks.text:
**Move…** takes keys to another tenant, or to a new tenant made for them. A new tenant can copy the source tenant's weight, group, limits, hours, budget, models and policies. This gives a heavy user a share of their own without handing out a new secret. Past usage stays with the tenant it was recorded under.

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9180/api/v1/keys/$KEY_ID/tenant \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tenant_id": "'"$NEW_TENANT_ID"'"}'
```

chunks.title: Tenants and keys
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A team, course or service that gets a share
  Tenants that share one group weight
  One credential, in one tenant
  Tenants and API keys in the dashboard

chunks.title: Tenants and keys
chunks.heading: Portal users
chunks.text:
People who sign in with SSO can manage their own tenant's keys without dashboard access. On **Users**, give the account the `user` role and link it to a tenant. They land in the portal, which has three pages:

| Page | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| `/portal/models` | The models the tenant may use. Upstream URLs and keys are never sent |
| `/portal/keys` | The tenant's keys with their last day of use. Users can create, turn off and delete keys, but not turn back on a key an administrator turned off |
| `/portal/usage` | The tenant's usage and its most recent requests |

See [Sign-in and SSO](/docs/dashboard/dashboard-sso).

A key is its prefix, `_`, then 56 hex characters: 48 random, then an 8-character CRC-32 checksum, so a mistyped key is refused before any lookup and secret scanners can recognise one. The prefix is `sk` unless you choose another under **Settings › Keys**: 1 to 3 lowercase letters or digits, starting with a letter, such as `obl`, `rc` or `air`. Changing it affects only new keys; keys with any prefix keep working, and so do keys made before v2.7.0, which are `sk_` and 48 hex characters with no checksum. An instance that made `obl_` keys under v2.7.0 keeps `obl` after upgrading. Set the starting value with `OBLETH_KEY_PREFIX`, or through `PUT /api/v1/settings/key-prefix`. A proxy that routes by the shape of a key must accept a new prefix before you change it. The gateway stores its SHA-256 hash and a display prefix (the first 18 characters) and returns the s

chunks.title: Tenants and keys
chunks.heading: Tenants
chunks.text:
A tenant is the unit fairshare divides between: every key belongs to exactly one tenant, and a tenant's weight sets its share of each model's pool against the other tenants in its group. See [How fairshare works](/docs/sharing/how-fairshare-works).

**Tenants** lists every tenant with its group and weight, keys, users, requests in the last day, spend against its budget, limits, and whether its access hours are open now. Filter by status, group, or what a tenant has set, such as a budget, access hours, a model list, guardrails, or being near a limit.

![The Tenants list: seven active tenants with their group and weight, keys, 24-hour requests, spend against budget, token rate and waiting requests, and access hours](/dashboard/tenants.png)

Each tenant has its own page at `/tenants/<name>`: requests and failures in the last day, its budget and where the current pace lands, running requests against fair share, a 30-day chart, its limits right now, the models it uses, its keys and people, and recent changes.

![A tenant's page: tiles for requests, failures, budget, running requests against fair share and tokens, a 30-day chart, the limits in force right now and the models it uses](/dashboard/tenant.png)

Below that, every setting sits on one page with **Find a setting** (`⌘K`) and one save bar:

| Setting | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Fairshare group and weight | Its share of each pool when everyone is busy. Weight defaults to `100`; the page previews the resulting share |
| T

chunks.title: Install with Docker Compose
chunks.heading: Install
chunks.text:
```bash
git clone https://github.com/thediymaker/obleth-gateway.git
cd obleth-gateway/deploy/docker
cp .env.example .env
```

Run every `docker compose` command from this directory, so Compose reads `.env` and merges a `docker-compose.override.yml` if you add one.

Compose refuses to start while a required value is empty, but the example file fills them with development values. Replace each one:

```bash
OBLETH_VERSION=v2.4.0
OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN=...          # openssl rand -hex 32
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=...
REDIS_PASSWORD=...              # URL-safe: openssl rand -hex 32
CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=...
DASHBOARD_ADMIN_EMAIL=you@example.org
DASHBOARD_PASSWORD=...          # at least 8 characters
DASHBOARD_SESSION_SECRET=...    # at least 32 characters
OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY=...       # openssl rand -base64 32
GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD=...      # only with the observability profile
```

The gateway connects to Redis at `redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD}@redis:6379`, so the password must not contain `@ : / ? # %` or spaces. Postgres takes its password only when its volume is first created; changing it later in `.env` does not change the database's password.

Set `COMPOSE_PROFILES` in `.env` (see [Profiles](#profiles)). For real models, drop `benchmark` and set the default upstream; each registered model's own `api_base` overrides it:

```bash
COMPOSE_PROFILES=edge
OBLETH_UPSTREAM_BASE_URL=http://my-model-server:8000/v1
```

```bash
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
curl -s http://localhost:8088/h

chunks.title: Install with Docker Compose
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
One host with Docker and Compose v2
  `deploy/docker/` in the gateway repo
  `ghcr.io/thediymaker/obleth-gateway/*`, tag `v2.4.0`

The Compose stack always runs the gateway, the dashboard, Postgres, Redis and ClickHouse. Everything else is behind a profile you opt into.

chunks.title: Install with Docker Compose
chunks.heading: Ports and exposure
chunks.text:
| Service | Host port | Bound to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data plane | 8088 | All interfaces |
| HAProxy (`edge`) | 80 | All interfaces |
| Dashboard | 3002 | All interfaces |
| Grafana (`observability`) | 3001 | All interfaces |
| Management API | 9180 | 127.0.0.1 |
| Metrics | 9091 | 127.0.0.1 |
| Postgres, Redis, ClickHouse | 5432, 6379, 8123 and 9000 | 127.0.0.1 |
| Prometheus, Jaeger | 9090, 16686 | 127.0.0.1 |

HAProxy in this stack listens on plain HTTP. Put TLS in front of the data plane and the dashboard before anyone else uses them; see [HAProxy](/docs/reference/haproxy) and [Security](/docs/operate/security).

chunks.title: Install with Docker Compose
chunks.heading: Profiles
chunks.text:
| Profile | Starts | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *(none)* | `obleth`, `control-plane`, `postgres`, `redis`, `clickhouse` | Always on |
| `benchmark` | `benchmark-backend`, a simulated model server | Trying things out and load tests; `mock` is an older alias |
| `edge` | `haproxy` on port 80 | A front door when you have no load balancer |
| `observability` | Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger, Postgres and Redis exporters | Metrics and traces on the same host |
| `slurm` | `obleth-provisioner` | Models launched on Slurm; see [Slurm provisioning](/docs/deployments/slurm-provisioning) |
| `compressor` | The neural prose compression sidecar | The compression boon's neural scoring |
| `sso-dev` | `dex`, a local OIDC provider | Developing dashboard SSO |

The example `.env` sets `COMPOSE_PROFILES=benchmark,edge,observability`. Leave it empty for the core services only. You can also add a profile for one command: `docker compose --profile slurm up -d`.

chunks.title: Install with Docker Compose
chunks.heading: Settings that matter in production
chunks.text:
| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_VERSION` | Pin a release such as `v2.4.0`. The default `latest` moves with each release; `dev` tracks unreleased builds. |
| `OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Encrypts upstream API keys, MCP credentials and upstream headers in Postgres. Unset, they are stored in plaintext and the gateway logs a warning. |
| `OBLETH_API_KEY_PEPPER` | A secret mixed into API-key hashes. Set it before you issue keys: changing it later invalidates every key. |
| `BETTER_AUTH_URL`, `TRUSTED_ORIGINS` | The URL people use to reach the dashboard. Sign-in from any other origin is refused. |
| `OBLETH_OTEL_ENDPOINT` | OTLP/HTTP collector for traces, for example `http://jaeger:4318`. Empty turns tracing off. |
| `OBLETH_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` | Alerts to Slack. |
| `OIDC_PROVIDERS` | Dashboard sign-in through your identity provider; see [Sign-in and SSO](/docs/dashboard/dashboard-sso). |

The Compose file fixes some gateway settings rather than reading them from `.env`: the global in-flight ceiling (4096), the default pool size (32), fairshare history (3600 s), the fairshare algorithm (`hierarchical`) and fail-open (`true`). To change one, set it under `services.obleth.environment` in a `docker-compose.override.yml`. [Docker Compose](/docs/reference/docker-compose) lists what is fixed and what is forwarded; [Environment variables](/docs/reference/environment-variables) has every setting.

chunks.title: Install with Docker Compose
chunks.heading: Upgrade
chunks.text:
Set the new `OBLETH_VERSION`, then `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`. Compose gives the gateway 345 seconds to drain in-flight requests before it stops. Read [Upgrades](/docs/operate/upgrades) first: some releases need a step before the new version starts.

Add `compressor` to `COMPOSE_PROFILES` and set `OBLETH_COMPRESSOR_URL=http://compressor:8080`; without the URL the gateway doesn't call the sidecar even when it runs. Its image bakes an ONNX model of about 600 MB, so the first pull or build is slow. It follows `OBLETH_VERSION`; `OBLETH_COMPRESSOR_VERSION` pins it to another tag. If the sidecar is unreachable, compression falls back to its built-in heuristics. See [Boons](/docs/boons/overview).

`deploy/docker/datastores.compose.yml` runs Postgres, Redis and ClickHouse alone, with named volumes, health checks and Redis append-only persistence, for a gateway that runs elsewhere (a Helm install with external datastores, or the binary):

```bash
cp datastores.env.example datastores.env    # set the passwords
docker compose --env-file datastores.env -f datastores.compose.yml up -d
```

Ports bind to `BIND_ADDR`, `127.0.0.1` by default. Change it to a private interface only behind a firewall, and never expose these ports to the internet. Connect with the `obleth` ClickHouse user from `datastores.env`, not `default`, which is limited to localhost.

chunks.title: First tenant and key
chunks.heading: Check that it worked
chunks.text:
- **Request Logs** in the dashboard shows the request with its tenant, key, tokens and timing. With the API: `GET /api/v1/usage/logs`.
- **Audit** shows the tenant and key you created. With the API: `GET /api/v1/audit`.
- **Fairshare** shows the model's pool and the tenant's share while requests run.

If the request fails, the status tells you where: 401 is the key, 403 a disabled key or model or a tenant outside its allowed models or hours, 404 an unregistered model. See [Troubleshooting](/docs/operate/troubleshooting).

| Step | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Tenant and key | Postgres (`tenants`, `api_keys`), with an audit row each |
| Key lookup entry | Redis, `obleth:key3:<hash>`, holding the tenant's and key's weights and limits |
| Per-minute token bucket | Redis, `obleth:budget:<tenant id>` |
| Usage row | ClickHouse, `usage` |

Minting a key writes the hash to Postgres, pushes the resolved key to Redis and publishes an invalidation so every gateway replica drops any stale copy. Creating a tenant writes only Postgres; its settings reach Redis inside each of its keys. If Redis loses an entry, the gateway re-pushes every key from Postgres every `OBLETH_REDIS_REWARM_SECS` (300 s) and on reconnect. See [Request lifecycle](/docs/how-it-works/request-lifecycle) for what happened to the request.

```bash
docker compose exec clickhouse clickhouse-client --user obleth --password "$CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD" \
  --query "SELECT tenant_id, model, admission, input_tokens, output_tokens, total_

chunks.title: First tenant and key
chunks.heading: In the dashboard
chunks.text:
Open **Tenants** and choose **Add tenant**. A name is enough; the weight defaults to 100 and every limit is off. You can change all of it later on the tenant's page.

Open **API Keys** and choose **New key**, or **New key** on the tenant's page. The secret appears once in a banner with **Copy** and **Copy as OPENAI_API_KEY=…**. Store it now: only its hash is kept.

Add one on the **Models** page if you haven't; see [Model registry](/docs/models/model-registry). Models added in the dashboard start switched off and turn on when their first health check passes.

![API Keys: a table of keys with tenant, status, last use, 30-day requests, spend, budget and weight](/dashboard/keys.png)

chunks.title: First tenant and key
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A running gateway and its admin token
  The dashboard, or the management API on port 9180
  A few minutes

A **tenant** is who gets a share of capacity: it carries the fairshare weight, group, limits and budgets. A **key** belongs to one tenant and is what a client sends. There is no shared or open key; every client needs its own key or an [identity token](/docs/clients/identity-tokens). The admin token (`OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN`) only works on the management API, never for inference.

chunks.title: First tenant and key
chunks.heading: With the management API
chunks.text:
```bash
TOKEN=dev-admin-token      # your OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN
API=http://localhost:9180/api/v1

TID=$(curl -s -X POST $API/tenants \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"my-team","weight":200,"tokens_per_minute":500000}' | jq -r .id)
```

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | required | Unique tenant name |
| `weight` | `100` | Fairshare weight against other tenants in its group |
| `fairshare_group` | `default` | The [group](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys) it competes in |
| `tokens_per_minute` | `0` (no cap) | Per-minute token rate |
| `max_in_flight` | none | Cap on this tenant's running requests, applied per model |
| `synthetic` | `false` | Marks test or benchmark traffic, left out of usage reports |

Schedules, budgets, model lists and guardrails are set afterwards; see [Tenants and keys](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys) and [Quotas and rate limits](/docs/sharing/quotas-and-rate-limits).

```bash
SECRET=$(curl -s -X POST $API/tenants/$TID/keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"prod"}' | jq -r .secret)
```

The response is `{"key": {…}, "secret": "sk_…"}`. Optional fields: `description`, `weight` (default 100, shares the tenant's slots among its keys), `max_in_flight` (per model), and a key budget (`budget_tokens`, `budget_cost_usd`, `budget_period`). See [API keys](/docs/sharing/tenants-and-keys).

chunks.title: Introduction
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
obleth is a gateway you run in front of model servers that have a fixed capacity: vLLM, SGLang, an inference gateway, or any OpenAI-compatible server you run yourself, on-prem or in your own cloud account. Clients send requests to one endpoint. obleth identifies the caller, decides who goes next when a model's backend is busy, forwards the request, and records what it cost.

These docs describe release **v2.4.0**.

![The dashboard Overview: requests, tokens, error rate, time to first token and spend, with a Needs attention card for a full pool and tenants waiting below their fair share](/dashboard/overview.png)

chunks.title: Introduction
chunks.heading: What it adds
chunks.text:
- **Fairshare admission per model.** Every model has its own pool of slots. When a pool is full, requests wait in a queue and each freed slot goes to the fairshare group, tenant and key furthest behind its weighted share. A busy model never holds up one with free capacity. See [Fairshare engine](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine).
- **Automatic routing.** Send `model: "auto"` and the gateway picks a registered model from the request's needs, cost and live load. See [Auto routing](/docs/routing/auto-model-routing).
- **Usage accounting.** Tokens, cost and energy are recorded per request. Per-minute token rates and term budgets are reserved at admission and settled to real usage afterwards; failed requests are not billed. See [Quotas and rate limits](/docs/sharing/quotas-and-rate-limits).
- **Boons.** Capabilities the gateway grants a model that lacks them: vision, structured output, compression, knowledge retrieval, image generation, tool use through MCP servers, and speculative drafting. See [Boons](/docs/boons/overview).
- **Guardrails.** Per-tenant scanning of request and response text for prompt injection, PII, banned keywords or harm, with block, redact or log actions. See [Guardrails](/docs/routing/guardrails).
- **One endpoint for many APIs.** The OpenAI API (chat, completions, embeddings, audio, images, rerank, moderations), the Responses API, the Anthropic Messages API for Claude Code and the Anthropic SDKs, the Videos API, typed [verdicts](/docs/clients/verdicts),

chunks.title: Introduction
chunks.heading: When it fits
chunks.text:
- Several teams, courses or services share models whose capacity you can't grow on demand.
- You want requests to wait their turn by weight when a model is full, instead of failing with 429.
- You want usage and cost attributed per tenant and key, in tokens.
- You want OpenAI and Anthropic clients to reach self-hosted models through one endpoint.

It is not built for spreading traffic across many hosted cloud providers, and its response cache is exact-match only, not semantic.

chunks.title: Introduction
chunks.heading: Where it sits
chunks.text:
- The **data plane** serves client traffic, authenticated with tenant API keys (`sk_…`) or identity-provider tokens.
- The **management API** creates tenants, keys and models, changes weights and reads usage. It takes a separate admin token.
- The **dashboard** is a web app that works only through the management API.

obleth decides *who* sends and in what order. It does not pick which replica serves a request: that stays with your inference gateway or load balancer. See [Inference gateways](/docs/models/inference-gateways) and [Architecture](/docs/how-it-works/architecture).

chunks.title: Introduction
chunks.heading: Where to go next
chunks.text:
- [Quick start](/docs/start/quick-start): run it locally with Docker Compose and send a first request.
- [Install with Docker Compose](/docs/start/docker) or [Install on Kubernetes](/docs/start/kubernetes) for a real install.
- [First tenant and key](/docs/start/first-tenant-and-key): the first thing to do after installing.
- [Connect clients](/docs/clients/openai-compatible-api): point SDKs and tools at the gateway.
- [Model registry](/docs/models/model-registry): register the models you serve.

The source, Compose files and Helm chart are in [obleth-gateway](https://github.com/thediymaker/obleth-gateway). See [License](/license) for the terms.

chunks.title: Install on Kubernetes
chunks.heading: After install
chunks.text:
Port-forward `svc/<release>-obleth` port 9180, or call it from inside the cluster.

Follow [First tenant and key](/docs/start/first-tenant-and-key). Each client needs its own `sk_…` key or an [identity token](/docs/clients/identity-tokens).

In the dashboard's Models page, the API or a manifest; see [Model registry](/docs/models/model-registry). In-cluster addresses such as `*.svc.cluster.local` are allowed by default. With `obleth.blockPrivateNetworks: true` (`OBLETH_BLOCK_PRIVATE_NETWORKS=1`), list your pod network in `obleth.allowedPrivateCidrs`; see [Security](/docs/operate/security).

Clients call port 8080 of `<release>-obleth`, or your Ingress, with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` or `x-api-key`.

chunks.title: Install on Kubernetes
chunks.heading: Choose where the datastores live
chunks.text:
| Scenario | Values file | Data survives a restart | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bundled, on PVCs | `values-persistent.yaml` | Yes | One cluster, no managed datastores yet |
| Bundled, ephemeral | `values-ephemeral.yaml` | **No** | Demos and CI; keeps the benchmark backend |
| External | `values-external.yaml` | Managed by you | Datastores you run or buy, with backups and HA |
| Production | `values-production.yaml` | Managed by you | External datastores plus pre-created Secrets, three gateway replicas, two dashboard replicas and a disruption budget |

**Bundled datastores** each run as one Deployment with the `Recreate` strategy. Their PVCs use the cluster's default StorageClass unless you set `<store>.persistence.storageClass`; if a datastore pod stays Pending, its PVC didn't bind. They have no backups and no failover. The bundled Redis runs with a 512Mi limit, `maxmemory 400mb` and `volatile-lru`, so only entries with a TTL are evicted. The bundled ClickHouse keeps 7 days of its own system logs (`clickhouse.systemLogRetentionDays`); give an external ClickHouse a retention of its own.

With `persistence.enabled: false`, every tenant, key, model and usage row is lost when a datastore pod restarts, including on `helm upgrade` or a node drain.

**External datastores** are set with `<store>.enabled: false` and `<store>.external.url`; the chart refuses to render without the URL. ClickHouse still needs `clickhouse.user` and `clickhouse.password`. Redis must present a

chunks.title: Install on Kubernetes
chunks.heading: Install
chunks.text:
Choose one of the [scenarios below](#choose-where-the-datastores-live) and download its values file from `deploy/k8s/obleth/examples/` for the release you install. Edit `obleth.upstreamBaseUrl` and the Ingress host.

```bash
helm install obleth oci://ghcr.io/thediymaker/charts/obleth --version 2.4.0 \
  -n obleth --create-namespace -f values-persistent.yaml \
  --set obleth.adminToken="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \
  --set obleth.encryptionKey="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  --set postgres.password="$(openssl rand -hex 16)" \
  --set redis.password="$(openssl rand -hex 16)" \
  --set clickhouse.password="$(openssl rand -hex 16)" \
  --set controlPlane.dashboardPassword="$(openssl rand -hex 16)" \
  --set controlPlane.dashboardSessionSecret="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
```

Without these values the chart refuses to render. `redis.password` goes into the Redis URL unescaped, so it must not contain `@ : / ? # %` or spaces; hex is always safe. To install from a checkout, use `./deploy/k8s/obleth` instead of the OCI reference. Keep the generated values: the next `helm upgrade` needs them, or use [pre-created Secrets](#production).

```bash
kubectl -n obleth port-forward svc/obleth-obleth 9180:9180
curl -s http://localhost:9180/api/v1/health    # ok
```

Services are named after the release: `<release>-obleth` (ports 8080, 9180, 9091) and `<release>-control-plane` (port 3000).

The chart creates none. Until you do, requests return 401 (no key) or 404 (no model). See [After install](#aft

chunks.title: Install on Kubernetes
chunks.heading: Optional components
chunks.text:
| Value | Default | Turns on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ingress.enabled` | `false` | An Ingress for the data plane (`ingress.className`, `host`, `tls`); the dashboard needs its own, see [Reach the dashboard](#reach-the-dashboard) |
| `networkPolicy.enabled` | `false` | NetworkPolicies: bundled datastores admit only the gateway (and the dashboard, for Postgres); the management API port admits only the dashboard and provisioner |
| `serviceMonitor.enabled` | `false` | A Prometheus Operator ServiceMonitor |
| `obleth.otelEndpoint` | `""` | OTLP/HTTP trace export |
| `obleth.capacityDiscovery.enabled` | `false` | Pool sizes that follow a model's ready replicas; see [Pool sizes](/docs/models/pool-sizes) |
| `provisioner.enabled` | `false` | The Slurm provisioner, a single replica; see [Slurm provisioning](/docs/deployments/slurm-provisioning) |
| `compressor.enabled` | `false` | The compression sidecar, wired to the gateway automatically |
| `benchmarkBackend.enabled` | `true` | The simulated model server; turn it off and set `obleth.upstreamBaseUrl` for real models |

chunks.title: Install on Kubernetes
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A Kubernetes cluster, kubectl and Helm 3
  `oci://ghcr.io/thediymaker/charts/obleth`, version `2.4.0`
  `deploy/k8s/obleth/examples/` in the gateway repo

The chart runs the gateway and the dashboard, and either runs Postgres, Redis and ClickHouse itself or connects to ones you run. Image tags default to `v` plus the chart's `appVersion`, so chart 2.4.0 runs the `v2.4.0` images.

chunks.title: Install on Kubernetes
chunks.heading: Production
chunks.text:
Production keeps real credentials out of values files and shell history by pointing the chart at Secrets you create, with `obleth.existingSecret` and `controlPlane.existingSecret`. The chart then renders no Secret of its own, so the Secret must hold every key the gateway reads:

```bash
kubectl -n obleth create secret generic obleth-secrets \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_DATABASE_URL="postgres://obleth:PASS@pg-rw.db.svc:5432/obleth" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_REDIS_URL="redis://:PASS@redis.db.svc:6379" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD="PASS" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_ENCRYPTION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_API_KEY_PEPPER="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL="" \
  --from-literal=OBLETH_JWT_ISSUERS=""

SESSION="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
kubectl -n obleth create secret generic obleth-control-plane \
  --from-literal=DASHBOARD_ADMIN_EMAIL="admin@example.org" \
  --from-literal=DASHBOARD_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -hex 16)" \
  --from-literal=DASHBOARD_SESSION_SECRET="$SESSION" \
  --from-literal=BETTER_AUTH_SECRET="$SESSION" \
  --from-literal=DATABASE_URL="postgres://obleth:PASS@pg-rw.db.svc:5432/obleth" \
  --from-literal=BETTER_AUTH_URL="https://dashboard.example.org" \
  --from-literal=TRUSTED_ORIGINS="" \
  --from-literal=OIDC_PROVIDERS=""

helm install obleth oci://ghcr.io/thediymaker/charts/obleth --version 2.4.0 \
  -n obleth -f values-produc

chunks.title: Install on Kubernetes
chunks.heading: Reach the dashboard
chunks.text:
The chart's Ingress covers only the data plane, so give the dashboard one of its own, pointing at `<release>-control-plane` port 3000:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: obleth-dashboard
  namespace: obleth
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx        # your Ingress class
  rules:
    - host: dashboard.example.org
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: obleth-control-plane
                port: { number: 3000 }
```

Set `controlPlane.betterAuthUrl` to the address people open, such as `https://dashboard.example.org`, and list every other address they use (a LAN IP, the other scheme) in `controlPlane.trustedOrigins`, comma-separated. Sign-in from an address in neither is refused with `Invalid origin`. Sign in with `controlPlane.dashboardAdminEmail` (default `admin@example.com`) and `controlPlane.dashboardPassword`.

Without an Ingress, port-forward the dashboard's Service:

```bash
kubectl -n obleth port-forward svc/obleth-control-plane 3000:3000
```

Then open `http://localhost:3000`, after adding it to `controlPlane.trustedOrigins` (or making it `controlPlane.betterAuthUrl`). Port-forwarding to the dashboard works from chart 2.1.0, which sets the dashboard to listen on all interfaces; in earlier charts it listened only on its pod's IP and the forward didn't connect.

chunks.title: Install on Kubernetes
chunks.heading: Replicas and capacity
chunks.text: Pool sizes, `obleth.globalMaxInFlight` (default 4096) and per-tenant and per-key caps hold across all gateway replicas together: the replicas share slots in Redis. Adding replicas or turning on the HPA (`hpa.enabled`) adds gateway capacity, not backend concurrency. See [Fairshare engine](/docs/how-it-works/fairshare-engine#multiple-gateway-replicas) and [Scaling](/docs/operate/scaling).

chunks.title: Install on Kubernetes
chunks.heading: Upgrade
chunks.text:
Use `helm upgrade --install` against the same chart source you installed from, with your own `-f` values file. Values in the chart's own `values.yaml` belong to that source. When a value in the chart-rendered gateway Secret changes, the gateway, Redis and ClickHouse pods roll on their own. After changing a pre-created Secret or the dashboard's Secret, run `kubectl rollout restart` on the affected Deployments yourself. Release-specific steps are in [Upgrades](/docs/operate/upgrades), and the Secret keys 2.0.0 added in [Upgrading from v1.x](/docs/operate/upgrade-from-v1).

The sidecar is CPU-only and stateless. One inference saturates at about four cores, so scale it with replicas rather than bigger pods, keep `compressor.numThreads` equal to `resources.limits.cpu`, and always set CPU limits: without them the scorer takes whole nodes and CPU autoscaling means nothing. Each pod holds about 900 MB of model in memory.

```yaml
compressor:
  enabled: true
  replicas: 4
  numThreads: 4
  resources:
    requests: { cpu: "4", memory: 1536Mi }
    limits:   { cpu: "4", memory: 2Gi }
  autoscaling:
    enabled: true
    minReplicas: 4
    maxReplicas: 24
    targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70
```

If the sidecar can't be reached, compression falls back to its heuristics and the request goes on. See [Boons](/docs/boons/overview).

chunks.title: Local development
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Stable Rust, Node.js and npm, and Docker for the datastores
  `obleth/` (gateway), `control-plane/` (dashboard), `benchmark-backend/`
  Data plane 8080, management API 9180, dashboard 3000

Running the code natively gives faster rebuilds and a debugger. The datastores still run in Docker from the Compose file.

chunks.title: Local development
chunks.heading: Run the benchmark backend
chunks.text:
A simulated OpenAI-compatible model server that streams tokens with a configurable delay, no GPU needed:

```bash
cd obleth-gateway/benchmark-backend
cargo run --release          # listens on 0.0.0.0:8081
```

chunks.title: Local development
chunks.heading: Run the dashboard
chunks.text:
```bash
cd obleth-gateway/control-plane
cp .env.example .env.local
npm install
npm run dev                  # http://localhost:3000
```

The dashboard reads `.env.local`, not `deploy/docker/.env`. The example points it at a gateway on `localhost:9180` and the same Postgres, and sets the sign-in values it refuses to start without: sign in as `admin@example.com` / `obleth-admin`. Set `OBLETH_PROXY_BASE_URL` (default `http://localhost:8080`) if your gateway's data plane listens elsewhere; the Playground uses it.

chunks.title: Local development
chunks.heading: Run the gateway
chunks.text:
The `obleth/` workspace builds two binaries, the gateway (`obleth`) and the Slurm provisioner (`obleth-provisioner`), so name the one to run:

```bash
cd obleth-gateway/obleth
export OBLETH_DATABASE_URL=postgres://obleth:obleth@localhost:5432/obleth
export OBLETH_REDIS_URL=redis://:dev-redis-password@localhost:6379
export OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_URL=http://localhost:8123
export OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_USER=obleth
export OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=obleth
export OBLETH_UPSTREAM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8081
export OBLETH_ADMIN_TOKEN=dev-admin-token
export RUST_LOG=info,obleth=debug
cargo run --release --bin obleth
```

The gateway applies its Postgres migrations and ClickHouse schema at start; there is no separate migration step. `OBLETH_CLICKHOUSE_USER` defaults to `default`, which the ClickHouse image limits to connections from inside its container, so set it to `obleth`. If ClickHouse is unreachable the gateway still starts and writes usage to its spill file (`OBLETH_WAL_PATH`, default `./obleth-telemetry.wal`) until it returns.

For a release binary, `cargo build --release --bin obleth` puts it at `target/release/obleth`.

chunks.title: Local development
chunks.heading: Run the tests
chunks.text:
```bash
cd obleth-gateway/obleth
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets
cargo test --workspace

cd ../control-plane
npm test
npm run build
```

Unit tests need no services. Integration tests run only when their URLs are set, and are skipped otherwise:

```bash
export OBLETH_TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgres://obleth:obleth@localhost:5432/obleth_test
export OBLETH_TEST_REDIS_URL=redis://:dev-redis-password@localhost:6379
```

The test database name must contain `test`; the tests refuse to run against any other. Point them at data you can lose. CI also runs `bash scripts/check-versions.sh` and a release build of `benchmark-backend/`; see `CONTRIBUTING.md` in the repo.

chunks.title: Local development
chunks.heading: Settings worth changing while developing
chunks.text:
| Variable | Default | Try |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OBLETH_DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` | `32` | `4`, to make requests queue |
| `OBLETH_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_SECS` | `60` | Lower, to see queued requests time out with 503 |
| `OBLETH_FAIRSHARE_ALGORITHM` | `hierarchical` | `weighted`, for flat tenant scheduling |
| `OBLETH_FAIL_OPEN` | `true` | `false`, to see budget checks fail closed when Redis is down |
| `OBLETH_OTEL_ENDPOINT` | unset | `http://localhost:4318` with a local Jaeger |

Every setting is in [Environment variables](/docs/reference/environment-variables).

Set `OBLETH_VERSION=dev` in `deploy/docker/.env` and run `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d` from `deploy/docker/`. Edge builds include the compression sidecar, which follows `OBLETH_VERSION` unless `OBLETH_COMPRESSOR_VERSION` is set.

chunks.title: Local development
chunks.heading: Start the datastores
chunks.text:
```bash
cd obleth-gateway/deploy/docker
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d postgres redis clickhouse
```

With the example `.env` they listen on `127.0.0.1`: Postgres and ClickHouse as `obleth` / `obleth`, Redis with the password `dev-redis-password`.

chunks.title: Local development
chunks.heading: Try it
chunks.text: Follow [First tenant and key](/docs/start/first-tenant-and-key) against `http://localhost:9180`, register a model with `"api_base": "http://localhost:8081"`, and send requests to `http://localhost:8080`.

chunks.title: Quick start
chunks.heading: If something fails
chunks.text:
- **401 `invalid api key`**: you sent the admin token, or a key that doesn't exist. Send the `sk_…` secret.
- **503 `authentication backend unavailable`**: the gateway couldn't reach Redis. Check the `redis` container, and that `REDIS_PASSWORD` hasn't changed since the volume was created.
- **404 `model '…' is not registered`**: register the model (step 3) or fix the `model` field. A disabled model returns 403.
- **Connection refused on 8080**: Compose publishes the data plane on 8088. Use `http://localhost` or `http://localhost:8088`.

More cases are in [Troubleshooting](/docs/operate/troubleshooting).

Sign-in checks the browser's origin against `BETTER_AUTH_URL` (default `http://localhost:3002`). Set it to the URL you browse to, or list extra origins in `TRUSTED_ORIGINS`, then run `docker compose up -d` again. See [Sign-in and SSO](/docs/dashboard/dashboard-sso).

chunks.title: Quick start
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Docker with Compose v2, git, curl and jq
  The bundled benchmark backend, a simulated model server
  About five minutes

The example `.env` holds development passwords. Use this stack on your own machine only; for anything others can reach, follow [Install with Docker Compose](/docs/start/docker).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/thediymaker/obleth-gateway.git
cd obleth-gateway/deploy/docker
cp .env.example .env
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
```

The example file turns on the `benchmark`, `edge` and `observability` profiles, so this starts the gateway, the dashboard, the three datastores, the benchmark backend, HAProxy, Prometheus, Grafana and Jaeger. To build from your checkout instead of pulling images, run `docker compose up -d --build`.

When `docker compose ps` shows the services healthy, check the gateway:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost/health               # ok
curl -s http://localhost:9180/api/v1/health   # ok
```

The management API takes the admin token from `.env` (`dev-admin-token` in the example). A tenant is who gets a share of capacity; a key is what a client sends.

```bash
TOKEN=dev-admin-token

TID=$(curl -s -X POST http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"my-team"}' | jq -r .id)

SECRET=$(curl -s -X POST "http://localhost:9180/api/v1/tenants/$TID/keys" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"laptop"}' |

chunks.heading: Ports
chunks.text:
| Service | URL |
| --- | --- |
| HAProxy (client entry) | `http://localhost` |
| Data plane, direct | `http://localhost:8088` |
| Management API | `http://localhost:9180` (this host only) |
| Dashboard | `http://localhost:3002` |
| Grafana | `http://localhost:3001` |

The full list is in [Endpoints and ports](/docs/reference/endpoints-and-ports).

chunks.heading: Stop the stack
chunks.text:
